About this book

Almost everyone who works with computers has learned networking twice: once as a diagram with seven layers, and once, years later and badly, at three in the morning. This book is an attempt to do it once, properly, with the packets on the page.

It is written for someone who can already deploy something and cannot yet explain why it is unreachable — who knows that 443 is HTTPS but not what a port is, who has typed ping a thousand times without knowing what it sends. It starts at “what is an address” and finishes at reading a packet capture of a failing TLS handshake.

The other twenty-four volumes in this series touch networking constantly — volume 15 configures nginx, volume 20 runs a DNS zone, volume 24 uses ssh and curl. All of them assume the network works. This is the volume that does not assume it.

The rule this book is built on

Every listing was executed before it was printed. That is easy to claim about a shell command and hard to claim about a packet capture, which is exactly why this book builds a real network to capture. Every frame, every sequence number, every retransmission and every hop count on these pages came out of a real Linux network stack moving real packets.

What this book will not do

It will not describe the author’s network. Not one listing here enumerates a real interface, a real route, a real open port or a real neighbour. That is not a redaction — it is the design. Every listing runs inside a network namespace, which the Linux kernel starts with nothing but a loopback interface, so ss in there is genuinely empty and ip addr genuinely shows only what the lab built. There is nothing to hide because inside the lab there is nothing there.

It will not print invented output. Where something could not be run — a hardware switch, a BGP session, a carrier-grade NAT — the book says so and explains the documented behaviour instead of fabricating a terminal. Every address in captured output comes from the ranges reserved for exactly this purpose: 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24 and 203.0.113.0/24 (RFC 5737), and 2001:db8::/32 (RFC 3849) — the build refuses to write a page containing anything else. The private ranges appear only in illustrations of home and office networks, because 192.168.1.1 is what you will actually see on yours, and every such illustration is labelled as not run.

How it is organised

Chapter 0 is the history, because almost every strange thing about networking is a decision someone made under a constraint that no longer exists. Chapter A builds the lab in front of you, so that when a later chapter prints a capture you know precisely what produced it. Then the layers, bottom to top — a frame, an address, a route, a connection, a name, a request — and finally two chapters on doing this under pressure.

Chapter 10 is the hinge. Once you have watched a three-way handshake happen and can name every field in it, most of the rest of networking stops being vocabulary and starts being consequences.

Every chapter ends the same way

A checkpoint of questions with real answers, and practice tasks to type. Networking punishes the gap between recognising a term and being able to use it, and only one side of that gap is any use when a service is down.

If you read one thing

Chapter 4, on masks and CIDR. It is arithmetic, it is genuinely dull, and it is the single most common thing senior engineers turn out not to know. Every firewall rule, every route, every cloud subnet and half of all “why can these two not talk” problems are that arithmetic.

About the author

CH

Cuong Hoang is a full-stack developer and the author, sole engineer and operator of cuongthai.com — 443,183 lines of code, 275 database tables, 99.97% uptime, one person.

Operating your own infrastructure means every network problem is yours, at whatever hour it happens. This book is what that taught, arranged in the order it would have been useful to learn it.

Chapter Zero · Orientation

Why Networks Look Like This

Networking is full of decisions that look arbitrary until you know what they were solving. Why is a packet about 1500 bytes? Why does a connection need three messages to start? Why do we number ports at all, and why is HTTP 80? None of it is arbitrary. Almost all of it was decided between 1961 and 1983, under constraints that have since vanished, by people who mostly expected to be replaced.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain packet switching, and what it replaced
  • Say what ARPANET actually demonstrated, and when
  • Describe the split of TCP into TCP and IP, and why it mattered
  • Explain why the OSI model is taught and the TCP/IP stack is used
  • Read a protocol number and a well-known port as historical artefacts
  • Name the constraint behind three things that still look strange

0.1 The thing that came before: circuits

Until the 1960s, “connecting two machines” meant what it meant for telephones: a circuit. You asked the network for a path, the network reserved a physical route end to end, and that route was yours until you hung up. While you held it, nobody else could use it — not the wire, not the switch capacity, nothing. If you said nothing for a minute, the network carried your silence at full cost.

For a phone call that is reasonable: two people talking use the line more or less continuously. For computers it is catastrophic. Machine traffic is bursty — a terminal sends a line, waits, receives a screen, sits idle while somebody reads. Measured over a minute, a 1960s interactive session might use under one per cent of a reserved line. The other ninety-nine per cent was paid for and thrown away.

There was a second problem, and it is the one that got the funding. A circuit has a fixed path. Break the path — a cut cable, a failed switch — and the call drops. For a military network in 1962, that is a design flaw with a specific name: the network has single points of failure, and an adversary who knows the topology knows exactly where to hit it.

The persistent myth about ARPANET and nuclear war

You will read that ARPANET was built to survive a nuclear strike. That is half true, and the half matters. Paul Baran’s work at RAND (1964) was explicitly about survivable communications under attack, and it is where the distributed, redundant-routing idea was worked out. But ARPANET itself was funded and built by ARPA’s Information Processing Techniques Office to share expensive computers between research sites — there were very few machines, they cost a fortune, and researchers wanted remote access to them. The survivability research and the resource-sharing network are two different projects that share an idea. Donald Davies at the UK’s National Physical Laboratory arrived at the same idea independently around 1965, and it is Davies who gave it the word we still use: packet.

0.2 Packet switching, and what it costs you

The alternative is to reserve nothing. Cut the data into small pieces, put a destination address on each piece, and hand each piece to the network separately. Every switch along the way looks at the address and makes its own local decision about where to send it next. No path is reserved; no state is held; a piece that arrives at a broken link is simply sent another way.

Everything good about the internet follows from that, and so does everything difficult. The network is now allowed to:

The network may…BecauseWhich is why we have
Lose a packetA queue filled up and it was droppedAcknowledgements and retransmission (ch 10–12)
Reorder packetsTwo packets took different routesSequence numbers (ch 10)
Duplicate a packetA retransmission raced the originalSequence numbers again
Delay a packet arbitrarilyIt queued behind other trafficTimeouts, and the tuning of them (ch 12)
Corrupt a packetA bit flipped on the wireChecksums at several layers
Fragment a packetA link ahead had a smaller limitMTU, MSS and path discovery (ch 14)

Table 0.1 The right-hand column is most of this book. Packet switching does not make these problems; it moves them, from the network’s hardware into the endpoints’ software. That trade — a stupid network and clever ends — is the single most consequential design decision in the subject, and it is why a company can invent a new protocol without asking anyone’s permission.

This is worth stating as a principle, because it explains the shape of everything that follows: the network promises to try, and nothing more. IP is a best-effort service. It will attempt delivery. It will not tell you whether it succeeded, it will not keep your packets in order, and it will not apologise. Every guarantee you have ever relied on — that a file arrives intact, that bytes arrive in the order they were sent — is manufactured at the two ends, on top of a network that offers none of it.

0.3 1969, and the first two letters

On 29 October 1969 a team at UCLA tried to log in to a machine at SRI, 550 km away, over the first ARPANET link. The operator typed L, then O, confirming each character by telephone. On G the SRI machine crashed. The first message ever sent over the ancestor of the internet was therefore LO — which is, as origin stories go, both accidental and hard to improve on.

By the end of 1969 there were four nodes: UCLA, SRI, UC Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. The host-to-host protocol they eventually ran was NCP, the Network Control Program. NCP worked, and it had a limitation that turned out to define everything after it: it assumed the network underneath was reliable, and it assumed there was only one network. Both assumptions were about to break.

0.4 The split that made the internet possible

By the early 1970s ARPANET was not the only packet network. There was a satellite network, and a packet radio network, and networks in other countries, each with its own conventions, its own packet sizes, and its own idea of an address. The problem stopped being “how do two computers talk” and became how do two networks talk — internetworking, which is where the word internet comes from.

In May 1974 Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication, describing a single Transmission Control Program that would run at the end hosts and let heterogeneous networks be stitched together by gateways. It was one protocol doing two jobs: moving packets across networks, and making the delivery reliable.

In 1978 that protocol was cut in half, and this is the moment the architecture of the modern internet exists. Reliability was separated from delivery:

LayerJobPromises
IPGet this packet to that address, somehowNothing. Best effort
TCPMake a reliable, ordered byte stream out of thatDelivery, order, integrity
UDPDo not make anything out of it. Just send itNothing, deliberately (ch 13)

Table 0.2 Splitting them meant you could keep IP and choose something else on top. Without the split there is no UDP, no video call that would rather drop a frame than wait for it, no QUIC, no DNS as we know it. The version number reached 4 during this work, which is why the first IP most people meet is IPv4 — versions 1 to 3 were iterations of the design, never deployed at scale.

0.5 The flag day: 1 January 1983

Migrating a live network from one protocol to another is the kind of thing that is now considered impossible. In 1983 it was done by decree. NCP was switched off and TCP/IP switched on across the whole ARPANET on 1 January 1983 — a flag day, meaning a hard cutover with no compatibility period. Hosts that had not converted simply stopped working.

It was possible because the network was about 400 hosts and every one of them had an administrator who could be telephoned. It is instructive to compare it with the transition that has not worked that way: IPv6 was specified in 1995 and, three decades later, runs alongside IPv4 rather than replacing it, because there is no longer anybody to telephone. Chapter 9 is about living with that.

Why “flag day” is now a warning

The term survives in software as a description of a change that cannot be rolled out gradually — everyone must switch at once. The 1983 cutover is the only famous one that worked, and it worked because of a property no modern system has: a complete, contactable list of every participant. When someone proposes a flag day for a system with users you cannot enumerate, 1983 is not the precedent. IPv6 is.

0.6 Meanwhile, in one building: Ethernet

Everything so far is about connecting networks. There was a separate problem: connecting the machines inside one building, where the distances are short, the wire is yours, and the economics are completely different.

In 1973 Robert Metcalfe at Xerox PARC wrote a memo describing what became Ethernet. Its central idea is almost rude in its simplicity: put every machine on one shared wire, let anyone transmit whenever the wire seems idle, and accept that two machines will sometimes transmit at once. When that happens — a collision — both stop, wait a random interval, and try again. No central coordinator, no reserved slots, no permission.

The name is a joke about the luminiferous aether, the medium nineteenth-century physicists believed light propagated through, and which turned out not to exist. Metcalfe’s cable did exist, but the point was the same: a passive medium everything is immersed in.

Modern switched Ethernet has essentially no collisions — each device gets a dedicated link to a switch, and the switch buffers. But the frame format Metcalfe designed, the 48-bit addresses, and the ~1500-byte payload limit are all still on your desk right now. Chapter 2 pulls one apart, and chapter 14 is about the consequences of that 1500.

0.7 The model that is taught, and the one that runs

Every networking course opens with the OSI seven-layer model, standardised by ISO in 1984. It is a genuinely good conceptual tool and it describes a protocol suite that lost. The suite that won — TCP/IP — has four layers, was specified largely in running code, and was already deployed before OSI was finished.

OSILayerTCP/IPWhat is actually thereChapter
7ApplicationApplicationHTTP, DNS, SSH, SMTP15, 18
6PresentationApplicationTLS sits awkwardly here16
5SessionApplicationNothing, in practice—
4TransportTransportTCP, UDP, QUIC9–13
3NetworkInternetIP, ICMP4–8
2Data linkLinkEthernet, ARP, Wi-Fi2–3
1PhysicalLinkCopper, fibre, radio—

Table 0.3 The bold rows are the ones you will spend your career in. Note what happens at the top: OSI’s layers 5, 6 and 7 collapse into one, because the split was never useful in practice — and TLS, the most important thing at that level, fits none of them cleanly. It is still worth learning the numbers, for one reason only: the industry talks in them. “An L4 load balancer” and “an L7 load balancer” are chapter 19, and the difference is exactly the difference between rows 4 and 7.

Why did the technically-blessed international standard lose to the research project? Several reasons, and the pattern is familiar: TCP/IP was already running when OSI was still being specified; it was free, with implementations in Berkeley Unix that anyone could take; it was simpler, having been trimmed by contact with reality rather than by committee; and it had a working address plan and a rough-consensus-and-running-code culture that shipped revisions in months rather than years. OSI was designed to be correct. TCP/IP was designed to be deployed, and deployment is the only correctness a network has.

0.8 The 1970s, still visible from your terminal

Three things that look strange, and the constraint behind each

Why is the maximum packet about 1500 bytes? Because the original Ethernet was a shared wire, and a long frame monopolised it — 1500 bytes was a compromise between efficiency and one machine hogging the cable. The wire is not shared any more. The number never moved. Chapter 14.

Why does a connection take three messages to open? Because both ends must agree on a starting sequence number, and each end needs to know the other received its number. Two messages cannot do that. Chapter 10.

Why does ping exist at all if it proves so little? Because in 1983 it was the diagnostic, and it was written in an evening by Mike Muuss to debug a network problem — named for sonar, which is exactly the right metaphor. Everything since is layered on top of an echo request. Chapter 7.

Checkpoint

In one sentence, what did packet switching trade away, and for what?

It gave up guarantees from the network in exchange for efficiency and resilience. A circuit promised you a path and reserved it; packet switching promises nothing, uses the capacity far better, and routes around damage. The cost is that loss, reordering, duplication and delay all become the endpoints’ problem — which is what TCP exists to solve.

Why was splitting TCP into TCP and IP in 1978 more important than TCP itself?

Because it made the transport layer replaceable. Once delivery (IP) is separate from reliability (TCP), you can put something other than TCP on top without touching the network: UDP for things that would rather lose data than wait, QUIC decades later for HTTP/3. Had they stayed one protocol, every one of those would have required changing the internet rather than changing an endpoint.

Someone says “we are an OSI layer 5 shop”. What should you conclude?

Politely, that they are speaking loosely. There is essentially nothing at layer 5 in a real TCP/IP stack — session management, where it exists, lives inside application protocols. In practice the industry uses only two of the seven numbers with any precision: L4 meaning “decides using addresses and ports” and L7 meaning “decides by reading the application data, e.g. the HTTP path”. That distinction is real and matters (chapter 19). The other five numbers are mostly vocabulary.

Why can we not simply have another flag day and finish the IPv6 migration?

Because a flag day requires a complete list of participants who can be compelled or contacted, and in 1983 ARPANET had roughly 400 hosts with named administrators. The internet now has billions of endpoints, no central authority over them, and hardware that will never receive another firmware update. Any change must therefore be incrementally deployable and backwards compatible — which is why IPv6 runs alongside IPv4 rather than replacing it, and why every successful protocol change since has been designed to work through equipment that does not understand it. QUIC runs over UDP for precisely this reason (chapter 18).

The protocol number for TCP is 6 and for UDP is 17. Why the gap?

Registration order, nothing more — the numbers between were assigned to protocols that were being worked on at the time and mostly did not survive (listing 0.1 shows several). There is no meaning in the values. What matters is that they are frozen: they appear in a field of every IP header, in firewall rules, in capture filters and in switch silicon, so the cost of changing one is unbounded and the benefit is zero.

Why does “stupid network, clever endpoints” matter to a working developer?

Because it is why you can deploy a new protocol at all. If guarantees lived in the network, adding one would mean upgrading every router between you and your users. Because they live at the ends, a browser and a server can agree on HTTP/3 and start using it while every device in between continues to see ordinary UDP packets it does not need to understand. It is also the reason your application, not the network, is responsible for retries, timeouts and idempotency — nobody else is going to do it.

Is it true that the internet was designed to survive a nuclear war?

Partly. Paul Baran’s 1964 RAND work on distributed communications was explicitly about surviving attack, and it is where the redundant-routing idea comes from. ARPANET, however, was funded to share scarce, expensive computers between research sites. The survivability idea fed into the design; it was not the project’s purpose. Both halves of the sentence get exaggerated in opposite directions, and the accurate version is more interesting than either.

If OSI lost, why is it still taught?

Because as a vocabulary it is genuinely useful and vendor-neutral, and because the industry standardised on its numbers even while ignoring its protocols. Saying “that is a layer 2 problem” communicates something precise in one phrase. The mistake is treating the seven layers as a description of software that exists: no shipping stack has a session layer, and TLS — arguably the most important protocol on the internet after TCP and IP — cannot be placed in the model without an argument.

Chapter A · Orientation

The Lab, and the Rules

A networking book has a credibility problem no other kind of technical book has. Anyone can typeset a packet capture. This chapter builds, in front of you, the network that produced every capture in this book — three machines, real Linux network stacks, no hardware, no privileges, and no contact whatsoever with the network this was written on.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Describe what a network namespace is, and why it makes this book possible
  • Read the lab topology, and recognise it in later chapters
  • Say why ss in the lab is empty, and why that is the point
  • Reproduce the whole lab yourself in about twenty lines
  • Know which listings ran in the lab and which reached the real internet
  • Recognise the documentation address ranges on sight

A.1 The problem, stated honestly

To show you a routing table, this book needs a machine with routes. To show you ARP resolving, it needs two machines on a segment. To show you a TCP handshake it needs a client, a server, and permission to capture packets between them. The obvious ways to get those are all unacceptable:

  • Use the author’s real network. Then every listing publishes a home or office network: real addresses, real MAC addresses, real hostnames, real open ports. Beyond the privacy problem, it is bad teaching — the output would be specific to one house.
  • Use a cloud VM. Better, but it still publishes a real machine, and it costs money to reproduce.
  • Type the output by hand. This is what most networking books do. It is also how errors become immortal: a plausible-looking capture with a wrong flag or an impossible sequence number gets copied for twenty years.

The fourth option is the one this book takes, and it is better than all three: build a real network that does not exist anywhere else, out of parts the Linux kernel gives away for free.

A.2 Network namespaces

Linux can give a process its own private copy of the entire network stack. That copy — a network namespace — has its own interfaces, its own IP addresses, its own routing table, its own ARP cache, its own firewall rules and its own table of open sockets. It shares nothing with the host’s network. It is not a simulation and not a virtual machine: it is the same kernel code, moving the same packets, with a separate set of data structures.

This is not an exotic feature. It is the mechanism every container uses. When you run a container and it has its own address and its own ports, this is what is happening. The lab uses it directly rather than through Docker.

A namespace begins with nothing but a loopback interface, and that fact is what makes this book publishable:

Why this needs no root

Creating a network namespace normally requires CAP_NET_ADMIN. The lab uses unshare -rn, which first creates a user namespace in which your unprivileged account is mapped to uid 0, and then creates a network namespace inside it. You are root, but only over things that namespace owns — which is a set of interfaces that did not exist a moment ago and will not exist a moment later. You cannot touch the host’s network from inside it, and neither can this book.

A.3 The topology

A.4 Building it yourself

Nothing here is hidden. The whole lab is one script, and if you have a Linux machine you can run it now. The essential twenty lines are these:

PieceWhat it gives you
unshare -rnA user namespace where you are root, plus a fresh network namespace
ip link add … type vethTwo interfaces joined back to back — a virtual cable
ip link set X netns PIDMoves one end of the cable into another namespace
nsenter -t PID -nRuns a command inside that namespace
sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forwardTurns a host into a router. It is one bit
type dummyAn interface with no peer, for when you only need an address

Table A.1 Six primitives, and every virtual network you have ever used is built from them — Docker’s bridge networking, Kubernetes pod networking, and this lab. Knowing them turns container networking from magic into arithmetic.

A.5 The rules this book follows

RuleWhyHow you can tell
Every listing is real outputA fabricated capture teaches a wrong detail foreverListings are labelled with the machine they ran on
Nothing describes the real machineIt is a published bookLab listings show only lab addresses
Only documentation addressesRFC 5737 and RFC 3849 exist for this198.51.100.x, 203.0.113.x, 192.0.2.x, 2001:db8::
Public internet only for public factsA root server’s address is not a secretLabelled terminal · Linux, not host-a · the lab
If it could not run, it is markedBetter an honest gap than an invented terminalCaptioned “shown rather than run”

Table A.2 The fourth row is the only place this book touches a real network, and only ever outbound to infrastructure that exists to be queried — a root name server in chapter 15, example.com, a public resolver. Those listings print public information about public hosts and nothing about the machine asking.

What the lab cannot show, and what this book does instead

Real latency and real loss. A veth pair is a memory copy: microseconds, and no loss ever. Where a chapter needs loss, it is induced deliberately — with an iptables rule that discards a fixed proportion of arriving segments, and the listing says so. The usual tool for this, tc netem, is not installed on the machine this book was built on, so nothing here uses it. Realistic delay the lab cannot produce at all: chapters that need a latency figure compute it from realistic numbers rather than measuring, and say which they are doing (ch 12).

Physical-layer anything. No cables, no radio, no duplex mismatch, no bad optic. Layer 1 is discussed, never demonstrated.

Hardware switches, VLANs on real gear, BGP with a real peer, carrier-grade NAT. A Linux bridge stands in for a switch and behaves the same way for everything in chapter 2; the rest are explained with their documented behaviour and marked as not run.

Checkpoint

Why is an empty ss -tuln the most important output in this chapter?

Because it is the proof of isolation. On any real machine that command lists every service listening — databases, dev servers, agents — which is both a security disclosure and useless for teaching. In the lab it returns a header and nothing else, which means the namespace genuinely has no connection to the host’s network stack. Every later listing inherits that guarantee: whatever appears in the output was put there by the listing.

What is a veth pair, in one sentence?

Two network interfaces created together and joined back to back, so that every frame written into one is received by the other — a virtual cable. Moving one end into another network namespace connects two otherwise isolated stacks, and that single primitive is what all container networking is built from.

The lab reports round-trip times in microseconds. Does that invalidate the captures?

No, and it is worth being precise about why. The timings are unrepresentative: there is no propagation delay, no queueing, no serialisation. Everything else — the frames, the addresses, the flags, the sequence numbers, the state transitions, the retransmission logic — is produced by the same kernel code that runs on a server handling real traffic. Where a chapter is about timing (chapter 12), delay is added artificially and the listing says so.

Why does the router have no default route?

Because it does not need one. A default route means “for anything I have no specific route for, send it here”. The router has directly connected interfaces on both of the only two networks that exist in the lab, so every possible destination matches a specific route. Adding a default would be meaningless: there is nowhere else. On a real router the default route points at the upstream provider, and chapter 6 walks through the decision properly.

If you ran the lab script and then closed the terminal, what would happen to the three machines?

They would cease to exist. A network namespace lives only as long as something references it — a running process, or an explicit bind mount. The two “other machines” are literally a sleep parked in a namespace; kill it and the namespace, its interfaces, its routes and its ARP cache are all freed by the kernel. This is why each listing in this book rebuilds the whole topology: it is cheaper than keeping it, and it guarantees every listing starts from an identical network.

Why use documentation address ranges rather than private ones like 192.168.1.0/24?

Because private ranges are in use. If a book prints 192.168.1.10, a reader who copies a firewall rule out of it may be pasting a rule about their own laptop. The RFC 5737 ranges — 192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24 — are reserved specifically so that documentation can use addresses guaranteed not to collide with anything real, and are not routable on the internet. Seeing them should tell you immediately that you are reading an example.

Practice · The Lab, and the Rules

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Create a network namespace with unshare -rn and run ip link inside it.Note what is there before you add anything.Easy
02In that namespace, run ss -tuln and then run it again outside. Compare.The difference is the whole chapter.Easy
03Create a veth pair and give both ends addresses in the same namespace, then ping across it.You do not need a second namespace to see a veth work.Easy
04Build the full three-machine lab from listing A.4 and ping host-b from host-a.Take it one block at a time; each block is one machine.Medium

07Explain to a colleague why docker network inspect shows a subnet.It is table A.1, used by a program instead of by you.Hard
Is this the same as what Docker does?

Yes, in mechanism. Docker creates a network namespace per container, makes a veth pair, puts one end in the container and attaches the other to a bridge (docker0), then adds NAT rules so containers can reach the outside. Every one of those pieces is in table A.1. The differences are management — image handling, lifecycle, DNS between containers — not networking. Once this chapter makes sense, docker network stops being a black box.

Could I do this on macOS or Windows?

Not natively; network namespaces are a Linux kernel feature. On macOS and Windows, run the lab inside a Linux VM — on Windows that means WSL2, which is a real Linux kernel and where everything in this book works unchanged. This is one of the places where the three systems genuinely diverge rather than merely spelling things differently, and it is why this volume, unlike volume 24, does not attempt to be cross-platform for its listings. The protocols are identical everywhere; only the tools for inspecting them differ, and the cheat sheet in chapter B gives the macOS and Windows equivalents for every command used here.

Chapter One · Part I

Layers, Seen in One Packet

Layering is normally taught as a diagram of stacked boxes, which is a picture of an idea rather than a picture of anything. This chapter does it the other way round: it captures one packet, prints every byte of it, and reads the same bytes four times — once as a frame, once as a datagram, once as a message, once as data. The layers are not boxes. They are offsets.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read a tcpdump line and say which layer each part came from
  • Point at the byte where one layer ends and the next begins
  • Explain how a receiver knows what is inside a packet, at every level
  • Calculate the overhead a layer adds, and why it matters at small sizes
  • Say what encapsulation costs and what it buys
  • Recognise the same structure in a protocol you have never seen

1.1 One packet, printed whole

Three separate protocols contributed to that one transmission, each wrapping the last:

LayerAdded byBytesWhere
LinkEthernet14Before everything, and not in the hex dump — tcpdump decodes it on the first line
InternetIPv420Hex offsets 0x00–0x13
Transport-ishICMP8Hex offsets 0x14–0x1b
Dataping8Hex offsets 0x1c–0x23 — the bytes we asked for with -s 8

Table 1.1 Eight bytes of payload cost 50 bytes on the wire. That is the price of layering, and at this size it is absurd — 42 bytes of headers to carry 8 bytes of data. It is also why chapter 13 exists: for a protocol sending tiny, frequent messages, header overhead is the design problem. Note that ICMP is in an awkward position: it rides directly on IP like a transport protocol, but it exists to serve IP itself. It is usually drawn at the network layer.

1.2 The IP header, byte by byte

OffsetBytesFieldValueMeans
0x0045Version + IHL4, 5IPv4; header is 5×4 = 20 bytes
0x0100DSCP + ECN0x00Traffic class. Zero means ordinary best-effort
0x0200 24Total length36Header and payload. 36 + 14 of Ethernet = 50 on the wire
0x04e2 54Identification57940Groups fragments of one datagram together (ch 14)
0x0640 00Flags + offset0x4000Bit 0x4000 is DF, “do not fragment” — central to ch 14
0x0840TTL64Decremented by every router. Hits zero, packet dies (ch 7)
0x0901Protocol1What follows this header. 1 = ICMP, 6 = TCP, 17 = UDP (ch 0)
0x0a04 12Header checksum0x0412Covers the header only, and is recomputed at every hop because TTL changed
0x0cc6 33 64 0aSource198.51.100.100xc6 = 198, 0x33 = 51, and so on
0x10c6 33 64 01Destination198.51.100.1Four bytes. This is all an IPv4 address is

Table 1.2 Generated from the bytes in listing 1.1, not typed. Two rows repay attention. Total length is 36 and the Ethernet frame is 50: the difference is exactly the 14-byte Ethernet header, which is how you can always check you are reading the right offsets. And protocol is the mechanism by which layering works at all — the receiver does not guess what is inside; it reads a number and dispatches.

An IPv4 address is a 32-bit number, and nothing else

Look at offsets 0x0c–0x0f: c6 33 64 0a. Those four bytes are 198.51.100.10. The dots are punctuation invented for humans; the wire has never seen one. Every mask, every subnet calculation and every “is this address in that range” question in chapters 4 and 5 is arithmetic on this single 32-bit integer, and it becomes easy the moment you stop seeing four numbers and start seeing one.

1.3 How the receiver knows what is inside

A layer boundary is not a place in memory. It is a promise about the next few bytes, made by a number in the current header. Follow that chain and you have the whole of demultiplexing:

AtThe fieldIts value hereSo next comes
EthernetEtherType0x0800IPv4 (0x86DD would be IPv6, 0x0806 ARP — ch 3)
IPv4Protocol1ICMP (6 would be TCP, 17 UDP)
ICMPType8Echo request (0 would be echo reply — ch 7)
TCPDestination port— not in this packetWhichever application bind()ed it (ch 9)

Table 1.3 Read downwards, that is the entire dispatch mechanism of the internet: each header names the format of what follows, so the receiver never has to guess and never has to understand more than one layer at a time. Read upwards, it is why a new protocol can be deployed without changing anything below it — QUIC (ch 18) was invented by choosing protocol number 17 and putting something new inside.

1.4 What layering costs, and what it buys

The cost is on the page above: 42 bytes of headers around 8 bytes of data. For a voice packet carrying 20 ms of audio, headers can genuinely exceed the payload, which is why specialised protocols exist to compress them over slow links.

The benefit is that no layer needs to know anything about the others. Consider what the packet in listing 1.1 does not contain:

  • The Ethernet header does not know it is carrying IP. It carries a number that happens to mean IP.
  • The IP header does not know or care that the link is Ethernet. Put the identical datagram on Wi-Fi, a VPN tunnel or a satellite link and not one byte of it changes.
  • ICMP does not know the addresses. It is handed a payload and a destination by the layer below.
  • Nothing anywhere knows there is a router in the path. The router will rewrite the Ethernet header completely and change exactly one byte of the IP header — the TTL — and the ends will never know.

That independence is why the internet survived the replacement of every physical technology it originally ran on. The IP header in listing 1.1 has the same layout as one from 1983. Everything underneath it has been replaced several times.

Checkpoint

Where exactly does the IP header end?

At the offset given by IHL, the low four bits of byte 0. It is a count of 32-bit words, so the header length is IHL×4. Almost always that is 5×4 = 20 bytes, but IP options can make it longer, which is why the field exists. Assuming 20 is the single most common bug in hand-written packet parsers — the correct move is always to read IHL. The same pattern appears in TCP with its data-offset field (ch 10).

A router changes the TTL. Why must it also recompute the header checksum?

Because the IPv4 checksum covers the header, and the TTL is in the header. Change one byte and the old checksum is wrong, so every router must recompute it at every hop — a real per-packet cost that was one of the arguments for removing the header checksum entirely in IPv6 (ch 9), on the grounds that the link layer and the transport layer both check integrity anyway.

Why does the IPv4 header contain a checksum over itself but not over the data?

Division of responsibility. A corrupted header could send the packet to the wrong host entirely, which no higher layer could detect, so IP protects its own header. Corrupted data is the transport layer’s problem, and TCP and UDP carry their own checksums covering the payload. Checking it twice would cost every router time for no gain — the end-to-end principle from chapter 0, applied to a single field.

You capture a frame whose EtherType is 0x0806. What can you say about the next byte?

That it is the start of an ARP message, not an IP header — so reading it as a version-and-IHL byte would be nonsense. This is the point of table 1.3: the meaning of a byte is never intrinsic, it is declared by the header before it. Chapter 3 decodes an ARP frame in full.

Someone proposes saving bandwidth by removing the IP header when both hosts are on the same LAN. What breaks?

Everything above it, immediately. Without the IP header there are no IP addresses, so the receiving kernel cannot decide which local address the packet was for, cannot dispatch on the protocol number, and cannot hand it to a socket. The layers above are written against IP, not against the wire. You would also have built something that can never leave the LAN, which is the same mistake that made NCP a dead end in chapter 0 — and, incidentally, the same overhead argument that keeps being made and keeps being wrong, because the ability to route is worth twenty bytes.

The same eight bytes of payload were carried by a frame of a much larger size. Where would you look first if that overhead mattered?

At whether you are sending the right number of packets, not at the headers — the headers are fixed and you cannot remove them. The real lever is batching: one packet with 800 bytes of payload costs the same headers as one with 8. That is why chatty protocols perform badly over long links and why Nagle’s algorithm exists (ch 12), and why a metrics agent that sends one packet per measurement is a problem worth finding.

Is ICMP a transport-layer protocol?

It is usually drawn at the network layer, and that is the better answer, but it genuinely does not fit cleanly. It rides directly on IP with its own protocol number (1), like TCP and UDP do, so structurally it looks like a transport protocol. But it carries no port numbers, is not used by applications to move data, and exists to report on IP’s own behaviour — it is IP’s error and diagnostic channel. The honest description is that ICMP is a companion to IP rather than a layer above it, and the model is the thing at fault, not ICMP.

Why is the annotation table in this chapter generated rather than written?

Because the kernel picks a new identification value for every packet, so the numbers in listing 1.1 change on every build. A hand-written table would agree with the listing on the day it was typed and quietly disagree afterwards — and a reader checking the book against the output would find the book wrong. Generating the table from the same captured bytes makes that class of error structurally impossible, which is a better guarantee than proofreading.

Chapter Two · Part I

Ethernet, Frames and MAC Addresses

Below IP there is a layer that has no idea the internet exists. It moves bytes between devices that share a wire, it addresses them by a number burned into the hardware, and it will not carry anything more than about 1500 bytes at a time. Almost every confusing thing about local networks — why a switch is not a router, why a broadcast storm is possible, why your VM has a strange MAC — lives here.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read a MAC address and extract the two flag bits from it
  • Explain what a switch learns, and when it floods instead
  • Distinguish unicast, broadcast and multicast at the link layer
  • Say why a switch cannot connect two different IP networks
  • Recognise a locally-administered address and know what made it
  • Name the field that limits a frame to 1500 bytes of payload

2.1 The frame

An Ethernet frame is almost insultingly simple. Six bytes of destination address, six of source, two bytes saying what is inside, then the payload, then a four-byte checksum the hardware computes and strips. There is no version number, no length field for the whole frame, no options, and no addresses that mean anything outside the local segment.

FieldBytesWhat it is
Destination MAC6Who should receive this frame
Source MAC6Who sent it
EtherType20x0800 IPv4, 0x86DD IPv6, 0x0806 ARP, 0x8100 VLAN tag
Payload46–1500The thing being carried. 1500 is the MTU (ch 14)
FCS4A checksum. Computed and checked by hardware; you will never see it

Table 2.1 14 bytes of header, and that is the whole of it. Two details repay attention. The payload has a minimum of 46 bytes — a leftover from collision detection on the original shared cable, which needed frames long enough to still be transmitting when a collision came back; short frames are padded, which is why a tiny packet still occupies 64 bytes on the wire. And the 1500 in the maximum is the single most consequential number in practical networking, because everything above must fit inside it or be split.

2.2 What a MAC address actually contains

Forty-eight bits, written as six hex bytes. They are conventionally split in half: the first three bytes are an OUI (Organisationally Unique Identifier), bought from the IEEE by the manufacturer, and the last three are assigned by that manufacturer to individual devices. That is how a MAC address can be globally unique without any central registry of devices.

Two bits in the first byte are flags, and they are the part almost nobody knows:

BitNameSet meansClear means
Least significant bit of byte 0I/GGroup — broadcast or multicastIndividual — one device
Second-least significant bit of byte 0U/LLocally administered — made upUniversal — from an IEEE OUI

Table 2.2 This is why virtual machines, containers and this book’s lab so often have addresses starting 02:, 06:, 0a: or 0e:. Those are exactly the byte values with the U/L bit set and the I/G bit clear — “I invented this address, and it belongs to one device.” Software that needs a MAC and has no hardware sets that bit, which is the polite way of promising not to collide with a real manufacturer.

The MAC address is not as fixed as people think

“Burned into the card” is the traditional description and it has been inaccurate for twenty years. The hardware has a default address in ROM, and the driver will happily use a different one: ip link set dev eth0 address 02:11:22:33:44:55 changes it until reboot. Phones now randomise their MAC per Wi-Fi network by default, precisely because a stable hardware identifier that is broadcast constantly is a tracking mechanism. Treat a MAC as a current identity on a segment, never as proof of which machine you are talking to — chapter 3 shows how cheaply it can be claimed.

2.3 One frame, three kinds of destination

KindDestination looks likeWho receives itExample
UnicastI/G bit clearOne interfaceEvery normal packet
Broadcastff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ffEveryone on the segmentARP requests (ch 3), DHCP discovery
MulticastI/G set, not all onesEveryone who subscribedIPv6 neighbour discovery, mDNS, routing protocols

Table 2.3 Broadcast is the expensive one and the reason segments are kept small. A broadcast frame is delivered to every device on the segment and every one of them must interrupt its CPU to look at it, even if it is of no interest. A network with thousands of machines on one segment spends real capacity on traffic nobody wanted — which is what “a broadcast domain” means, and why networks are split into several (ch 5).

2.4 What a switch does, watched from empty

A switch has no addresses of its own on the data path and does not participate in IP at all. It does one thing: it remembers which port each source MAC address arrived on, and uses that table to forward frames out of one port instead of all of them.

The rules are short enough to state completely:

  1. A frame arrives on a port. Record its source MAC as reachable via that port.
  2. Look up the destination MAC. If it is known, send the frame out only that port.
  3. If it is not known, or it is broadcast/multicast, send it out every port except the one it came from. This is called flooding.
  4. Forget entries that have not been seen for a while, typically five minutes.

That is a complete description of an unmanaged switch. Here it is happening:

Why the first frame to a machine is always flooded

Follow the rules above for a switch that has just been powered on. The first frame has an unknown destination, so it is flooded to every port. The reply teaches the switch where the original sender is. From then on traffic in that direction is targeted. This is why a completely idle machine can be temporarily unreachable after a table entry ages out, why a switch under a MAC-flooding attack degrades into a hub — fill the table and everything must be flooded — and why moving a server to a different port works instantly: the first frame it sends re-teaches the switch.

2.5 Why a switch cannot do a router’s job

The two devices are often in one box, which makes them easy to confuse. They operate on different fields and answer different questions.

SwitchRouter
ReadsDestination MACDestination IP
Table built byListening — automaticConfiguration or a routing protocol
Scope of its addressesThis segment onlyThe whole internet
Changes the frame?No. Forwards it unchangedYes. New link header every hop
Changes the packet?NoDecrements TTL, recomputes header checksum
Can join two IP networks?NoYes. That is the definition
Fails byFlooding — wasteful but worksDropping — no route, no delivery

Table 2.4 The decisive row is the fourth. A switch is transparent: the frame that leaves is the frame that arrived. A router rebuilds the link layer at every hop, which is exactly what listing 1.3 showed — same IP addresses at both ends, completely different MAC addresses. Everything else follows from that.

Checkpoint

You see a device with MAC 0a:1b:2c:3d:4e:5f. What can you say immediately?

That it is almost certainly virtual. 0a is 00001010: the least significant bit is 0 (individual, so a normal device) and the second bit is 1 (locally administered) — meaning the address was invented by software rather than allocated to a manufacturer. Hypervisors, containers, bridges and Wi-Fi randomisation all produce these. You will not find an OUI lookup for it, because there is nothing to look up.

A switch receives a frame for a MAC it has never seen. What does it do?

Floods it — sends it out every port except the one it arrived on. This is correct behaviour, not a failure: it is the only way to reach a destination whose location is unknown, and the reply will teach the switch where that destination is. The cost is that for one frame, the switch behaved like a hub. An attacker who deliberately fills the forwarding table with fake addresses forces this state permanently, which is how MAC flooding turns a switched network back into a shared one.

Why is a broadcast frame more expensive than a unicast one, beyond the extra copies?

Because of what it does at the receivers. A switch can decline to forward a unicast frame to ports that do not need it, and a network card can filter unicast frames not addressed to it in hardware without waking the CPU. A broadcast must be delivered to every device on the segment and passed up to every operating system to be examined and usually discarded. The cost is paid by every machine, not just the sender — which is why the size of a broadcast domain is a design decision rather than an accident.

Can two machines with the same IP but different MACs coexist on one switch?

The switch will not object at all — it never reads IP addresses, so as far as it is concerned these are two ordinary devices. IP is where it breaks: ARP requests for that address will get two different answers, and which one a given host caches is a race. The symptom is the classic intermittent, direction-dependent failure that seems to follow no pattern, and the diagnosis is ip neigh showing an address whose MAC keeps changing (ch 3).

Why does a frame have a minimum payload size of 46 bytes?

Collision detection on the original shared cable. A sender had to still be transmitting when a collision from the far end of the maximum-length segment propagated back, or it would never notice the collision had happened. That set a minimum frame time, and therefore a minimum frame size of 64 bytes including headers. Modern switched Ethernet has no collisions and does not need this at all, but the frame format cannot change, so short frames are simply padded. It is a fossil of a problem that no longer exists — exactly the pattern from chapter 0.

Your laptop and a server are on the same switch but cannot reach each other, and both have correct addresses. What class of problem is this?

Most likely not a switch problem at all. If both are genuinely on the same segment, the switch will flood the first frame and learn from the reply; there is very little for it to get wrong. Look at IP: are the two addresses actually in the same subnet according to their masks (ch 4)? A pair like 192.0.2.10/24 and 192.0.2.200/25 looks adjacent and is not — one of them will send to the gateway instead of directly, and the return path may not exist. That specific misconfiguration is common enough to check first.
