Are MAC addresses really globally unique?

In principle, for hardware from a manufacturer that follows the rules: the IEEE sells each vendor an OUI and the vendor is responsible for not repeating the remaining 24 bits. In practice duplicates do occur — from cheap unbranded hardware, from cloned firmware, and from cloned VM images, which is a common and confusing cause of a duplicate MAC appearing on one segment. It matters less than it sounds: the addresses only need to be unique within a single broadcast domain, because they are never seen outside one.

If a switch does not read IP, how does a “layer 3 switch” exist?

It is a router with a switch’s pricing and port count. The marketing name describes hardware that does normal layer-2 switching at wire speed and can also make routing decisions between VLANs in silicon rather than in software. Nothing about the two functions has merged — the box simply contains both, and which one handles a given frame depends on whether the destination is in the same VLAN. The distinction in table 2.4 still holds for every individual frame.

Chapter Three · Part I

ARP, or How an IP Address Finds a MAC

Chapter 2 addressed neighbours by a 48-bit MAC; chapter 1 addressed a packet by a 32-bit IP. Nothing yet connects the two. A host that wants to send to 198.51.100.1 holds an IP and must put a frame on the wire, and a frame needs a destination MAC it does not know. ARP is the short conversation that fills that gap — a broadcast question, a unicast answer, a small cache of the results — and it is held together entirely by trust, which is the other half of this chapter.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read an ARP request and its reply off the wire and name every field
  • Explain why the question is a broadcast and the answer a unicast
  • Interpret the neighbour-cache states and say what each makes the kernel do
  • Prove that a host off-segment is reached by ARPing the gateway, not the destination
  • Describe how a gratuitous ARP rewrites a cache nobody asked to update
  • Say why ARP has no authentication, and what spoofing does with that

3.1 The question and the answer, on the wire

The whole of ARP is two frames. A host wants the MAC behind an IP it can see on its own segment, so it shouts the question to everyone and the one machine that owns that IP answers privately. Watch it happen: flush the cache so there is nothing to reuse, start a capture, and send one ping.

The hex is not decoration. An ARP message is 28 bytes with a rigid layout, and every value in listing 3.1 sits at a fixed offset. Here is the request, decoded from exactly the bytes above:

OffsetBytesFieldValueMeans
0x00ff ff ff ff ff ffEthernet dstff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ffBroadcast: goes to everyone on the segment
0x0602 00 00 00 0a 0aEthernet src02:00:00:00:0a:0aThe asker
0x0c08 06EtherType0x0806ARP. No IP header follows; the ARP message starts here
0x0e00 01HW type11 = Ethernet
0x1008 00Protocol type0x08000x0800, the same value that means IPv4 in an EtherType
0x1206HW len6A MAC is 6 bytes
0x1304Proto len4An IPv4 address is 4 bytes
0x1400 01Opcode11 = request; the reply carries 2
0x1602 00 00 00 0a 0aSender MAC02:00:00:00:0a:0aThe asker’s own MAC, so the reply comes straight back
0x1cc6 33 64 0aSender IP198.51.100.10The asker’s own IP
0x2000 00 00 00 00 00Target MAC00:00:00:00:00:00All zeroes: the blank we are asking to fill
0x26c6 33 64 01Target IP198.51.100.1The IP we want a MAC for

Table 3.1 Generated from the request bytes in listing 3.1, not typed. The field worth staring at is target MAC at 0x20: 00 00 00 00 00 00, six zero bytes. That hole is the whole point of the message — the sender holds the target IP and its own two addresses, and asks the segment to fill in the one value it lacks. The hardware and protocol type fields exist because ARP was never tied to Ethernet and IP; it is a general “resolve an address of one family to another” mechanism, and IPv4-over-Ethernet is merely the only pairing almost anyone uses.

3.2 Why broadcast the question and unicast the answer

The asymmetry in listing 3.1 is the tightest design under one constraint. A host that needs a MAC has no idea which machine owns the target IP — that is exactly what it is trying to learn — so it cannot address the question to anyone in particular. The only envelope that reaches a machine whose address you do not yet know is the one addressed to all of them. The question must be a broadcast.

The answer is the opposite case. By the time a host replies, it knows precisely who asked, because the request carried the asker’s MAC and IP in its sender fields. Broadcasting the reply would make every other machine take an interrupt over a frame between two parties, so the reply is a unicast — and the request conveniently supplied everything needed to send it. Look back at the two frames in listing 3.1 and the roles have simply swapped: the responder’s own MAC, the answer the asker wanted, now sits in the sender fields, while the target fields carry the asker’s details so the unicast lands. The target MAC that was six zero bytes in the request is filled in, because by now both parties are known.

There is no request-and-reply binding, and that will matter later

Nothing in the reply proves it answers your request. There is no transaction id, no nonce, no field tying frame two to frame one — the receiver believes any well-formed reply for an IP it cares about, including one it never asked for. That makes the cache in the next section cheap to keep and, in section 3.5, trivial to poison. Hold the thought: ARP has no memory of having asked.

3.3 The neighbour cache and its states

Broadcasting a question for every packet would flood the segment, so the answer is remembered in a table the kernel calls the neighbour cache (ip neigh). Each entry has a state recording how much the kernel currently trusts it, and those states are a small machine worth knowing — “why is this host briefly unreachable” is usually an answer written in them. The natural lifetime is minutes, awkward to watch, so this listing shrinks the timers to seconds and says so; everything else is the real mechanism.

StateMeansWhat the kernel does with a packet for it
INCOMPLETEA first resolution is in flightQueues the packet; broadcasts requests and waits
REACHABLEConfirmed within the reachable timeSends immediately to the cached MAC
STALEKnown, but not confirmed latelySends anyway, and schedules a check
DELAYA stale entry was just usedSends, then waits briefly for upper-layer proof before probing
PROBEActively re-checkingSends unicast requests to the known MAC
FAILEDNo answer ever cameDrops the packet — the target is silent or absent

Table 3.2 The Linux neighbour states. The one that catches people is DELAY: rather than probe the instant an entry goes stale, the kernel sends the packet and waits a moment for the transport layer to confirm the neighbour — a returning TCP ACK is proof it is alive, so no ARP probe is needed at all. Only if nothing confirms it does the entry move to PROBE and the unicast questions begin. An entry that never answers reaches FAILED: the wire is fine, but nobody is home.

3.4 The key insight: you ARP for the gateway, not the destination

Here is the point on which more confused debugging hangs than any other in this chapter. ARP is a link-layer mechanism: it resolves addresses only on the same segment, because the question is a broadcast and broadcasts do not cross routers. So what happens when host-a, on 198.51.100.0/24, pings host-b on 203.0.113.0/24?

It does not, and cannot, ARP for host-b. It consults its routing table, finds host-b reachable only via the gateway, and ARPs for the gateway instead. The proof is one capture:

Destination on my segmentDestination off my segment
Example here198.51.100.1203.0.113.20
Routing saysDirectly connectedvia 198.51.100.1
ARP asks forThat IPThe gateway’s IP
Frame destination MACThe host’s own MACThe gateway’s MAC
Packet destination IPThe hostStill the far host, unchanged
Ends up in the cacheThat hostOnly the gateway

Table 3.3 The right-hand column is why a machine reaches the entire internet with a cache holding one entry: its gateway. It also splits a family of symptoms in two. If nothing off-segment works but the gateway pings fine, ARP is fine and the fault is routing. If host-a cannot even resolve the gateway — an INCOMPLETE or FAILED entry for 198.51.100.1 — the problem is the local wire. The cache tells you which half of the world to suspect.

3.5 A protocol that believes anything it is told

Return to the note in section 3.2: a host accepts any well-formed reply, even one it never requested. An unrequested reply has a name — a gratuitous ARP — and a legitimate purpose: when a machine changes its MAC, or a standby fails over and takes on a shared IP, it broadcasts one so every cache updates at once instead of waiting to go stale. Here is host-a changing its MAC and announcing it, watched from the router:

The spoof is the same frame, sent by the wrong machine

ARP has no authentication: no signature, no secret, no check that the sender owns the IP it claims. A gratuitous reply saying “the gateway is at my MAC” is indistinguishable from a legitimate one. Below, a third machine on a shared segment does exactly that — and its attack tool is a dozen lines: build one Ethernet frame, build one ARP reply, send it in a loop.

3.6 Proxy ARP, in one listing

One deliberate use of ARP’s willingness to answer is worth naming, because you will meet it and it looks like a fault. In proxy ARP, a router answers requests for addresses that are not its own — on behalf of a machine reachable through it — handing out its own MAC. A host ARPs for a destination it believes is local, the router quietly says “that’s me”, and forwards what arrives.

Checkpoint

Why is an ARP request sent to the broadcast address but its reply sent as a unicast?

Because of what each side knows at the time. The requester is trying to find the MAC behind an IP, so it cannot address the question to that machine — the broadcast is the only envelope that reaches a host whose MAC you do not yet have. The responder is in the opposite situation: the request carried the asker’s MAC and IP, so it knows exactly who to answer and unicasts back, sparing every other machine an interrupt. The asymmetry is not a quirk; it is the minimum broadcasting the problem requires.

You ping a host three subnets away and capture a single ARP request on your segment. For which IP?

For your gateway, not the distant host. ARP’s broadcast cannot cross a router, so a host resolves only addresses on its own segment. Your routing table says the distant host is reachable via the gateway, so the kernel resolves the gateway’s MAC and sends the frame there, leaving the packet’s destination IP set to the distant host. This is why a machine reaches the whole internet with one neighbour-cache entry, and why “can you ARP the gateway?” is the first question when nothing off-segment works.

An entry in ip neigh reads STALE. Is that a problem?

No — STALE is a normal resting state, not a failure. The entry is still cached and usable; it just has not been confirmed within the reachable time, so the kernel sends to it and then arranges to re-check. On the next use it enters DELAY, waits briefly for an upper layer (a returning TCP ACK, say) to prove the neighbour alive, and sends a unicast probe only if nothing does. A STALE entry that keeps working costs no extra packet. The state to worry about is FAILED: probing got no answer at all.

What is a gratuitous ARP, and why would a well-behaved machine send one?

It is an ARP reply nobody requested — a host announcing its own IP-to-MAC mapping to the segment unprompted. The legitimate reasons are all about updating other caches quickly: a server has changed its MAC, an interface has come up, or a high-availability pair has failed over and the standby, now holding the shared service IP, needs every peer to send to the new hardware at once rather than waiting for entries to go stale. It also detects duplicate addresses — if anyone answers your announcement, someone else already holds that IP.

Why can ARP not tell a legitimate gratuitous reply from an attacker’s?

Because it authenticates nothing. An ARP reply has no signature, no shared secret, and no field asserting the sender owns the IP it claims — and no link to any earlier request, so an unsolicited reply is accepted on the same terms as a solicited one. A failover host announcing “the service IP is now at my MAC” and an attacker announcing “the gateway is at my MAC” put identical bytes on the wire. The design assumed a trusted local segment — reasonable for a 1980s LAN, and the root of ARP spoofing today. Every defence adds trust from outside the protocol: static entries, or a switch that polices replies.

You see two hosts on one segment answering ARP requests for the same IP with different MACs. What are the two innocent explanations before you reach for “attack”?

First, a genuine duplicate IP: two machines were misconfigured with the same address, both answer, and whichever reply a host cached last is the one it uses — the intermittent, direction-dependent failure from chapter 2. Second, proxy ARP: a router answering on behalf of a host replies for that host’s IP with its own MAC, so the address is legitimately answered by two pieces of hardware. Only after ruling those out is deliberate spoofing the explanation — and the wire looks the same in all three cases, which is exactly the problem with a protocol that carries no intent.

Go deeper — the primary sources
  • RFC 826 — Address Resolution ProtocolIETF
  • arp(7): the Linux neighbour cacheman7.org
  • RFC 5227 — IPv4 Address Conflict DetectionIETF

Practice · ARP, or How an IP Address Finds a MAC

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Flush your neighbour cache and capture the ARP exchange when you ping your gateway.ip neigh flush all, then tcpdump -e -n arp and one ping.Easy
02In that capture, confirm the request went to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff and the reply did not.The reply’s destination is your own MAC.Easy
03Run ip neigh and identify the state of every entry.Map each against table 3.2.Easy
04Ping a host on a different subnet and watch which IP your machine ARPs for.It will be the gateway, not the host. Predict it before you look.Easy
05Leave an entry untouched and watch it go from REACHABLE to STALE, then use it and watch the probe.The re-check is a unicast request, not a broadcast.Medium
06Add a static neighbour entry with ip neigh add ... nud permanent and explain what it defends against.A permanent entry ignores ARP replies entirely.Medium
07Read arp[6:2] in a tcpdump filter and explain why it selects requests.It is the opcode, two bytes into the ARP message.Medium
08Explain why ARP spoofing needs the attacker on the same segment as the victim, using table 3.2.ARP broadcasts do not cross routers.Hard
Why does a host on the far side of a router never appear in your neighbour cache?

Because you never resolve it, and you never resolve it because you cannot. ARP broadcasts its question, and a broadcast is confined to the local segment — routers do not forward it. When your routing table says a destination is reachable via a gateway, the kernel resolves the gateway’s MAC and addresses the frame there, leaving the packet’s destination IP set to the far host. The router then strips the link header and builds a fresh frame on the next segment, where it, not you, does the ARP for the next hop.

So the neighbour cache stays small and local however much of the internet you talk to: it holds only machines on segments you are directly attached to, usually a gateway or two plus a few local peers. That makes it the most useful fact for triage. An INCOMPLETE entry for your gateway means the local wire is broken and nothing off-segment can work; a healthy gateway entry with failures beyond it means ARP is fine and the fault is routing. The cache draws the line between “my problem” and “the network’s problem”.

If ARP has no authentication, why has it not been fixed?

Because the fix costs more than the disease for most networks, and cheaper mitigations exist where it matters. ARP was designed for a segment of mutually trusting machines, and on a home or small-office LAN that roughly holds — an attacker already on your segment has easier targets than cache poisoning. Cryptographic authentication would impose a key-distribution problem on every LAN, for a protocol whose whole appeal is that it needs zero configuration and works the instant a cable is plugged in.

Instead, trust is added from outside the protocol where the stakes are high. Enterprise switches offer dynamic ARP inspection: they record the IP-to-MAC bindings handed out by DHCP and drop any reply that contradicts them, so a forged “the gateway is at my MAC” never reaches the victim. Hosts can pin critical entries as permanent. And IPv6 dropped ARP entirely for Neighbour Discovery, securable with SEND — though almost nobody deploys that either, for the same reason: the segment is usually trusted, and when it is not, the switch is the better place to enforce it.

Chapter Four · Part II

IP Addresses, Masks and CIDR

The front matter promises that if you read one chapter it should be this one, and the reason is unglamorous: a great deal of “why can these two machines not talk to each other” is a mask, computed wrongly by somebody who was never taught how. An address is one 32-bit integer, a mask is a boundary drawn through it, and the rest is AND, OR and a comparison.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Convert an IPv4 address to its 32-bit integer and back again
  • Compute a network address, a broadcast address and a host range with AND and OR
  • Say exactly what changes when a prefix goes from /24 to /25, /30 or /32
  • State the one question a host asks its mask, and when it asks it
  • Diagnose a mask mismatch from the symptom, before you open a capture
  • Recognise the reserved ranges on sight and say what each one is for

4.1 An address is one integer

Chapter 1 found the destination address at offset 0x10 of the IP header, as four plain bytes. That is the whole truth of it: an IPv4 address is a 32-bit unsigned integer, and the dotted quad is a display convention invented so people could read and dictate these numbers without mistakes. No dot has ever crossed a wire.

The notation is base 256, most significant digit first. It survives from an era when the space was carved on byte boundaries: the leading bits of the first octet chose a “class”, and the class chose how many bytes were network. CIDR replaced that in 1993 and lets the boundary fall anywhere; only the notation stayed.

OctetValuePlace valueContributes
198198224 = 16,777,2163,321,888,768
5151216 = 65,5363,342,336
10010028 = 25625,600
101020 = 110
total3,325,256,714

Table 4.1 The dots separate the digits of a base-256 number, and this is the multiplication they stand for — generated from the same four bytes the listing used. The whole space is 232 = 4,294,967,296 addresses, fewer than there are people, which is why chapter 8 exists. And because the number is ordinary, comparing and range-testing addresses are ordinary integer operations.

An address parser is an attack surface

The listing shows one host answering to 198.51.100.1, 3325256705, 0306.063.0144.01 and 198.51.25601. That is inet_aton() as documented: one, two, three or four parts, and a leading 0 means octal. Now put a check that matches host strings against a forbidden range in front of a library that resolves with inet_aton(). The two disagree about what the string means and the request goes somewhere it should not. Never compare address strings; parse to the integer first.

4.2 The mask is a boundary, not a filter

A mask is a second 32-bit integer whose bits are all ones and then all zeros, the change happening exactly once. The ones cover the part of the address that identifies the network, the zeros the part that identifies a host inside it. Because the ones are contiguous and leading, the only information a mask carries is how many there are — so it becomes one number after a slash, and /24 and 255.255.255.0 are two spellings of one thing.

Address AND mask gives the network address; network OR NOT mask gives the broadcast address. Here is a fifteen-line ipcalc that does nothing else, run four times:

PrefixMaskAddressesUsableWhat it is used for
/8255.0.0.016,777,21616,777,214An old class A block
/16255.255.0.065,53665,534192.168.0.0/16 is this size
/24255.255.255.0256254The default assumption almost everywhere
/25255.255.255.128128126A /24 cut in half — section 4.4
/28255.255.255.2401614A small DMZ, or a bank of load-balancer addresses
/30255.255.255.25242A point-to-point link between routers
/31255.255.255.25422The same, wasting nothing (RFC 3021)
/32255.255.255.25511One host: loopbacks, host routes, firewall rules

Table 4.2 Generated, not typed. Each step of one in the prefix halves the block, which is why there is no such thing as a network of 100 addresses. Two rows break the “minus two” rule: a /31 has two usable addresses, because a link with exactly two ends needs neither a network nor a broadcast address (RFC 3021), and a /32 has room for neither.

Why the ones have to be contiguous

Nothing in the AND requires it — 255.0.255.0 is perfectly computable, and some very old systems allowed it. It is forbidden now because routing (ch 6) works by longest-prefix match, which ranks routes by how many leading bits they pin down — and that ranking is only meaningful if a mask is a count of leading bits. Accept contiguity and a route becomes a pair of integers and a lookup becomes a trie walk. CIDR is that decision.

4.3 The one question a mask answers

A mask does not filter anything. It does not decide who may talk to you, it drops nothing, and it is not consulted when a packet arrives. It is used at one moment only: when this host has a packet to send and must decide how to send it.

Is the destination address, masked, equal to my own address, masked?

If yes, resolve the destination’s MAC address with ARP (ch 3) and put the frame on the wire. If no, send the frame to the router’s MAC address instead, leaving the destination IP address untouched. Watch that decision change when the mask is the only thing that changes:

What the mask doesWhat people believe it does
Decides direct-or-via-the-router when sendingDecides who may reach this host
Is consulted by the sender, onceIs checked on every arriving packet
Says which addresses ARP is attempted forSays which addresses will be answered
Belongs to an interfaceBelongs to the network, agreed by all
Has no effect on the packetIs carried in the packet somewhere

Table 4.3 The right-hand column is where mask bugs come from, and the fourth row is the dangerous one: a mask is configured per interface, and no protocol checks whether the machines on a segment agree. Two hosts on one cable may disagree about the size of the network they share, and nothing will complain. The last row is why no capture can show you a mask.

4.4 Two hosts that look adjacent and cannot talk

This is the failure the chapter exists for. Two machines on the same switch, addresses differing by one octet, every cable good, the switch forwarding perfectly. They cannot exchange a single packet, and every tool that reports on the link layer says the link layer is fine.

Chapter A’s lab is the wrong shape for this, so the listing builds a Linux bridge — a real switch, as chapter 2 showed — with two fresh machines on it: 198.51.100.10/24 and 198.51.100.200/25. Host-a’s own address goes first, so those two are the only addresses here.

Why not even ARP worked, and what that hides

ARP is a link-layer protocol with no business caring about masks, so the reasonable prediction is that the MAC address resolves fine and only IP fails. The last line of the listing says otherwise: net.ipv4.conf.pc2.rp_filter = 2, Linux’s reverse-path filter in loose mode. An ARP request whose sender is an address this machine could not route a reply back to is discarded as a “martian” and never answered. Values are 0 off, 1 strict, 2 loose, and distributions disagree about the default — which is why one misconfiguration looks different on different systems.

4.5 Where the packets actually went

“100% packet loss” says nothing about which direction failed, and the instinct it produces — check the cable, the switch, the firewall — is wrong here. The packets arrived, and were received, parsed and understood. The receiver had no way to answer, because in its opinion the sender lives beyond a router that does not exist.

SymptomWhat it points at
Traffic works one way and not the otherA mask or route problem on the silent side
ARP resolves, echo requests arrive, no replies leaveThe receiver has no route back — this chapter
ARP never resolves, and both hosts are on one switchMasks disagree and reverse-path filtering is on
Error: Nexthop has invalid gatewayThe gateway is outside the interface’s prefix
Some hosts on the subnet reachable, others notYour prefix is narrower than everyone else’s
It broke when the subnet “was made bigger”Someone widened the prefix on some hosts and not others

Table 4.4 A mask fault has a signature, and it is asymmetry. Because the mask is consulted only when sending, a host with a wrong mask stays perfectly reachable by anything that could already reach it — it is its own replies that go missing. Which is why the first move is not a capture but printing the prefix on both machines and doing the AND.

The two-minute version, for when something is down

Run ip -br addr on both machines and write down the two address/prefix pairs. Mask each address with each prefix. If the network addresses differ, or the prefixes differ at all, stop — you have found it. If they agree, ask each machine ip route get <the other> and look for via where you expected dev, or the reverse. Faster than a capture that will only show you listing 4.5 again.

4.6 The addresses that are not ordinary

Some ranges of the space are reserved, and every one of them is a prefix — so recognising them is the same AND against a fixed constant. There is no separate mechanism, no flag, nothing in the packet. An address is special because of its leading bits and for no other reason.

RangeNameWhat it is for
0.0.0.0/8This networkUnspecified: a socket bound to every address (ch 9)
10.0.0.0/8Private (RFC 1918)16,777,216 addresses. The cloud and data-centre default
172.16.0.0/12Private (RFC 1918)Note the /12: 172.16 to 172.31 only
192.168.0.0/16Private (RFC 1918)65,536 addresses. Home routers, almost universally
100.64.0.0/10Shared space (RFC 6598)Carrier NAT, so an ISP can number customers safely
127.0.0.0/8LoopbackNever leaves the host. All 16.7 million of them
169.254.0.0/16Link-local (RFC 3927)Self-assigned when DHCP fails. Must never be routed
192.0.2.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24Documentation (RFC 5737)Reserved so books cannot name a real host
224.0.0.0/4Multicast224.0.0.1 is every host on this link
240.0.0.0/4ReservedThe old class E. Never allocated, now unusable
255.255.255.255/32Limited broadcastEveryone on this link. Used by DHCP before a lease

Table 4.5 The three RFC 1918 ranges are the reason chapter 8 exists: they are not globally routable, so a host using one cannot be reached from the internet without NAT. And 169.254 is worth knowing as a symptom — a machine that gave itself a link-local address asked for a DHCP lease and got no answer.

Checkpoint

Are 198.51.100.10/24 and 198.51.100.10/25 the same host?

Same 32-bit address, two configurations that behave differently. At /24 the host will ARP for anything from .1 to .254; at /25 only for .1 to .126, sending the rest to its gateway. Note the trap listing 4.2 shows: masking 198.51.100.10 gives 198.51.100.0 at both prefixes. Identical network address, and still not the same network — a network is a pair, a base and a length, and dropping the length loses half the information.

Why can a mask never appear in a packet capture?

Because masks are not transmitted. Nothing in the IPv4 header carries one (table 1.2 again), and no protocol on a normal network exchanges them. A mask is a local property of an interface, used by its owner to decide how to send. That is why mask faults are hard: the evidence is in each host’s configuration, not on the wire. A capture shows the consequence — an ARP you did not expect, replies that never come — never the cause.

Two hosts on one switch, 198.51.100.10/24 and 198.51.100.200/25. Which is misconfigured?

You cannot tell from the addresses alone, and that is the point. If the segment is really a /24 the second host is wrong; if it is really 198.51.100.128/25 the first has both the wrong prefix and an address outside the real subnet. Check the router’s interface prefix first: it is the one machine whose opinion has to be right, because every other host sends its off-link traffic there.

Widening a mask from /25 to /24 is described as “letting more machines in”. What is wrong?

The direction. A mask governs what this host does when it sends, so widening it means “I will now try to reach these addresses directly instead of through the router”. It grants nobody access to anything. If those addresses really are on this link it works and saves a trip through the gateway; if they are not, this host will now ARP into the void instead of handing the packet to a router that knew the way.

A host is configured 198.51.100.10/30 with a gateway of 198.51.100.1. What happens?

The configuration is rejected before it can do damage, as listing 4.3 shows: Error: Nexthop has invalid gateway. That /30 covers 198.51.100.8 to 198.51.100.11, and .1 is not in it. A gateway must be directly reachable — the whole idea of a next hop is that you can put a frame in front of it without asking anyone. In production this is a machine that boots with no default route, with the reason already in the logs.

Why is 169.254.10.5 on a server a diagnosis rather than a configuration?

Because almost nobody sets one deliberately. A link-local address is what a host gives itself when it asked for a DHCP lease and no server answered: it picks one at random, checks nobody else is using it, and carries on with an address guaranteed never to be routed. It is not the fault but the symptom — a dead DHCP server, a broken relay, or a VLAN the machine should not be in.

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

02For 203.0.113.77/26, work out the network, broadcast and host range on paper.Then check it with the calculator from listing 4.2.Easy

06Fix it by changing the mask on the left machine instead of the right.Narrowing the left mask also works. Ask what it costs the rest of the segment.Medium
07Give an interface a /32 and try to add a default route. Read the error.Then add an on-link route explicitly and try again.Medium
08Write the classifier from listing 4.6 from memory, and add the three RFC 1918 ranges.The tie-break for overlapping ranges is longest prefix, not list order.Hard
Why is a network written as a pair — a base address and a prefix — rather than just a base address?

Because the base address alone does not determine the network. 198.51.100.0/24 and 198.51.100.0/25 share a base address and are two different networks holding different sets of hosts, 256 addresses against 128. Listing 4.2 shows it directly: the same address masked at two prefixes gives the same network address and two different broadcast addresses. Drop the prefix and you have lost the size, and size is half the definition.

It is also what makes longest-prefix match possible: given several candidate networks that all contain an address, the length is what ranks them. A route is a prefix, a firewall rule is a prefix, a cloud subnet is a prefix, and comparing two of them means comparing both halves. A base address with no length is just an address.

Two machines on one segment with different masks. Why does the failure so often look intermittent?

Because the mask is consulted only on transmission, so the fault is one-directional, and whether you notice depends on which machine starts the conversation. A monitoring check that only ever pings from the correctly configured side succeeds forever; a backup job that opens a connection from the wrong side fails every time. If the wrongly configured host has a default route its replies still go out, through a router that may or may not have a path back, so some traffic completes with odd latency and some vanishes.

Layer 2 makes it worse by working perfectly. Listing 4.5 captures the ARP exchange succeeding, the MAC addresses being learned and the echo requests arriving intact; anything reporting on link health will report health. The habit worth building is that “works one way only” is not intermittent at all — it is a deterministic asymmetry, and asymmetry between two hosts on one wire means routing or masks, in that order, every time.

Chapter Five · Part II

Subnetting

A subnet is a set of addresses that have agreed they can reach each other without help, and subnetting is cutting one such agreement into several. Everything strange about it — the two addresses you must never use, the host counts that are always two short, the /31 that breaks the rule on purpose — falls out of one fact: the boundary between “which network” and “which host” is a bit position, not a number. Every boundary here is computed rather than asserted.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Split a prefix into equal subnets and compute every boundary yourself
  • Explain what the all-zeros and all-ones host addresses mean, and what breaks
  • Calculate usable hosts for any prefix, including the /31 and /32 exceptions
  • Show that a broadcast stops at a subnet boundary even on a single wire
  • Lay out a VLSM allocation that neither overlaps nor wastes
  • Choose a VPC CIDR block you will not regret in two years

5.1 The cut, computed

Chapter 4 established the only thing an IPv4 address is: a 32-bit integer, plus a prefix length saying how many leading bits identify the network. 203.0.113.0/24 means the top 24 bits are fixed and the bottom 8 free — 256 consecutive addresses on a multiple of 256.

Subnetting is one operation: move the prefix boundary to the right. Take a bit that identified a host and let it identify a network instead. One place gives two networks of half the size; two places, four of a quarter the size. RFC 950 standardised this in 1985, for organisations holding one huge allocation and needing more than one wire inside it.

Because the boundary is a bit position and not a number, two constraints follow:

  • A subnet’s size is a power of two. There is no /26.5: you cannot make a subnet of 100 addresses, you make one of 128 and leave 28 idle.
  • A subnet starts at a multiple of its own size. 203.0.113.64/26 is legal; 203.0.113.50/26 is not a subnet at all. Software corrects you silently, which is worse than an error.

A real split, computed from the integer rather than quoted:

Split intoSubnetsAddresses eachUsable eachTotal usableLost to network + broadcast
/2412562542542
/2521281262524
/26464622488
/278323024016
/2816161422432
/29328619264
/306442128128

Table 5.1 What splitting one /24 costs. The address count never changes, but every subnet pays a fixed toll of two, charged per subnet rather than per host. At /30 you have spent half the block to buy 64 broadcast domains. That trade is the design question of this chapter, and the last row is why section 5.5 exists.

5.2 The kernel does the same arithmetic

None of that is a convention agreed between humans. It is arithmetic, and every IP stack performs it independently — so you can check listing 5.1 without trusting it. Hand a kernel four host addresses, one per interface, never mention a network or broadcast address, and ask what it worked out. The brd + below means “derive the broadcast address”; it takes no argument, because an address and a prefix admit only one answer.

The prefix on an address and the prefix on a route are different statements

203.0.113.65/26 on an interface says two things at once. 203.0.113.65 is this machine’s address, one host. The /26 is a claim about the wire: everything from .64 to .127 is out there with me and I may address it directly. That is why changing only the mask on one host breaks connectivity in one direction and not the other: it has changed its opinion of who is local while its neighbours have not. Chapter 21 treats that as a named diagnosis, because the symptom looks like anything but a mask problem.

5.3 The two you never assign, and what actually breaks

Every textbook states the rule: in a subnet of n addresses, n−2 are usable. The two are not the same kind of reservation at all.

The all-zeros host is barely an address. It is the name of the subnet — what you write in a route, a firewall rule or a VPC definition when you mean the whole range. The all-ones host genuinely is an address with a destination: every host in the subnet at once, the directed broadcast. That one bites, because it is enforced not by the machine you configure but by every other machine on the segment:

AddressFormallyMeansAssignable to an interface?
All host bits 0{network, 0}The subnet itself, as written in a route or a ruleLinux allows it; RFC 1122 does not, and other stacks reject it
All host bits 1{network, −1}Directed broadcast — every host in that subnetNo. Every peer treats traffic to it as broadcast
255.255.255.255Limited broadcastThis wire only, never forwardedNo. Used by DHCP before a client has an address
0.0.0.0This host / unspecifiedA source before configuration; a wildcard in bind() (ch 9)No

Table 5.2 The operational distinction is between the first two rows. All-zeros is a notational reservation that Linux lets you break — a trap, because the configuration works in your lab and is rejected by the first real router it meets. All-ones is enforced: it fails at once, on machines you did not configure.

5.4 One wire, two subnets, and a broadcast that stops

The sharpest way to see that a subnet is a decision rather than a place is to put two of them on one piece of cable. Nothing at the link layer objects: a switch (ch 2) never reads an IP address, and a broadcast frame goes to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, which every interface on the segment must receive. So the frame arrives everywhere, and what happens next is decided by each receiver alone from its own mask.

Three machines share one bridge below: two in 203.0.113.0/26, one in 203.0.113.64/26. A capture runs on the odd one out while the broadcast is sent, so we can watch the frame reach it rather than guess.

This is also why a router will not forward a directed broadcast

203.0.113.63 is a routable destination right up until the last hop, where some router would have to turn it into a link-layer broadcast. Routers stop doing that by default because it was the amplifier in the smurf attack: one echo request with a forged source, sent to a large subnet’s broadcast, and every host replies to the victim. The consequence for you is duller — a service relying on broadcast discovery works in the office and finds nothing across a VPN or between two cloud subnets. That is a subnetting symptom, not a firewall one (ch 17).

5.5 The /31, and why the rule has an exception

Look again at the last row of table 5.1. A point-to-point link — a cable, a tunnel, a circuit between two routers — needs exactly two addresses, and the smallest subnet giving two usable ones under n−2 is a /30. Half of it goes on a broadcast address that can never be useful, because a broadcast to “every host on this link” is a unicast to the only other machine there.

A provider with ten thousand such links throws away twenty thousand addresses on nothing. RFC 3021 fixed that: on a point-to-point link a /31 is legal — two addresses, both usable, no network and no broadcast address, because one host bit leaves no room for the distinction to mean anything. Linux implements it:

/30/31
Addresses42
Usable22
Wasted20
Broadcast addressx.x.x.3, meaningless on a two-host linkNone exists
Where it fitsAnything, including a shared segmentPoint-to-point links only
SupportUniversalLinux and modern router platforms; not always old firmware or IPAM tools

Table 5.3 The case for the /31 is arithmetic; the case against is operational. It halves the address cost of every link, enormous at provider scale, but it confuses any tool computing usable hosts as n−2 without a special case — that expression returns zero, and inventory systems have reported such links as having no capacity.

5.6 VLSM, and the CIDR you choose before you know anything

Listing 5.1 cut the /24 into four equal pieces. Real networks are not: if one department has 100 machines and another 10, four /26s of 62 usable addresses each is at once too small for the first and eight times too large for the second.

VLSM — variable length subnet masking — is cutting subnets of different sizes from one block. It is not a feature you enable; it is what CIDR always allowed once routing protocols began carrying a prefix length with every route rather than inferring it from the address class (ch 4). Its one discipline is the alignment rule of section 5.1, and the way to satisfy it is to allocate largest first.

That is the whole argument about cloud CIDR blocks. When a platform asks for one before you have created a single machine, it is not being pedantic: the block is what it programs into its virtual router, what every subnet must be carved from, and what other networks are checked against when you peer. On AWS a VPC block may be /16 to /28, five addresses are reserved in every subnet rather than two, and the primary block cannot be changed after creation.

DecisionChoosing /16Choosing /24
Addresses65,536256
Subnets available at /24256 — one per zone per tier, for years1 — you are already out
Cost while unusedNothing. Private addresses are not billedNothing
Adding a zone laterCut another /24 from the spare spaceAdd a secondary block, or rebuild
If both sides of a peering chose the same popular defaultPeering is impossible without NAT (ch 8)Same failure, arriving sooner

Table 5.4 The asymmetry is the point. Too large costs nothing: unused private addresses have no price and are invisible outside your network. Too small costs the worst kind of migration, renumbering every instance and every hard-coded address on a live system. What deserves thought is not the size but the position, because two networks that overlap cannot be joined however much spare space each has.

Checkpoint

Why is the usable host count 232−prefix − 2 rather than 232−prefix?

Because two bit patterns in the host field already have meanings: all zeros is the subnet’s own identifier, all ones the directed broadcast. Neither is available to a machine. The misconception worth correcting is that these are reservations someone made. They are the smallest and largest value the host field can hold, and would have existed whether or not anyone found a use for them — listing 5.1 prints them as the 000000 and 111111 rows of the same six bits.

You assign 203.0.113.50/26 to a server. What have you actually configured?

An address in 203.0.113.0/26, which is legal: .50 is a good host address in the first subnet. What you have not done is create a subnet starting at .50, because a /26 must begin at a multiple of 64. Nothing warns you — the kernel silently computes the network as 203.0.113.0/26, as listing 5.2 shows. The failure surfaces later, when someone assumes .50 began a block and allocates from it, overlapping the next subnet.

Two machines on one switch, at 203.0.113.10/26 and 203.0.113.70/26. Can they talk?

Not directly, though there is a cable between them. Each computes the other’s address against its own mask, finds it outside the local subnet, and hands the packet to its default gateway instead of ARPing for it (ch 3). With a router holding a leg in both subnets it works but takes a pointless trip; without one it fails. Listing 5.4 is this situation, and its capture is the point: the frames do reach the other machine, so nothing at the link layer separates them.

A colleague says a /31 is invalid because it has no usable addresses. What is the error?

Applying n−2 outside its range. The subtraction exists because a network and a broadcast address must be carved out, and RFC 3021 observes that on a point-to-point link neither is needed: a broadcast to “all hosts on this link” is a unicast to the one other machine. Listing 5.5 shows a working link between 192.0.2.0 and 192.0.2.1, the kernel producing no broadcast address even when asked. The rule is n−2 down to /30, and n at /31 and /32.

You ping a subnet’s broadcast address from outside that subnet and get nothing back. Is the network broken?

Almost certainly not. Routers have not forwarded directed broadcasts by default for a long time, because it made every large subnet an amplifier: forge the source, send one packet to a broadcast address, every host replies to your victim. Separately, most hosts ignore broadcast pings — the machines in listing 5.4 answered only because the setup command turned that off. A silent result tells you nothing about reachability; test with a unicast ping instead.

Why would anyone choose /16 for a VPC that will hold thirty machines?

Because the block costs nothing and cannot be changed. Private address space is not scarce, not billed, and invisible outside your network, so an unused address has no price. Meanwhile a VPC’s primary CIDR is fixed at creation on the major platforms, and outgrowing it means renumbering a live system. Too big costs nothing; too small costs a migration. The question worth care is which range, because overlapping with a network you later need to peer with is the one failure address space cannot solve (ch 8).

Go deeper — the primary sources
  • RFC 950 — Internet Standard Subnetting ProcedureIETF
  • RFC 3021 — Using 31-Bit Prefixes on IPv4 Point-to-Point LinksIETF

Practice · Subnetting

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Split 203.0.113.0/24 into eight subnets and list every network and broadcast address.Eight means three borrowed bits, so /27, stepping by 32.Easy
02For 198.51.100.0/22, give the address range, the broadcast address and the usable count.Four /24s worth. The mask is 255.255.252.0.Easy
03Assign an address with ip addr add ... brd + and check what the kernel derived.ip -4 addr show. Try it at /26, then /31.Easy
04Say which subnet 203.0.113.130 is in if the block is split into /26s.130 divided by 64 is 2, remainder 2. So the third subnet.Easy
05Build listing 5.4 and add a fourth machine in the second subnet. Predict who answers the broadcast.Then broadcast to each subnet’s address in turn and check.Medium
06Configure a /31 link between two namespaces and confirm there is no broadcast address.brd + on both ends, then look for a brd field.Medium
07Plan a VLSM layout for departments of 60, 30, 12 and 6 hosts inside one /24.Largest first, and check each block starts on a multiple of its own size.Medium
08Take a subnet calculator you trust and find an input where it disagrees with your arithmetic./31 and /32 are where most of them are wrong.Hard
Why does allocating largest-first matter, if the total fits either way?

Because of the alignment rule, not the total. Every block must start at a multiple of its own size, so a large block has few legal starting positions and a small one has many. Place a /28 at 203.0.113.0 first and the next legal start for a /25 is 203.0.113.128, stranding the 112 addresses between: the machines would fit, but no /25 may begin at .16. Largest-first lands each big block on the first boundary that accepts it, which is why listing 5.6’s rounding step never moved anything.

It is the fragmentation problem a memory allocator has, with the same remedy. It is also why you should leave deliberate gaps rather than packing perfectly: listing 5.6 fits six subnets into a /24 with twelve addresses spare, which looks efficient and means the next request cannot be met at all.

If the broadcast address is so rarely used, why not reclaim it and make every subnet two addresses larger?

Because the reservation is not held by any single machine that could be persuaded to give it up. Every host on the segment holds it independently, in its own mask, on operating systems from twenty vendors. Listing 5.3 is the demonstration: the machine that owned 203.0.113.63 accepted the configuration happily, and the one that broke was the machine trying to reach it, which computed “that is a broadcast” from arithmetic it will always do.

The /31 is the shape a real fix has to take. It found one case — a link with exactly two hosts — where the distinction is provably meaningless, wrote a rule for that case only, and let deployment be incremental, because a /31 link needs only its two routers to agree. Compare IPv6 (ch 4), which dropped broadcast entirely for multicast, and could only do that because it had no installed base to convince.

Chapter Six · Part II

Routing

A host does not know how to reach the internet. It knows one thing: for a given destination, which machine on its own wire to hand the packet to next. That is the whole of routing, repeated at every hop by a machine that also does not know the path. This chapter reads a real routing table field by field, proves which entry wins when several match, and then breaks the network by deleting one line.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read every column of a routing table and say what it controls
  • Predict which of several overlapping routes will be used, and confirm it
  • Use ip route get to settle an argument in one command
  • Explain what a default route is, and what happens when there is none
  • Tell connected, static and dynamic routes apart in a live table
  • Recognise asymmetric routing and say why it breaks a stateful firewall

6.1 The table, field by field

A routing table is not a map. It holds no path and no knowledge of anything beyond the next machine along. Each line answers one question — if the destination falls inside this prefix, where do I hand the packet and out of which interface? — and a host that has answered it has finished its job. Every other hop is somebody else’s decision, which is the design that let the internet scale.

FieldExample hereWhat it decides
destination203.0.113.0/24, defaultThe prefix this line covers. default has length zero, so it matches everything
via (gateway)via 198.51.100.1The next machine to hand the frame to. Absent means the destination is on this link
devdev eth0The interface it leaves by, and so the wire ARP runs on (ch 3)
protokernel, boot, static, dhcpWho installed it. A label only; the kernel never chooses on it
scopelink, global, hostHow far the destination is: this wire, a gateway, or this machine
srcsrc 198.51.100.10The source address stamped on packets taking this route, if the application chose none
metricmetric 100A tie-break only, between routes to the same prefix. Lower wins

Table 6.1 The seven fields, in the order ip route prints them. src is the one that surprises people, because it changes the packet rather than its path — section 6.4 uses exactly that to prove which route a packet took.

6.2 Three tables, one decision

There is not one routing table. Before the kernel consults the table you have just read, it walks a short list of rules, each naming a table to try. That list is untouched on almost every machine — but knowing it exists explains behaviour that is otherwise magic, such as why a packet addressed to your own machine never leaves it.

PriorityTableNumberHolds
0local255Every address this machine holds, and its broadcast addresses. Written by the kernel
32766main254What ip route shows: connected routes, your static routes, whatever a daemon installed
32767default253Empty on virtually every machine. A rule naming an empty table does not match; the search carries on

Table 6.2 Three tables, tried in this order, first match wins. The gap between 0 and 32766 is room for rules you add: policy routing — “traffic from this source uses that uplink” — is no more than a rule in that gap naming a fourth table. When a machine routes a packet in a way the main table cannot explain, ip rule show is what explains it.

6.3 Longest prefix wins

Several routes will often match the same destination. The rule for choosing between them is one sentence with no exceptions: the route with the longest prefix wins. Not the first listed, not the lowest metric, not the most recently added. The most specific.

Said in binary it stops sounding arbitrary. A /32 pins all thirty-two bits and describes one address; a /0 pins nothing. Preferring the longest match is preferring the entry whose author knew the most, and it is what makes a default route safe to keep.

Destination asked forRoutes that matchWinnerWhy
203.0.113.20/0, /24, /32203.0.113.20 via eth032 bits pinned — the longest
203.0.113.21/0, /24203.0.113.0/24 via eth1The /32 is a different address
198.51.100.99/0, connected /24198.51.100.0/24 dev eth0Connected wins on length, not on being connected
9.9.9.9/0 onlydefault via 198.51.100.1Nothing more specific exists

Table 6.3 Read the third row twice. A connected route is not special-cased anywhere in the kernel: it wins because /24 is longer than /0, and would lose to a /32 pointing elsewhere. That is how a VPN captures traffic to one server without touching anything else — and how one mistyped host route makes exactly one machine unreachable while its neighbours work.

6.4 Changing the table while packets are moving

Routes are not configuration that needs a restart. The table is consulted per packet, so a change lands on the very next one. Each route below carries a different src, so the source address arriving at host-b names the wire the packet left by — a witness at the far end, not an opinion from the machine that decided.

6.5 The default route, metrics, and having no route at all

A default route is not special machinery. It is an ordinary entry whose prefix is 0.0.0.0/0, and it wins only when nothing more specific matched — which is what lets an ordinary machine hold two routes instead of a million. When two routes to the same prefix exist the metric breaks the tie and lower wins, but nothing in that comparison asks whether the chosen next hop is alive.

OriginWritten byprotoDisappears when
ConnectedThe kernel, when an address is configuredkernelThe address is removed or the link goes down
StaticYou, a file read at boot, or config managementboot, staticSomething deletes it — which may be never, even when the path is broken
DHCPThe DHCP client, from the server’s router optiondhcpThe lease is not renewed
DynamicA routing daemon speaking OSPF, BGP or IS-IS — none runs in this labospf, bgp…The daemon withdraws it, seconds after the path fails

Table 6.4 The proto column is a label and nothing more: the kernel stores the number and never chooses on it. It matters because it is how a daemon recognises its own routes in order to withdraw them, and how you tell at a glance whether a line came from a human or from software.

This lab runs no routing protocol, and this chapter will not pretend otherwise

Nothing in this book has run OSPF or BGP. The lab has three machines and hand-written routes, and every decision shown here was made by a table somebody typed. Doing it honestly needs a daemon and a topology big enough for a path to fail; inventing the output would be worse than omitting it.

The division of labour is what to carry away. A dynamic protocol forwards nothing: it talks to its neighbours, works out which prefixes are reachable and how, then installs ordinary routes into the table you have read all chapter — where they win or lose on longest prefix and metric exactly like the ones you typed. OSPF runs inside one organisation; BGP runs between them.

6.6 Asymmetric routing, and the firewall it breaks

Nothing so far required the replies to retrace the requests. Each hop decides independently, for the destination in front of it — and a reply has a different destination, so it may quite reasonably take a different path. Traffic that leaves one way and returns another is asymmetric routing. It is everywhere on the public internet, and by itself it works.

It stops working the moment something on the path needs to see both directions. A stateful firewall does: it permits a returning packet because it remembers the outbound one. Put such a device where only half the conversation passes and it will do exactly what you configured, and drop everything.

Device on the pathSees requestsSees repliesConsequence
Router 1YesNoFine while stateless. A stateful rule here drops nothing: no reply ever reaches it
Router 2NoYesBreaks the moment it becomes stateful: every reply belongs to no known flow
host-a and host-bYesYesBoth endpoints see the whole conversation, so neither notices anything wrong

Table 6.5 The second row is the one that matters. Symptoms in the wild: ping and UDP often survive while TCP hangs after the handshake, and both firewalls look correctly configured, because individually they are. Diagnose by capturing on both paths (ch 20) and noticing that no single device holds both halves. The fix is a routing change, not a firewall change.

Checkpoint

Your table has default via 10.0.0.1, 203.0.113.0/24 via 10.0.0.2 and 203.0.113.20/32 via 10.0.0.3. Where does a packet to 203.0.113.20 go?

To 10.0.0.3. All three match and the /32 pins the most bits, so it wins; order in the table is irrelevant. The misconception worth killing is that the default route is a fallback consulted after something failed. It is not: it is an ordinary entry with a zero-length prefix, evaluated in the same lookup as the others, and it loses to every route that matches at all — without ever asking whether 10.0.0.3 is alive.

Why does the router in listing 6.1 have no default route, when both hosts do?

Because it does not need one. It is directly connected to both networks in this lab, so every destination that exists here is already matched. A default route means “for everything I do not know about, ask that machine”, and a router at the edge of its world has nobody to ask. The same holds at the top of the real internet, where a core router carries a full BGP table and no default — the “default-free zone”. No default is a claim of completeness, not a misconfiguration.

ping says connect: Network is unreachable. How much of the network was involved in that message?

None of it. That error came from your own kernel, from the connect() call, before a byte reached a wire: the lookup matched nothing, so the socket could not be set up. It is a local diagnosis, and the fault is in your own table — no default route, or an interface that never came up. Contrast an ICMP destination-unreachable, which comes from a router that did receive your packet (ch 7). The two are constantly confused, and they point at machines several hops apart.

What does the metric on a route actually compare?

Only other routes to the same prefix, and only after longest-prefix match has narrowed the field. It is a local preference, not a distance: nothing measures or validates it, and a low-metric route with a dead next hop is chosen over a working one, as listing 6.5 showed. It never lets a /0 beat a /24, however low you set it, and Linux has no “administrative distance” ranking route sources against each other the way some vendor platforms do.

Traffic leaves through firewall A and returns through firewall B. TCP hangs after the handshake but ping works. What is happening?

Asymmetric routing meeting stateful inspection. Firewall B sees the returning half of a conversation whose opening it never observed, so those packets belong to no known flow and are dropped as invalid — the counters in listing 6.6. ping can survive because ICMP is often permitted outright rather than by state. It hangs after the handshake because the opening exchange may still be let through as a new flow, while everything later is judged against state that does not exist. The fix is to make the paths symmetric; loosening the rules until it works removes the firewall without admitting it.

You add ip route add 203.0.113.0/24 via 198.51.100.99, where .99 does not exist. What does the kernel say?

Nothing at all. The route is accepted and installed: a next hop only has to sit inside a directly connected subnet to be valid, and whether anything answers there is checked neither at insertion nor afterwards. Packets go to eth0, ARP asks for .99 (ch 3), nothing answers, and they are discarded locally. The symptom is total loss with a table that reads perfectly — which is why ip route get is only half a diagnosis: it gives you the decision, and ip neigh tells you whether it can be carried out.

If longest prefix always wins, what is the metric for?

For the case longest prefix cannot decide: two or more routes to the identical prefix. That happens constantly — a laptop on Wi-Fi and Ethernet at once has two default routes, and a daemon that learns one prefix from two neighbours installs two. Longest prefix ties between them by definition, so something else must choose, and lower metric wins.

What it is not is a measurement. Nothing verifies a metric against reality, and a low-metric route with a dead next hop is chosen over a working one until something removes it. That is the difference between a metric inside a routing protocol — derived from bandwidth or hop count, withdrawn when the path fails — and a metric on a static route, which is a number you typed. The kernel cannot tell them apart, which is why static routes outlive the paths they describe.

Why do routers not simply remember the whole path to a destination?

Because then every router would have to agree with every other about every path, and the table would need rebuilding globally whenever any link anywhere changed. The internet works on a per-hop, per-packet decision instead: each router reads only the destination address, consults only its own table, and picks only the next machine. Nobody holds a path, so nobody has to be told when one changes — the routers next to the failure update their tables, and packets arriving afterwards are forwarded differently.

The cost is what section 6.6 is about. Because no device holds the path, none is guaranteed to see both directions of a conversation — and anything that needs to, such as a stateful firewall, a NAT (ch 8) or a connection-tracking load balancer (ch 19), is building state on a network that promised none. Each imposes a symmetry IP does not provide, and each fails the same way when routing stops cooperating.

Chapter Seven · Part II

ICMP, ping and traceroute

IP has no way to tell you that it failed. An undeliverable datagram is simply gone, and nothing in the header has room to say why. ICMP is the answer to that: a small protocol riding on IP whose only job is to report on IP’s own behaviour. Two of the most useful tools in networking are built from it — one of them by abusing a field designed for something else entirely — and a great deal of modern breakage comes from administrators who decided ICMP was optional.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read an ICMP message off the wire and name its type and code
  • Explain what a router does when a TTL reaches zero, and prove it happened
  • Describe exactly how traceroute discovers a path nobody told it about
  • Say what each Destination Unreachable code means and who sent it
  • Explain why a failed ping is weak evidence and a successful one is weaker
  • Predict precisely what breaks when a firewall drops all ICMP

7.1 The protocol that reports on IP

Chapter 1 took an IP header apart and found no field for “this went wrong”. That was deliberate: IP promises nothing and owes you no explanation. But a network whose failures are entirely silent is unusable, so a companion protocol carries them. ICMP has IP protocol number 1, so it rides inside IP datagrams exactly as TCP (6) and UDP (17) do — yet it is not a transport protocol, because no application uses it to move data. It exists so IP can talk about itself.

Every ICMP message begins the same way: one byte of type, one of code, two of checksum, then four bytes whose meaning depends on the type:

OffsetRequestReplyFieldWhat it is
0x140800TypeThe whole meaning of the message
0x150000CodeA sub-type. Idle for echo; decisive for type 3 (table 7.6)
0x1617 861f 86ChecksumOver the ICMP message only; IP checksums its header separately
0x183b f23b f2Identifier15346. Steers the reply to the right ping
0x1a00 0100 01Sequence1. Ping prints it as icmp_seq
0x1c…6b c8 8e 6a…6b c8 8e 6a…PayloadArbitrary, echoed back byte for byte

Table 7.1 Generated from listing 7.1’s bytes, so it cannot drift from them. ICMP has no port numbers, so the identifier (15346) and sequence (1), identical in both directions, are the only thing letting a host with three pings running send each reply to the right one. The checksum went from 0x1786 to 0x1f86: exactly 0x0800 larger, which is precisely the amount the type byte shrank by.

TypeNameKindWhere you meet it
0Echo replyqueryThe second half of every ping
3Destination unreachableerrorCarries a code saying which kind. Sections 7.5, 7.6
4Source quencherrorA congestion signal. Deprecated; nothing sends it
5Redirecterror“Use a different gateway for that” (ch 6)
8Echo requestqueryWhat ping sends
11Time exceedederrorA TTL reached zero. All of section 7.3
12Parameter problemerrorA header field the receiver could not parse

Table 7.2 A query is self-contained. An error reports on someone else’s packet, so it must quote enough of it to be identified: the IP header plus eight bytes, which for TCP or UDP is exactly the two port numbers — the rest of the four-tuple that names a socket (ch 9). One rule follows: an ICMP error is never sent about an ICMP error, or one malformed packet could bounce between two routers for ever.

7.2 TTL is a hop count, not a timer

The field at offset 0x08 of an IP header is called Time To Live, and the name is a historical accident: it was meant to be a lifetime in seconds, with each router subtracting the time it held the packet. Nobody implemented that, because measuring how long you held a packet is expensive and pointless, so routers subtract one and move on. IPv6 renamed the field Hop Limit, which is what it always was. Its purpose is not politeness: chapter 6 showed how easily two routers can be made to point at each other, and without a hop count the first packet to fall into that loop stays there for ever. TTL bounds the disaster at 255 wasted forwardings, and then tells somebody.

You seeWhere it comes fromWhat you may conclude
ttl 64 leaving a hostLinux and macOS start hereNothing. A starting value is not a measurement
ttl 128Windows starts hereA guess at the sender’s operating system
ttl 255The maximum; common on appliancesThat it will survive a long path
ttl=63 in a ping reply64 minus oneOne router coming back — if it started at 64
ttl=61 in a ping reply64 minus threeThree routers. Listing 7.3 shows exactly this
ttl 0 on a wireNowhere. You will never see itA router discarded it and sent type 11 instead

Table 7.3 Counting hops from a reply TTL is a useful field trick and an unreliable one, for the reason in the last column: you subtract an observed value from an assumed one. It survives only because the three common starting values are far apart, so 61 is obviously 64−3 and not 128−67. And a reply’s TTL measures the path back, which need not match the way out.

7.3 The trick: how traceroute sees a path nobody told it about

Nothing in IP lets you ask which routers your packets will cross. There is no such query and no router keeps a list for you; the path is an emergent property of dozens of independent forwarding decisions, and no single machine knows all of it.

Traceroute extracts it anyway, from two facts. A router that decrements a TTL to zero sends back a type 11 Time Exceeded — and an ICMP error carries the address of the router that generated it. So send TTL 1 and the first router names itself; send TTL 2 and the second does. Keep going until something answers that is not a Time Exceeded, and you have walked the path a hop at a time with no router cooperating in the slightest. Each merely complained about a packet it had to throw away.

Three machines is not a path worth tracing, so this listing builds a longer one: host-b becomes a router with two more machines behind it, on 192.0.2.0/24 cut into /30s.

ProbeTTLUDP portDies atWhat comes back
1133434the first routerType 11 from 198.51.100.1
2233435the second routerType 11 from 203.0.113.20
3333436the third routerType 11 from 192.0.2.2
4433437nowhere — it arrivesType 3, port unreachable, from 192.0.2.6

Table 7.4 One traceroute, decoded from the capture above. The design has a consequence people find shocking: each row names the interface the probe arrived on, because that is the source address the router chose for its error. A router with six interfaces identifies itself differently depending which way you approach it. And this is the forward path only — the errors came back by whatever route existed, about which you learn nothing.

Why UDP, and why those odd port numbers

UDP to a very high, conventionally unused port makes the last hop unambiguous: routers reply type 11, and only the destination itself can reply port unreachable. The alternative, used by traceroute -I and Windows’ tracert, sends echo requests and stops on an echo reply — simpler, and easier to block silently. Modern practice increasingly uses TCP probes to the real port (traceroute -T -p 443), because a path that carries HTTPS may drop UDP and ICMP outright, and then the only honest trace is one made of the traffic you care about.

7.4 Loss that is not loss: reading mtr

mtr is traceroute in a loop with statistics. It finds the hops the same way and then keeps probing them all, reporting loss and latency per hop. For watching a path that is intermittently bad it is far better than running traceroute repeatedly. It also produces the most misread output in networking: people see 60% loss on hop 2 and open a ticket about hop 2. Almost always, nothing is wrong with hop 2.

pingtraceroutemtr
AnswersCan I exchange small packets with this host?Which routers does my traffic cross?Is the path getting worse, and roughly where?
UsesType 8 out, type 0 backTTL 1,2,3…, type 11, ending in type 3The same, repeated
Loss figure to trustThe end-to-end oneNone — stars mean very littleOnly the last row
Common misreading“It pings, so it works”“It stops at hop 4, so hop 4 is broken”“Hop 2 has 60% loss”
Run it forThirty secondsOnce, to see the shapeMinutes, while the problem is happening

Table 7.5 The rule that survives all three tools: loss at an intermediate hop only matters if it also appears at every hop after it. A router reporting 60% on its own row and 0% below it is telling you about its rate limiter, or a CPU deprioritising work it considers optional — generating errors about other people’s packets is the first thing a busy router stops doing well. Real loss propagates downwards.

7.5 Destination Unreachable, and the silence that tells you nothing

Type 3 is the workhorse. Unlike Time Exceeded, which means one thing, it carries a code saying which of several quite different failures occurred — and its source address tells you which device decided. Reading both is most of the diagnostic value ICMP offers. Here are four failures that all look like “ping does not work” from a distance, and a fifth that looks identical and is not a failure at all:

CodeNameWho sends itWhat it means
0Net unreachableA router with no route for that networkA routing gap, usually a missing or withdrawn route (ch 6)
1Host unreachableThe last router before the destinationThe network exists; that address does not answer ARP
2Protocol unreachableThe destination hostNothing there handles that IP protocol number. Rare; not shown here
3Port unreachableThe destination hostNothing bound to that UDP port. Traceroute’s finish line, listing 7.3
4Fragmentation needed, DF setA router whose next link is too smallCarries the next-hop MTU. Section 7.6, and all of ch 14
13Administratively prohibitedA firewallSomeone decided no, and was polite enough to say so

Table 7.6 Codes 0 and 1 are the pair people confuse. Net unreachable means the routing system had nowhere to send it, from somewhere in the middle; host unreachable means the packet reached the destination’s own segment and the last router could not find the machine. Same tool, same-looking failure, two completely different investigations. Code 13 is a gift: a firewall that rejects rather than drops turns a ten-minute mystery into a one-line answer.

What a successful ping actually proves

That an 84-byte ICMP packet reached the far end and one came back, so a route exists both ways and nothing objected to type 8. That is the complete list. It does not prove the service is running, that TCP can be established, or — as the next section shows — that a full-sized packet can get through at all. A failed ping proves even less, because ignoring echo requests is a default on plenty of hosts. Test with the protocol and port you actually depend on. Ping is a first question, never an answer.

7.6 Fragmentation Needed, and the cost of blocking ICMP

Links do not all carry the same maximum packet. Ethernet takes 1500 bytes of payload; a VPN or a tunnel wraps its own headers round yours and leaves less. A sender that does not know the smallest link on the path can either fragment everything down to a safe minimum, which is wasteful, or send full-sized packets with the DF (don’t fragment) bit set and let the network complain.

Every modern stack does the second, and the complaint is a type 3 code 4 message. It is unique among ICMP errors in carrying a number the sender needs rather than mere news: the MTU of the next link. That value makes Path MTU Discovery work, and Path MTU Discovery is what makes the DF bit safe to set. Chapter 14 covers the consequences; this is the mechanism, and what happens when you throw it away.

The failure this produces, and why it takes so long to diagnose

Read that again as a TCP connection rather than a ping. The handshake is three tiny packets, so it succeeds. The request is small, so it arrives. The response is large, so it is sent at full size, dropped silently, retransmitted at full size, dropped again — for ever. The symptom is a connection that opens instantly and then hangs, on some sites, for some users, while ping and DNS and the dashboard look perfect. This is the PMTU black hole, and it is nearly always a well-meaning rule that dropped “ICMP” as a category. The fix is a policy: never drop type 3 code 4, and never drop type 11. Blocking echo requests is defensible and cheap; blocking ICMP wholesale breaks path MTU discovery, breaks traceroute, and turns every later problem into an investigation. Where the errors truly cannot be trusted to arrive, the answers are MSS clamping and packetisation-layer probing, both in chapter 14.

Checkpoint

A router discards your packet because its TTL hit zero. Which address does the Time Exceeded come from?

The router’s own — specifically the interface the packet arrived on, which it picks as the source of the error it generates. That is the entire foundation of traceroute: the router is not answering a question, it is filing a complaint, and a complaint is signed. It also explains a confusing feature of traceroute output: a router with many interfaces names a different address depending which way you approach it, so two people tracing the same router can legitimately see two different addresses.

Traceroute shows * * * at hop 4, then continues normally to hop 9 and the destination. What is broken?

Nothing. Hop 4 forwarded your packets perfectly — hops 5 to 9 answered, and their answers came back through hop 4. What hop 4 declined to do is generate Time Exceeded messages, by configuration, or because its rate limiter refused, or because a filter dropped the reply on the way back. Listing 7.4 shows a rate limiter doing this to a healthy router. A gap followed by answers is not loss; loss is a gap that continues to the end.

Why does an ICMP error quote the packet that caused it, and why is eight bytes past the IP header the magic number?

Because the error arrives unsolicited, from a machine you may never have addressed, about a packet you sent some time ago; without a copy you could not tell which of your connections was affected. The quoted IP header gives the addresses and the protocol, and the first eight bytes after it are, for TCP and UDP alike, the two port numbers. Addresses plus ports is the four-tuple that names a socket (ch 9), so eight bytes is the minimum that delivers the bad news to the right connection instead of merely counting it.

Monitoring pings a server every 30 seconds and has never alerted. A user says the site hangs on large pages. Where do you look?

At the MTU, before anything else. Small packets fine, large packets vanishing for ever with no error, is the PMTU black hole from section 7.6, and monitoring will never catch it because monitoring sends small packets. Reproduce it with ping -M do -s 1472, then bisect the size downwards; the largest that works plus 28 bytes of IP and ICMP headers is the real path MTU. Then find whoever is dropping type 3 code 4, or clamp the MSS (ch 14).

Ping returns Destination Host Unreachable from a router. What has that told you, precisely?

That the packet was routed correctly all the way to the last router before your destination — a great deal of good news — and that this router ARPed for your target on the local segment and heard nothing (ch 3). Routing is fine; the machine is not answering on that address, so it is off, or on a different address or VLAN. Contrast Destination Net Unreachable, which means the packet never got near the destination at all.

Someone proposes blocking all ICMP at the perimeter because “ICMP is a security risk”. What is your response?

That the category is wrong. Refusing echo requests (type 8) hides you from casual scanning and costs a diagnostic; that is a real trade-off reasonable people accept. Dropping every type is different, because two are load-bearing: type 3 code 4 is the only way a sender learns the path MTU, and losing it gives connections that establish and then hang for ever (listing 7.6); type 11 is the only way any hop can be identified at all. A correct policy names types, not protocols.

  • RFC 1191 — Path MTU DiscoveryIETF
