Practice · ICMP, ping and traceroute

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Ping your default gateway and note the reply TTL, then ping something several hops away.The difference is the hop count of the return path.Easy
02Capture a ping with tcpdump -nn -v -X icmp and find the type byte in the hex.First byte after the 20-byte IP header: 08, then 00.Easy
03Run ping -t 1 at a host beyond your gateway and read the message.Your gateway names itself. That is traceroute’s first row.Easy
04Run traceroute and traceroute -I to the same host and diff them.UDP probes and ICMP probes get filtered differently.Easy
05Capture a traceroute and confirm each probe’s TTL rises by one.Filter udp or icmp and use -v, or the TTL will not print.Medium
06Find a host that ignores ping but answers TCP, and prove both.nc -vz host 443. Many cloud instances are set up this way.Medium
07Determine the path MTU to a host by bisecting ping -M do -s N.Add 28 to the largest N that works: 20 of IP, 8 of ICMP.Medium
08Drop inbound ICMP, then demonstrate a PMTU black hole through it.Shrink an MTU in the path first. Listing 7.6 is the recipe.Hard
Why does traceroute send UDP to strange high ports instead of pinging each hop?

Because it needs two unmistakably different answers. An intermediate router must say “I discarded this” (type 11), and the destination must say “this is as far as it goes” in a way no intermediate device could imitate. UDP aimed at a port in the 33434-and-upwards range, which by convention nothing uses, gives exactly that. The incrementing port also gives each probe a unique identity, so replies can be matched with several in flight.

Echo-based tracing, used by traceroute -I and Windows’ tracert, works too and stops on an echo reply. It survives firewalls that block UDP and dies on firewalls that drop echo requests, so neither is strictly better. Better advice is to trace with the protocol you care about: traceroute -T -p 443 is the only variant describing the path your application will actually take.

An mtr shows 0% at hops 1 and 2, 45% at hop 3, 44% at hop 4 and 43% at the destination. Is hop 3 the problem?

Yes, and this shape is what says so. The loss appears at hop 3 and persists through every hop after it, including the destination row — the only row that measures the real end-to-end path. Packets are genuinely being lost at or just after hop 3, and everything downstream inherits that loss because those packets never reach it. The drift from 45% to 43% is sampling noise, not a second fault.

Contrast listing 7.4, where an intermediate row reported heavy loss and the destination reported none. That means the opposite: the device is declining to generate errors as fast as you are asking, while the traffic it forwards is untouched. Generating ICMP errors is optional work on a router’s slowest path and is the first thing sacrificed under load, so a busy core router lossy on its own row and nowhere else is uninteresting. The rule is whether the loss propagates downwards.

Chapter Eight · Part II

NAT

Your laptop almost certainly has an address that several million other laptops also have, and it works anyway. That is not a bug being tolerated; it is a rewrite happening in a box between you and everything else, on every packet, in both directions, invisibly. This chapter builds that box with one rule, watches the same packet on both sides of it, opens the table that makes it reversible, and goes through what it broke.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain why address translation exists, in terms of a number that ran out
  • Build a working source NAT and prove the rewrite from a capture
  • Read a translation-table entry and name both of its tuples
  • Say why NAT must be stateful, and what happens when the state expires
  • Describe port overloading and predict when a port must be rewritten
  • Name four things NAT breaks and the workaround each one produced

8.1 Four billion, and why that was not enough

An IPv4 address is 32 bits (ch 1). That was decided when the network being designed had a few dozen sites on it, and 32 bits was already thought extravagant. Do the arithmetic and the problem is obvious in hindsight:

BlockAddressesWhat it is for
10.0.0.0/816,777,216RFC 1918 private. The usual cloud VPC default
172.16.0.0/121,048,576RFC 1918 private. The forgotten one, which is why docker0 lives here
192.168.0.0/1665,536RFC 1918 private. The home-router default, and why your laptop is 192.168.x.x
100.64.0.0/104,194,304RFC 6598 shared address space — not yours, not public, for carrier-grade NAT
198.51.100.0/24256RFC 5737 documentation addresses. What this book’s lab is built from

Table 8.1 The first three come with an explicit deal: use these numbers, nobody will route them, and do not expect them to be unique outside your own network. That last clause is the whole of NAT’s job description. The fourth is the one people miss — it is what an ISP puts on its side of its NAT, so finding it on a traceroute means two translations, not one.

The lab has to fake the private side, and says so

Every listing here runs in the chapter A lab, where host-a is 198.51.100.10 and host-b is 203.0.113.20. Those are documentation addresses, not private ones: the build refuses to print a real RFC 1918 address, since a listing containing one would mean the book had captured a home network rather than the lab. Read 198.51.100.0/24 as “the inside”. NAT translates whatever it is told to.

8.2 Source NAT, built in one rule

The mechanism is simpler than its reputation. A router sits between two networks. On the way out it replaces the packet’s source address with its own; on the way back it replaces the destination address with the original. Everything else — the table, the ports, the breakage — falls out of having to do the second half.

On Linux the outbound rewrite hangs on the POSTROUTING hook, after the routing decision, so the kernel already knows which interface the packet leaves by and therefore which address to pretend to be. MASQUERADE is SNAT that reads that address off the interface at packet time instead of being told it in advance.

FieldInside wireOutside wireRewritten?
Source address (request)198.51.100.10203.0.113.1Yes — the whole of SNAT
Destination address (request)203.0.113.20203.0.113.20No
Destination address (reply)198.51.100.10203.0.113.1Yes — the rewrite undone
ICMP idsame valuesame valueNo — nothing competed for it
Header checksum——Necessarily (ch 1), but no -v, so not printed
Payload bytesunchangedunchangedNo — and section 8.5 is why that matters

Table 8.2 Read against listing 8.2 line by line. The bottom two rows are the honest ones: the checksum must change because the address it covers changed, but these captures lack -v, so the table declines to claim the listing proves it. The payload row is the assumption half this chapter’s difficulties rest on.

8.3 The table that makes it reversible

Now the hard question. A reply arrives at the router addressed to 203.0.113.1 — the only address the outside world ever saw. Which machine behind it is that reply for?

Nothing in the packet says; the information was destroyed on the way out. The only way to answer is to have written it down, which is why NAT cannot be stateless the way routing is. A router forwards knowing only a destination and a configured table; a NAT must remember every conversation it rewrote. That memory is conntrack, and it is readable:

Piece of a rowExample from listing 8.3What it does
Protocoltcp 6, udp 17, icmp 1The IP protocol field from ch 1
Timeout431998 / 28Seconds until deletion. Reset by traffic
StateESTABLISHEDTCP only, tracked from the flags (ch 10, ch 11)
Original tuplesrc=198.51.100.10 … sport=9001What the inside host actually sent
Reply tupledst=203.0.113.1 … dport=9001The packet the router is waiting for
[ASSURED]on the TCP rowTraffic went both ways; do not evict this one first

Table 8.3 The two tuples are the entire idea: outbound packets match the original and are rewritten, inbound packets match the reply and are rewritten back. A NAT is a bidirectional dictionary with an expiry date on every entry, and every strange NAT behaviour is that dictionary being full, stale, or missing what someone hoped for.

Thirty seconds is why your VoIP call needs a keepalive

TCP is remembered for days because it announces its own end (ch 11) and the router can watch for it. UDP announces nothing, so the router guesses that half a minute of silence means over. Any long-lived UDP conversation with quiet periods — a SIP registration, a game session, a VPN — has its mapping deleted underneath it, after which return packets reach a router that no longer knows who they are for. All of them therefore send traffic only to keep a NAT entry alive; WireGuard’s PersistentKeepalive has exactly that one job.

8.4 Port overloading, and the collision that forces it

Table 8.3 quietly answered a question nobody asked: why is the port in the reply tuple at all? Because after translation every machine behind the NAT has the same address, so the address cannot distinguish two conversations. What is left is the port.

A NAT therefore translates the pair (address, port), which is why the accurate name is PAT — port address translation — or, in vendor literature, NAT overload. Usually nothing changes: if no other flow claims port 9001 toward that destination, the inside host keeps it. The rewrite happens only on a collision, so let us cause one:

What the outside seesWhat identifies a flowConsequence
Many source portsAbout 64,000 per protocolA ceiling on what one public address can carry
No inside addresses, everNothing — they were overwrittenServer logs record the NAT, not the user
A per-flow table entryRouter memoryA cheap router dies of table exhaustion, not bandwidth

Table 8.4 Rows one and three are where real outages come from: one machine opening thousands of short-lived connections can exhaust the port space or the table using almost no bandwidth, and the symptom is connections failing while ping stays perfect. Row two is why a website cannot reliably tell two people behind one NAT apart.

CGNAT: the same trick, applied to you without asking

Not run in this lab, and it cannot be — it needs an ISP. When a provider runs out of public addresses it stops giving you one: your router’s outside interface gets an address from 100.64.0.0/10 and a second, enormous NAT sits upstream, so everything here happens twice. What changes is not speed but capability. You cannot forward a port to anything, whatever your router’s settings page offers, because the carrier NAT drops the packet first. You also share an address with strangers, so their IP-based bans become yours:

8.5 What NAT broke, and the workarounds it caused

NAT saved IPv4 and, in doing so, repealed the assumption every protocol before it was written against: that a host knows its own address, and that the address a packet claims is where it came from. Both failures are visible in one listing:

What brokeWhyWhat it produced
Inbound connectionsNo entry exists until you send firstPort forwarding (below); UPnP IGD, NAT-PMP and PCP to request one
Knowing your own addressThe kernel reports the inside addressSTUN — ask an outside server what it sees
Peer-to-peerBoth peers are inside; neither can be dialledHole punching; TURN relays when it fails; ICE tries both
Addresses in payloadsNAT rewrites headers onlyHelpers such as nf_conntrack_ftp, and passive FTP, which sends no address
Attribution in logsEveryone shares one addressX-Forwarded-For-style headers further up (ch 19)
End-to-end integrityA rewriting middlebox looks like an attackerAn argument for encrypting everything (ch 18)

Table 8.5 The third row is worth a minute. Hole punching works only because of the table in listing 8.3: if both peers transmit outward at roughly the same moment, each NAT records a mapping for the other before the other’s packet arrives, so what would have been an unsolicited inbound packet is instead a reply to something already there. It is a race deliberately entered into, and it is why video calls need a signalling server first.

The first row has a direct fix, and it is the other half of the nat table. DNAT on PREROUTING rewrites the destination of inbound packets, before routing, so the router sends them onward instead of to itself. That is all port forwarding is:

NAT is not a firewall, though it does an impression of one

It is tempting to conclude that NAT protects the machines behind it. It does not intend to. The inbound connection failed because the router had no entry to translate it with, not because a policy said no — the refusal is a lookup missing. Nothing in the nat table has an opinion about whether that connection should be allowed, so once a mapping exists traffic flows unexamined. Chapter 17 writes the rules that do have an opinion, in a separate table.

Checkpoint

Why can a router forward a packet without keeping state, while a NAT cannot?

Because forwarding only reads a field already in the packet: destination in, table lookup, packet out. A router could be rebooted between two packets of one connection and behave identically. A NAT destroys information — the original source address and port are overwritten and exist nowhere else — so reversing the operation on the reply requires having written the original down first, which is what listing 8.3’s two tuples are. It is also why a NAT reboot kills every connection through it while a router reboot merely delays them.

A UDP application works for thirty seconds and then stops receiving replies, every time. Where do you look?

At the NAT’s UDP timeout, which listing 8.3 showed as about 30 seconds against 432,000 for established TCP. UDP gives the router no way to know a conversation ended, so it deletes the mapping after a short silence; return packets are then addressed to a port that maps to nothing and are dropped. The fix is periodic outbound traffic to refresh the entry. The suspiciously round thirty seconds is the tell — a real network fault does not keep time that well.

Two machines behind one NAT both connect out from source port 9001. What does the router do, and what would break if it did nothing?

It keeps 9001 for whichever flow claimed it first and rewrites the other to a free port, exactly as listing 8.4 captured. If it did nothing, both conversations would produce the same reply tuple — same protocol, same public address, same port, same server — and an inbound packet matching it could not be attributed to either machine. The port is not an optimisation; it is the only field left that can tell the flows apart once the source addresses are erased.

Why does FTP need special handling through a NAT when HTTP does not?

Because FTP puts an IP address in its payload and HTTP does not. Listing 8.5 shows the consequence: the header source was rewritten to 203.0.113.1 while the PORT 198,51,100,10,35,41 string arrived untouched, telling the server to connect back to an address that is unreachable and probably belongs to someone else. NAT works on headers and cannot know that bytes further along are an address. The fixes are a helper that parses FTP, or passive mode, in which the client always dials out. The lesson outlives FTP: any protocol carrying its own addressing, SIP included, needs a helper on every middlebox or a redesign.

Your ISP gives your router an address in 100.64.0.0/10. What can you no longer do?

Accept inbound connections at all. That block is RFC 6598 shared address space, so you are behind carrier-grade NAT: your router’s outside address is not public either, and there is a second translation upstream you do not control. A port forward on your own router still works perfectly and still achieves nothing, because the carrier’s NAT has no entry for that port and drops the packet long before it reaches you. Self-hosting and inbound VPN are finished; peer-to-peer falls back to hole punching and then to relays.

Someone says their network is secure because everything is behind NAT. What is wrong with that?

It confuses a missing table entry with a policy. Unsolicited inbound packets fail because the NAT has nothing to translate them into, not because anything decided they should be refused — and the moment a mapping exists, traffic passes with no rule consulted. Mappings get created by outbound traffic from a compromised machine inside, by UPnP requests, and by forwards someone configured and forgot. None of that is auditable, because it is not a policy. NAT also does nothing about traffic between machines on the inside, where lateral movement happens.

If NAT causes this much damage, why did we not just deploy IPv6 instead?

Because NAT worked immediately, for one person, at no cost to anyone else. IPv6 needs your ISP, your router, your operating system, your applications and the server at the far end to all support it before you get any benefit — a coordination problem with nobody able to move first. Buying a NAT router requires only you, and pays off that afternoon. Every year NAT relieved the pressure was another year IPv6 did not become urgent.

The costs were real but paid by people with no say: developers who had to invent STUN, TURN, ICE and hole punching; users who cannot host anything; and the end-to-end model itself, now an aspiration rather than a description. IPv6 was standardised before the crunch became acute, so this was not a failure to see the problem — it was a failure to make the good solution cheaper than the expedient one, which is a much harder kind of failure.

Why is inbound traffic blocked by default, given that no rule says to block it?

It is not blocked; it is undeliverable, which looks identical from outside and is not the same thing. An inbound packet arrives addressed to the router’s public address. The router checks its table for an entry whose reply tuple matches, and for an unsolicited packet there is none, because entries are created by outbound traffic. With no entry there is no inside address to rewrite the destination to, so the packet is handled locally — in listing 8.6, Connection refused. A lookup missed; nothing had an opinion.

The distinction tells you what will change the behaviour. Anything that creates an entry — an outbound packet from a machine inside, a UPnP or PCP request, a DNAT rule, a helper opening a data connection — makes traffic flow, and none consults a security policy, because there is none. That is why chapter 17’s filter table is separate, with its own default policy: to turn an accident that usually blocks inbound traffic into a decision that always does.

Chapter Nine · Part III

Ports and Sockets

Almost everyone is first taught that a port is a numbered door in the side of a machine, and almost every confusion about servers, load and firewalls comes from that picture. A port is not a door and nothing goes through it. A connection is identified by five numbers, only one of which is the server’s port — and seeing that on a real machine ends a dozen unrelated mysteries at once.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Name the five values that identify a connection, and read them out of ss
  • Explain how one server port can hold thousands of connections at once
  • Say why the largest port number is 65535, by pointing at the header
  • Choose a port for a service that the kernel will not take for itself
  • Diagnose “it works on my machine” from one line of ss -tln
  • Say what a Unix domain socket gives you that a TCP socket cannot

9.1 A port is not a door

Here is the picture most people carry: the machine has 65535 numbered doors, a service stands behind one, and clients queue up to walk through. It explains nothing. If a port were a door, two clients could not use it at once, a busy web server would need thousands, and “port 443 is in use” would be a capacity problem rather than a misconfiguration.

What exists instead is the socket: a kernel object with an address at each end. When a packet arrives the kernel must decide which socket it belongs to, and it does so by comparing five values:

( protocol , source IP , source port , destination IP , destination port )

That is the five-tuple, the last link in chapter 1’s dispatch chain. Two connections may share four of the five and still be entirely separate. The server’s port is one number out of five, and the one that never varies.

ElementIn listing 9.1Chosen byVaries?
ProtocolTCPThe applicationRarely (ch 13)
Source address203.0.113.20, .21 on one rowRouting, on the clientYes — one or more per client
Source portA different number every rowThe kernel, automaticallyYes — every connection
Destination address198.51.100.10The client (ch 15)No, for one server
Destination port9101Convention or configurationNo. Never.

Table 9.1 Read the last column. Four values are fixed on a server and one varies per connection, which is why the arithmetic works: a server port holds as many connections as there are distinct client address-and-port pairs, and there are some 281 million million of those. The famous 65535 limits outbound connections from one client to one destination — section 9.3 does that sum — not how many people can talk to your server.

9.2 Sixteen bits, and where they live

Ports are not a property of the machine. They are two fields in a header, and every question about them — how many exist, why 65535 — is answered by looking at the fields.

OffsetBytesFieldValueMeans
0x0906IP protocol66 = TCP. What tells the kernel a port pair follows at all
0x148f 4cSource port366840x8f×256 + 0x4c = 36684
0x1623 8dDestination port91010x238d. The number the server bound
0x183c 05 e8 dfSequence number1007020255Four bytes. Chapter 10

Table 9.2 Generated from the bytes above. The answer to “why 65535?” is in the Bytes column: a port field is two bytes. Sixteen bits hold 65536 values, and 0 is reserved to mean “choose one for me”, so the largest you can bind is 65535 — and there is no room for a bigger one, since the offset of every field after it is fixed everywhere. Note also that nobody chose source port 36684: it fell out of the kernel’s ephemeral range, which is the next section.

The port pair is why NAT can exist

A NAT device (ch 8) rewrites a packet’s source address to its own and — the part that makes it work — rewrites the source port to a value it picked, so it can map that port back to the original host. Nothing else in the packet has room for the mapping, and it is why a NAT box has a hard limit measured in ports rather than hosts: it spends the same 16 bits you do.

9.3 Three ranges, and the one that will bite you

65536 numbers, divided by convention into three ranges. The division is a registry kept by IANA, not a rule the kernel enforces — nothing stops you serving HTTP on 31337. What the kernel does enforce is a permission boundary at 1024, and a range it keeps for itself.

RangeIANA calls itWho is in itWhat it means for you
0–1023System, or well-known22 ssh, 25 smtp, 53 dns, 80 http, 443 httpsBinding one needs a capability, not just a free port
1024–49151User, or registeredDatabases, brokers, anything with a vendorRegistration is a courtesy; collisions are yours
49152–65535Dynamic, or privateNobody. Reserved for automatic allocationNever a service. The client side’s scratch space

Table 9.3 The registry is why /etc/services exists, and why a firewall rule can be written before anyone runs the software. The third row is the one people ignore: those ports are for clients, and a service parked there can lose its port to an outbound connection allocated the same number. Linux, as the next listing shows, does not respect that boundary either.

The sum that decides how many outbound connections you get

That range holds 60999 − 32768 + 1 = 28232 ports. A source port need only be unique within a five-tuple, so that is how many connections one client address can have to a single destination address and port — not in total. Ten thousand to one database is comfortable, thirty thousand is not, and the fix is more addresses rather than a wider range. When a proxy logs EADDRNOTAVAIL, this is the sum it ran out of — and TIME-WAIT sockets (ch 11) still count.

9.4 Listening sockets and connected sockets are different objects

A listening socket has a local address and no peer, and never carries data. Its job is to match an incoming SYN and manufacture a new socket when the handshake completes. A connected socket has both ends filled in — a full five-tuple — and is what the application reads and writes. So the handshake is finished by the kernel, and completed connections queue up until the program calls accept(). If it never does, they sit there, established and unread.

ColumnOn a LISTEN socketOn an ESTAB socket
Local Address:PortWhat was bound; a wildcard is normalOne address of this machine
Peer Address:Port0.0.0.0:* — no peerThe other end. The half that varies
Recv-QConnections awaiting accept()Bytes arrived but unread
Send-QThe backlog given to listen()Bytes sent but unacknowledged (ch 12)
How manyOne per bound addressOne per client, indefinitely many

Table 9.4 The same two columns mean different things in different states. Non-zero Recv-Q on a listening socket means the application is not accepting fast enough — look at the process, not the network. Non-zero Recv-Q on an established socket means it is not reading fast enough: a different bug in the same program. A growing Send-Q means the far end is not acknowledging, which belongs to chapter 12.

9.5 bind(), and the two ways it ruins an afternoon

bind() takes an address and a port, and the address half is the one nobody thinks about. 127.0.0.1 means “connections arriving on loopback”; 0.0.0.0, the wildcard, means “any interface this machine has, including ones added later”. The difference is invisible while you test on the machine the server runs on, and total from anywhere else.

bind() addressss -tln showsReachable fromUse it when
127.0.0.1127.0.0.1:portThis machine, over loopback onlyAn admin port that must never leave the host
0.0.0.00.0.0.0:portEvery address the machine has, now or laterAn ordinary service. The usual choice
A specific addressThat address and portTraffic for that address onlyA multi-homed host answering on one network
::*:portIPv6, and IPv4 too on a default LinuxAnything modern. One socket, both families

Table 9.5 The first two rows are listing 9.5. The habit worth forming is to read the address half of ss -tln first: it settles in a glance a question that otherwise costs an hour of firewall archaeology. A container sharpens it — a process bound to 127.0.0.1 inside one is unreachable even from the host, because the host’s loopback is a different one.

9.6 The socket with no port at all

Everything above assumed the address family AF_INET. There is another, used constantly and noticed rarely: AF_UNIX. The identical API — socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), read(), write() — but the address is a filesystem path, and nothing touches a network stack. Run a database, a container runtime or a system logger on Linux and you have used one.

TCP socketUnix domain socket
AddressIP address + 16-bit portA filesystem path, or a name with no file
How many can existBounded by ports and tuplesBounded by the filesystem
Access controlFirewall rules, by address (ch 17)File permissions, by user
Peer identityAn address, which can be spoofedpid, uid, gid — from the kernel
Reaches another machineYes. That is the pointNo. No packet can carry a path
Cost per messageChecksums, queues, headersA copy between two buffers

Table 9.6 The last two rows are the trade. A Unix socket cannot leave the machine: no field in any IP header can hold /tmp/app.sock, so there is nothing to route on. In exchange it skips the network stack, gets authentication free, and is unreachable by anyone who cannot already read a directory on your disk. Linux also allows an abstract name with no directory entry at all, printed with a leading @: nothing is left behind on a crash, and nothing protects it either.

Checkpoint

A web server has 40,000 connections open. Has it run out of ports?

No, and it is not close. All 40,000 share the single listening port — listing 9.1 shows four doing exactly that. What must be unique is the whole five-tuple, and the varying part is the client’s address and port. The 65535 limit applies to the client side, per destination: one client machine can hold about 28,000 connections to one server address and port. A server failing at 40,000 is short of file descriptors, memory or accept-queue capacity, never ports.

Why is the highest port 65535 rather than 65536?

Because the field is 16 bits, giving 65536 values including zero, and zero is spoken for. Port 0 is the request “allocate me one” — listing 9.3 binds to 0 four times and gets four real ports back. So the usable range is 1 to 65535, and 65536 is not a port that failed a permission check but a number that will not fit the two bytes table 9.2 points at. Nobody can widen the range either: the offset of every following field is fixed everywhere.

Your service works on your laptop and your colleague gets “connection refused”. Where do you look first, and why not the firewall?

At the local address in ss -tln. A firewall usually drops packets, which the client sees as a timeout; an immediate refusal means a machine actively answered that nothing is listening for that tuple — the signature of a server bound to 127.0.0.1, which listing 9.5 reproduces. The confirming test is one command: connect from the server itself to its own external address. If that is refused too, no network device is involved.

What is the difference between a socket in ss -tln and one in ss -tn?

They are different objects with different lifetimes. The listening socket has a local address, no peer, and exists to match incoming SYNs; it never carries application data. Each connected socket has a complete five-tuple and is what the program reads and writes. accept() returns a new connected socket, not the listener, which is why the listener stays free for the next client. Confusing the two produces the belief that a busy server needs many ports.

A restarted service reports Address already in use although nothing is running. What happened?

A socket from the previous process still occupies the port, almost always in TIME-WAIT — listing 9.5 shows exactly that, on a port whose server has exited. TIME-WAIT exists so stray packets cannot reach a new connection reusing the same tuple (ch 11), and lasts a minute or two. SO_REUSEADDR tells the kernel to allow the bind anyway. Killing processes and rebooting treat a problem that was never a process.

Why can a Unix domain socket tell you which user is on the other end when TCP cannot?

Because both ends are processes on the same kernel, so the kernel already knows their credentials and can report them — SO_PEERCRED in listing 9.6, returning a pid, uid and gid the peer never had a chance to claim. Over TCP the only identity in the packet is a source address, chosen by the sender and rewritten in the path (ch 8), so identity must be built on top: certificates and tokens (ch 16). That is a security advantage of a path over a loopback port, not a performance one.

Practice · Ports and Sockets

02Print your ephemeral range from /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_local_port_range.Subtract: how many outbound connections per destination does that allow?Easy

If ports are only 16 bits, why is that not a limit on how big a service can get?

Because what must be unique is the tuple, not the port. Every connection shares your server’s destination address and port and differs in the client’s, so a listening socket is bounded by the number of distinct client endpoints, not by 65535. Listing 9.1 is that in miniature: four established sockets, one listening socket, one port. A million connections on 443 is unremarkable.

The 16-bit limit does bite, but on the client side and per destination. One machine connecting to a single address and port can use each ephemeral port once — about 28,000 on a default Linux, with TIME-WAIT sockets still holding theirs. That is why a loaded proxy is given several source addresses, and why a wider range only postpones it.

When should a service listen on a Unix domain socket instead of a loopback port?

Whenever every client is a process on the same machine, which is more often than people assume: a database serving an application on the same host, an agent reading a local daemon, a container runtime taking commands from a CLI. The API is identical, so the change is usually one configuration line. You gain a service that occupies no port and cannot be port-scanned, access control by file permissions rather than firewall rules, and a server that can ask the kernel for the peer’s uid.

Not when a client might ever be on another machine: no IP packet has a field that can carry a path. The other cost is operational. A socket file is shared state, so a crash can leave a stale one that blocks the next start, and every client needs access to its directory — awkward across users or mount namespaces. Loopback TCP leaves no name behind, and that is what you trade away.

Chapter Ten · Part III

TCP: the Handshake

Everything TCP promises — bytes delivered in order, exactly once, with nothing missing — rests on three packets that carry no data at all. This chapter captures those three packets, decodes every field and every option in them, and then breaks the handshake four different ways, because a handshake that fails tells you more than one that works.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read a three-packet handshake and say what each packet proves to whom
  • Point at the bytes in a SYN that hold the sequence number, the flags and the window
  • Explain why two messages cannot open a connection and three can
  • Say why the initial sequence number is random, and what breaks when it is not
  • Tell the SYN queue from the accept queue, and read both with ss
  • Distinguish a filtered port from a closed one by the shape of the failure

10.1 Three packets, and not one fewer

A TCP connection does not exist on the wire. It exists as a pair of matching data structures, one in each kernel, and the handshake is the procedure that creates both of them and gets them to agree. Nothing is transmitted that a router or a switch treats specially; the three packets below are ordinary IP datagrams with the TCP protocol number (ch 1) and a flag bit set.

What makes them a handshake is what each one proves. Watch for that rather than for the flag names.

#DirectionFlagsCarriesProves
1host-a → host-b[S]host-a’s ISN, its options, its windowNothing yet. It is a request
2host-b → host-a[S.]host-b’s ISN, and an ack of host-a’sTo host-a: host-b exists, is listening, and received host-a’s ISN
3host-a → host-b[.]An ack of host-b’s ISNTo host-b: host-a is real and received host-b’s ISN

Table 10.1 The right-hand column is the whole design. After packet 2 only host-a knows the connection is viable; host-b has sent a number and has no idea whether it arrived. Packet 3 is not politeness, it is the moment host-b learns that its own half of the connection is real — and it is why the handshake costs a full round trip before a single byte of application data can move, a cost that TLS 1.3 (ch 16) and QUIC (ch 18) were both designed to claw back.

In […]BitMeaning
SSYNSynchronise: “this packet carries my initial sequence number”
.ACKThe acknowledgement field is meaningful. Set on every packet after the first
FFINThis end has no more data to send (ch 11)
RRSTAbort. There is no connection here and there never will be
PPSHDeliver what you have to the application now, do not wait for more
UURGUrgent pointer is valid. Effectively dead; treat its use as a red flag
W, ECWR, ECEExplicit congestion notification (ch 12)

Table 10.2 How to read the bracket. [S] is SYN alone, [S.] is SYN together with ACK, [.] is a bare acknowledgement carrying nothing. The dot is easy to miss and it is the most common flag in any capture, because after the handshake every single packet in both directions has ACK set — there is always something to acknowledge.

10.2 Every field in a SYN

The summary line is a rendering, not the packet. Underneath it the TCP header is a fixed 20 bytes followed by a variable-length options block, and the SYN is the one packet where that options block matters, because it is the only chance either end gets to state what it supports.

Here is one SYN with the bytes attached. The IP header takes the first 20 bytes (ch 1); everything from offset 0x0014 onwards is TCP.

TCP offsetIn the dumpBytesFieldValueWhat it does
0x000x001488 42Source port34882Chosen from the ephemeral range by the kernel (ch 9)
0x020x001623 8eDestination port91020x238e is 9102. This is the whole of “which service”
0x040x0018b7 e9 45 a3Sequence number3085518243The ISN. Randomly chosen for this connection — see 10.4
0x080x001c00 00 00 00Acknowledgement0Zero, and ignored: the ACK flag is clear, so this field means nothing
0x0c0x0020a0Data offset10The high nibble of a0, counted in 32-bit words: 10×4 = 40 bytes of TCP header, so 20 bytes of options
0x0d0x002102Flags0x02One bit per flag from table 10.2. 0x02 is SYN and nothing else
0x0e0x0022fa f0Window64240How many bytes host-a can receive right now. Not scaled in a SYN
0x100x002466 81Checksum0x6681Covers the header, the payload and parts of the IP header
0x120x002600 00Urgent pointer0Valid only if URG is set, which it never is
0x140x002802 04 05 b4…Options20 bytesDecoded in table 10.4

Table 10.3 Generated from the bytes in listing 10.2 rather than typed, so it cannot drift from them. Two rows are worth stopping at. Data offset is the same idea as IHL in the IP header: the header is variable length and this field is the only way to find where it ends, so anything that parses TCP and assumes 20 bytes will misread every packet that carries options — which is every packet in this book. And the window here reads 64240 literally; the scaling factor negotiated a few bytes further on does not apply to the packet that negotiates it.

Why the TCP checksum reaches down into the IP header

TCP’s checksum is computed over a pseudo-header that includes the source address, the destination address and the protocol number from the IP header, none of which are part of the TCP segment. The reason is that TCP has no addresses of its own but is absolutely dependent on them: a connection is identified by the four-tuple, and a segment delivered to the right port on the wrong host would otherwise pass every check. Folding the addresses into the checksum makes that undetectable case detectable. It is also the reason a NAT box (ch 8) cannot rewrite an address without recomputing the TCP checksum — layering leaks here, deliberately, and it has been argued about ever since.

10.3 An option is an offer, not an announcement

The 20 bytes of options in listing 10.2 are a list of type–length–value records. A parser that does not recognise a kind can skip it using the length byte and carry on, which is how new options were added to a protocol from 1981 without breaking anything that predates them.

KindLenBytesOptionValueWhat it commits to
2402 04 05 b4Maximum segment size1460The largest segment payload host-a is willing to receive. 1460 = the 1500-byte Ethernet MTU minus 40 bytes of IPv4 and TCP header (ch 14)
4204 02SACK permitted—Says host-a can send selective acknowledgements — “I got bytes 1–1000 and 2001–3000” — so a single lost segment need not stall everything behind it (ch 12)
81008 0a af 3a 6e 92 00 00 00 00Timestamps2939842194 / 0Host-a’s clock, and the echo field — zero here because there is nothing yet to echo. Used for round-trip measurement and for detecting sequence numbers that have wrapped
1—01No-operation—One byte of filler with no meaning. Here it is what makes the options block add up to a whole number of 32-bit words
3303 03 0aWindow scale10Shift every future window field left by 10 bits, i.e. multiply by 1024. Without this the window could never exceed 65535 bytes

Table 10.4 Decoded from the same 20 option bytes printed in listing 10.2, in the order they appear. The No-operation row is the part that surprises people: it carries nothing and means nothing. The data-offset field counts 32-bit words, so the options block must be a whole number of them, and a stack also uses these fillers to line up an option’s multi-byte values — which is why the timestamps in listing 10.3 are preceded by two of them once the other options are gone. That is what all those nops in a real capture are: alignment padding, not a message.

Now the critical part, which the word “negotiation” usually hides: an option in a SYN is a request. It takes effect only if the SYN-ACK contains it too. Either end can veto any option by simply not repeating it, and the veto is silent.

10.4 The number that has to be unguessable

Each end picks a starting point for its own byte numbering. It could pick zero. The reason it does not is worth taking seriously, because it is one of the few places where a protocol field exists purely as a security measure.

Consider what an attacker who can send packets but cannot see the replies is able to do if initial sequence numbers are predictable. They can forge a SYN from a trusted address, guess the sequence number in the SYN-ACK they will never see, and send a plausible third packet — and the server now has an established connection it believes is with someone else. That attack is not hypothetical; it is why the field is randomised, and it is why the randomisation must be per-connection rather than per-boot.

This is why it is three and not two, and not four

Two is not enough: after message two, host-b has sent a sequence number and has no evidence it arrived, so it cannot start numbering data against it and cannot tell a real client from a forged source address. The listing above is precisely that state, and host-b is stuck in it. Four is unnecessary: message three carries host-a’s acknowledgement of host-b’s number, and there is nothing left for host-b to confirm — if message three is lost, host-b simply retransmits message two until it is not. Three is the minimum number of messages in which two independently chosen numbers can each be sent and acknowledged, which is the general shape of the problem and not a fact about TCP.

10.5 The two queues behind listen()

A server that has called listen() but has not yet called accept() will still complete handshakes. The kernel does it, without the application’s involvement, and parks the finished connections until someone asks for one. That means there are two distinct queues, they fill for different reasons, and they fail in different ways.

SYN queueAccept queue
HoldsHalf-open connections — SYN seen, third packet not yetFully established connections waiting for accept()
State in ssSYN-RECVESTAB, but no file descriptor yet
Entered whenA SYN arrivesThe third packet arrives
Left whenThe third packet arrives, or it times outThe application calls accept()
Sized bynet.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlogThe backlog argument to listen(), capped by net.core.somaxconn
Filled byA slow or absent client — or a SYN floodA slow application. The network is fine; the code is not calling accept()
Overflow looks likeSYN-ACK retransmissions, then nothingThe SYN is dropped. The client sees a timeout

Table 10.5 The row that matters operationally is the second-to-last. An accept queue overflows because your program is not accepting fast enough — it is blocked, or single-threaded, or wedged on a lock — and the symptom appears at the client, several machines away, as a connection timeout. The network is blameless and will be blamed anyway.

10.6 The two ways a handshake fails

There are only two, and telling them apart is most of TCP diagnosis. Either something answers the SYN with a refusal, or nothing answers it at all. They are produced by completely different causes, they take completely different amounts of time, and the error your application prints is the fastest way to distinguish them.

You seeOn the wireAlmost always means
Connection refused, instantlySYN, then [R.]You reached the host. Nothing is bound to that port — wrong port, or the process is down (ch 9)
Connection timed out, after seconds or minutesSYN, SYN, SYN, silenceA firewall dropping rather than rejecting (ch 17), a wrong address, a dead host, or a full accept queue
No route to hostNo TCP at allLocal routing or ARP failed before a packet left (ch 3, ch 6)
Handshake completes, then nothingS, S., ., then silenceTCP is fine. The application above it is not — it accepted and then hung
[R.] arriving after the handshakeS, S., ., R.Something is deliberately tearing the connection down — a middlebox, or a server that rejected what it read (ch 11)

Table 10.6 The first two rows are the ones to internalise, because the difference between reject and drop is a firewall policy decision that someone made on purpose. Rejecting is friendlier and faster to diagnose; dropping hides whether the host exists at all, at the cost of turning every misconfiguration into a multi-minute timeout. When a deployment “hangs” and a rollback “fixes” it, this table’s second row is the first hypothesis worth testing.

Checkpoint

Why can a connection not be opened with two packets?

Because after two packets only one end knows the connection is real. Host-a has sent its sequence number and seen it acknowledged, so host-a is satisfied; host-b has sent its own number into the dark. If host-b started sending data at that point it would be numbering it against a baseline the other end may never have received, and it would have no evidence that the source address in the SYN was genuine rather than forged. Listing 10.4 shows exactly that state: host-b sitting in SYN-RECV, replaying its SYN-ACK, holding memory for a connection it cannot use. The third packet is what ends that.

tcpdump shows ack 1. Has one byte been transferred?

No. That 1 is relative, and it is relative to an initial sequence number that tcpdump subtracted for you because it saw the SYN. The absolute value is the peer’s ISN plus one, as listing 10.1 shows with -S. The reason it is +1 rather than +0 is that the SYN flag itself consumes one sequence number despite carrying no data — otherwise there would be no way to acknowledge it, and the whole handshake would have nothing to confirm. FIN consumes one for the same reason (ch 11).

A capture shows win 501 on an established connection. How many bytes can the sender push?

Unknowable from that line alone, and probably far more than 501. If window scaling was agreed during the handshake, the real window is 501 shifted left by the factor in the SYN — with the shift of 10 seen in listing 10.3, just over half a million bytes. The scaling factor appears only in the SYN and SYN-ACK, so a capture that starts after the handshake cannot resolve the window at all. That is a concrete reason to start captures before the connection, not after, and a concrete reason to check the kernel’s own view with ss -ti alongside.

Your service is healthy, its port is open, and clients report connection timeouts. Where do you look?

At the accept queue before the network. A timeout with no RST means SYNs are being discarded, and one of the ordinary causes is an application that is not calling accept() fast enough — the kernel completes handshakes, fills the queue to backlog+1, and then silently drops further SYNs, which on the wire is identical to a firewall drop. ss -ltn on the server shows the queue depth in Recv-Q and the backlog in Send-Q, and nstat shows TcpExtListenOverflows climbing. Both are server-side facts that no amount of client-side debugging will surface.

Why must the initial sequence number be random per connection rather than per boot?

Because the threat is an attacker who can send packets but cannot see replies. If they can predict the sequence number a server will choose, they can forge a SYN from a trusted address, never see the SYN-ACK, and still send a correct-looking third packet — completing a handshake on behalf of a host that never spoke. A per-boot random base does not help: they observe one connection legitimately, learn the base, and predict every subsequent one. The number has to be unpredictable for this four-tuple at this moment, which is why kernels derive it from a secret keyed hash of the four-tuple plus a clock, as the six unrelated values in listing 10.4 show.

You configure a large receive buffer on a server and throughput does not improve. What might the handshake tell you?

Check whether window scaling was actually agreed. It is offered in the SYN and confirmed in the SYN-ACK, and if either end omits it — a sysctl, an old stack, or a middlebox that strips options it does not recognise — the window field caps at 65535 no matter how much memory you allocated. Listing 10.3 shows one end declining and the other end silently going along with it, which is the hard part: nothing is logged and nothing fails, throughput is just quietly limited to a window per round trip. On a link with any real latency that ceiling is the whole story (ch 12).

Why does a RST arrive instantly when a timeout takes minutes, if both are “failures”?

Because they are produced by different machines. A RST is generated by the destination host itself: the SYN arrived, the kernel looked for a socket bound to that port, found none, and answered immediately. The cost is one round trip and the answer is definitive — the host exists, and it does not want this connection. A timeout is the absence of an answer, and absence cannot be detected, only waited out. The sending kernel has no way to distinguish a dropped SYN from a slow path, so it retransmits on a schedule and only declares failure when its retry budget is exhausted.

That asymmetry is why the two errors mean such different things in an incident. Connection refused localises the problem precisely: routing worked, the host is up, the process is not. Connection timed out localises nothing — it is equally consistent with a typo in an address, a firewall rule, a dead host, a broken return path, and a server whose accept queue is full. It is also expensive: as listing 10.6 shows, the kernel default holds the caller for over two minutes, which is long enough to exhaust a thread pool upstream and turn one unreachable dependency into a whole-service outage.

If the kernel completes handshakes without the application, what is accept() actually for?

It hands an already-finished connection to the program. By the time accept() returns, the three packets are long gone: the kernel completed the handshake on its own, created the connection state, and queued it. accept() allocates a file descriptor for it and removes it from the queue. This split is deliberate — it lets the kernel absorb bursts without the application being scheduled, which is why a server can survive a spike of simultaneous clients that arrive faster than it can loop.

The consequence is that “the connection succeeded” and “the server is processing my request” are entirely separate events, and a client cannot distinguish them. A completely wedged application still completes handshakes until its backlog fills, so monitoring that only checks whether the port accepts connections will report a hung service as healthy. Listing 10.5 is that failure in miniature: three clients believing they are connected to a server that has never once called accept(). The useful signals are the queue depth on the LISTEN row and the overflow counter, not connectivity.

Chapter Eleven · Part III

TCP: Closing, and the State Machine

Opening a connection is the part everyone can draw. Closing it is the part that fills the ticket queue: four segments rather than three, either end may start it, one end is left holding a timer for a minute afterwards, and the most common TCP fault in production is a state that appears only when your own code forgets to call close().

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Read a four-way close and name the state each end is in after every segment
  • Explain what a FIN promises, and use a half-close on purpose
  • Observe every TCP state with ss, including the ones that last microseconds
  • Say what TIME-WAIT protects against and why 2×MSL is the number
  • Diagnose client-side port exhaustion and know why the fix belongs on the server
  • Read a CLOSE-WAIT count as a bug report about your own application

11.1 Four segments, not three

A TCP connection is not one channel. It is two independent byte streams glued together by a single four-tuple, one each way, and they are shut down separately. That is why a close takes four segments where the handshake (ch 10) takes three. In the handshake the middle segment can carry the server’s SYN and its acknowledgement of the client’s, because the server learns both facts at once. A close cannot: host-a announcing that it has nothing more to send says nothing about whether host-b has finished, and only host-b’s application knows that.

SegmentSent bySender then inReceiver then in
FINwhoever closes firstFIN-WAIT-1CLOSE-WAIT
ACKthe other end’s kernel, at onceCLOSE-WAITFIN-WAIT-2
FINthe other end’s applicationLAST-ACKTIME-WAIT
ACKthe first closer’s kernelTIME-WAIT, 2×MSLCLOSED — gone

Table 11.1 Lines 6 to 9 of listing 11.1. The second row is sent by the kernel instantly; the third only when the peer’s application gets round to calling close(), which may be never — that gap is section 11.5. The fourth is not symmetric: the side that closed first pays for a minute in TIME-WAIT while the side that answered is already gone. Who closes first is a design decision, not an accident.

The state names are backwards from how they feel

FIN-WAIT sounds like “waiting to send a FIN”, and CLOSE-WAIT like “waiting for the network to close this”. Both readings are wrong and both cost hours. FIN-WAIT-1 means I sent my FIN and am waiting for it to be acknowledged; FIN-WAIT-2, it was acknowledged and I am waiting for the peer’s FIN; CLOSE-WAIT, the peer has finished and I am waiting for my own application to call close(). Read each name as what this end is waiting for.

11.2 Half-close, and what a FIN really promises

A FIN is not “goodbye”. It promises one thing about one direction: “I will send no more bytes.” It does not oblige the peer to stop sending and it does not stop you reading — the second capture in listing 11.1 is the proof, where host-a sent a FIN and then read 21 bytes out of the same socket.

That is what shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR) is for, and why it is a separate call from close(). close() destroys the descriptor and so necessarily ends both directions; shutdown(SHUT_WR) touches only the outgoing stream and leaves the descriptor open and readable. The pattern it enables is old and still everywhere: “here is my whole request — the end of it is the FIN”, which lets a server read to end-of-file with no length header and no delimiter at all.

Used carelessly it leaves a socket in FIN-WAIT-2 indefinitely, and listing 11.4 shows the subtlety directly: a socket half-closed with shutdown() whose descriptor is still open has no timer at all and waits for the peer’s FIN for ever, while one orphaned by close() gets the tcp_fin_timeout countdown. The kernel will put a deadline on an abandoned connection; it will not second-guess one your process still holds a descriptor for.

CallSends a FIN?Still readable?Still writable?Descriptor
shutdown(fd, SHUT_WR)YesYesNoStill yours
shutdown(fd, SHUT_RD)No — local onlyNoYesStill yours
close(fd)Yes, if this was the last referenceNoNoReleased
close() with SO_LINGER 0No — sends RSTNoNoReleased

Table 11.2 Only the first row is a half-close. SHUT_RD surprises people: it puts nothing on the wire, because TCP has no way to say “stop sending to me” — it only makes local reads return end-of-file. The last row is section 11.6, and the only way to end a connection without a FIN.

11.3 Eleven states, and how to see all of them

TCP is specified as a state machine and, unusually, that is exactly how it is implemented: every socket in your kernel sits in one named state and ss -tan prints it. There are eleven, and each one is an accusation about something different.

StateWaiting forNormal lifetimeIf it is stuck, suspect
LISTENIncoming SYNsThe life of the process—
SYN-SENTThe SYN-ACKOne round tripA dropped SYN: firewall, wrong address, dead host (ch 17)
SYN-RECVThe final ACKOne round tripClients not completing: a SYN flood, or a one-way path
ESTABLISHEDData, or a closeAs long as you like—
FIN-WAIT-1Our FIN to be acknowledgedOne round tripThe peer or the path vanished mid-close
FIN-WAIT-2Their FINUntil their app closesTheir application never closed. Their bug, seen from here
CLOSINGOur FIN to be acknowledgedRare; one round tripBoth ends closed at the same instant
CLOSE-WAITOur own close()UnboundedUs. This machine, this process (11.5)
LAST-ACKOur FIN to be acknowledgedOne round tripThe peer stopped listening mid-close
TIME-WAITNothing. A timer60 s on LinuxNormal. Only a problem if local ports run out (11.4)
CLOSED—Not a socket at allYou will never see this in ss

Table 11.3 Read the last column downwards and it is a diagnosis. Almost every row accuses the network or the peer; exactly one — CLOSE-WAIT — accuses the machine you are standing on, and that is the one people misread. Note too that CLOSED is not something ss can show you: a closed connection is not a socket in a state, it is the absence of a socket. Chapter 21 starts a diagnosis from this column.

Two states last long enough to sample easily. Here is the close from listing 11.1 again, watched from both ends by a loop that prints only when something changes:

The remaining states are not exotic; they are just brief. Below, three connections are broken in three different ways: host-a throws away the SYN-ACK on port 9111, goes deaf on port 9112 the instant the connection is up, and hides its FIN from host-b on port 9113 so that host-b closes as though it had never been asked to.

11.4 TIME-WAIT: not a leak, and not your enemy

The end that closes first does not get to leave. It sits in TIME-WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime — the longest a segment is assumed able to survive in the network — for two reasons, both about correctness rather than tidiness. First, the final ACK might be lost, in which case the peer retransmits its FIN and something must be there to acknowledge it again, or the peer’s close fails with a reset instead of completing. Second, an old segment might still be wandering: the four-tuple is about to become reusable, and a delayed duplicate arriving inside a new connection with sequence numbers that fitted the new window would be accepted as data. Waiting 2×MSL guarantees the old connection’s stragglers have expired — one MSL for one to arrive, one more for anything it provokes.

The original specification suggests an MSL of two minutes, making TIME-WAIT four. Linux uses 60 seconds, a constant compiled into the kernel with no sysctl attached — which is worth demonstrating, because the most repeated piece of TCP advice on the internet, lower tcp_fin_timeout to shorten TIME-WAIT, is simply false:

What people sayWhat is true
“TIME-WAIT is a socket leak”It is a bounded timer. Each one disappears 60 s after it appeared, with no action by anyone
“Thousands of them means something is wrong”Thousands is what a busy client looks like. At 500 connections a second with a 60 s timer, 30,000 is the steady state
“Lower tcp_fin_timeout to fix it”That sysctl governs FIN-WAIT-2 and nothing else, as listing 11.4 shows on one screen
“Turn on tcp_tw_recycle”It silently broke clients behind NAT and Linux removed it — the ls above shows there is no such file to write to
“The server is running out of ports”A server listens on one port. The client spends a local port per connection, and the client hits the wall
“SO_REUSEADDR makes TIME-WAIT go away”It lets a listener bind() a port that has TIME-WAIT sockets on it. They are untouched; only the bind check is relaxed

Table 11.4 The last two rows cost the most time. If a restarted service cannot bind its own port you want SO_REUSEADDR — a one-line fix, and the reason every server in this chapter sets it. If a client cannot make connections the sysctls are a distraction; the real levers are to reuse connections rather than open new ones (ch 18), to widen ip_local_port_range, to spread across more destinations so the four-tuple differs, or to have the server close first and move the cost to the side with room for it (ch 19).

11.5 CLOSE-WAIT means your application did not call close()

Ten of the eleven states are left when a packet arrives or a timer expires. CLOSE-WAIT is left by a line of your code. The peer has sent its FIN, your kernel has already acknowledged it automatically, and the connection waits — with no timeout, no retransmission and no complaint — for the application to call close(). If it never does, the socket stays until the process exits. That makes a rising CLOSE-WAIT count the most specific diagnostic in this chapter: not a network problem, not the peer’s problem, and not tunable. A leaked file descriptor with a name.

Why the count only ever goes up

A leaked ESTABLISHED socket looks like a busy server, so nobody notices. A leaked CLOSE-WAIT socket is unmistakable, because a healthy server passes through that state in microseconds and has no reason to accumulate any. Two things follow. The fix is never a sysctl; it is a missing close(), usually on an error path, usually in code that closes correctly when nothing goes wrong — typically a connection object escaping its scope into a list, a cache or a retry queue, exactly as kept does above. And it will eventually take the process down: each socket is a file descriptor, and at the descriptor limit accept() starts failing, so the service stops taking work while looking entirely healthy from outside.

11.6 RST: the alternative to all of the above

There is also the other kind of ending. A reset is one segment with the RST flag set, meaning “this connection does not exist and will not be discussed”. It is not acknowledged, not retransmitted, carries no data, and destroys the connection at both ends immediately, discarding anything still queued. There is no state for it in table 11.3 because there is nothing to wait for. It is also never packet loss — loss is what TCP silently retransmits around. A reset is a decision, taken by software at one end or by a middlebox between, and three quite different situations produce one:

CauseThe peer seesIs it a bug?
SYN to a port with no listenerECONNREFUSED from connect()No — that is how a refusal is supposed to look
Any segment for a connection the receiver has no record ofECONNRESETNo, but one end forgot: a reboot, or a NAT or firewall state table expiring (ch 8, ch 17)
close() with unread data in the receive queueECONNRESET on the next readUsually — the application abandoned a request half-read
close() with SO_LINGER set to 0ECONNRESETOnly if you meant it. It throws away unsent data
Writing to a socket the peer already resetEPIPE, or SIGPIPENo — it is the second symptom of the first reset

Table 11.5 The second row is the one to remember at three in the morning, because it is the only one that is nobody’s code’s fault. A long-idle connection through a NAT device or a stateful firewall can be forgotten in the middle of the path while both ends still believe in it; the next segment either vanishes or draws a reset from equipment with no idea what the connection is. That is the real argument for TCP keepalive and for application heart-beats. Read the whole table as a list of suspects: when ECONNRESET appears in a log the question is never “is the network bad?” but “who sent the RST, and which of these reasons did they have?” — and a capture answers that in one line (ch 20).

Checkpoint

Why does a close take four segments when the handshake takes three?

Because the connection is two independent byte streams, each shut down separately, so there are two FINs and two ACKs. The handshake gets away with three because the server piggybacks its SYN on the ACK of the client’s — it learns both facts at one instant. A close cannot: when one end says it has finished sending, the other’s application decides when to emit the second FIN, and listing 11.1 shows that decision as a half-second gap which is a sleep() in the server, not the network. When the peer does close immediately the ACK and the second FIN merge and a close takes three segments — an optimisation, not the rule.

A colleague says your server is leaking, because ss shows 18,000 sockets in TIME-WAIT. What do you check first?

Whether that machine is the one making connections or the one receiving them, because TIME-WAIT only ever appears on the side that closed first. On an outbound machine — a gateway, a job runner, a proxy dialling upstreams — 18,000 is simply what busy looks like: 300 new connections a second with a 60-second timer gives exactly that as a steady state. The number is not a symptom; the symptom would be connect() failing with EADDRNOTAVAIL, and without that you have found a statistic. It is also not a leak in any sense, since every one of those sockets destroys itself 60 seconds after it appeared, whatever anybody does.

Why does lowering tcp_fin_timeout not shorten TIME-WAIT on Linux?

They are different states with different timers. tcp_fin_timeout bounds how long an orphaned socket sits in FIN-WAIT-2 waiting for a peer that may never close — it protects you from someone else’s bug. TIME-WAIT is 2×MSL, and on Linux that is a kernel constant with no sysctl attached. Listing 11.4 puts both on one screen under tcp_fin_timeout=8: one counts down from under eight seconds, the other from 59. The advice survives because the two states look alike in ss, which unhelpfully labels both timers timewait.

Your service has 4,000 sockets in CLOSE-WAIT and it is climbing. Where is the bug?

In your code, on this machine. CLOSE-WAIT means the peer sent a FIN, your kernel acknowledged it automatically, and the socket is waiting for your application to call close() — a wait with no timeout and no retry. Nothing the peer does and nothing in /proc will clear them. Look for a connection object escaping into a list, a cache or a retry queue, or an error path that returns before closing; it is nearly always code that closes correctly when everything works. The urgency is real, because each one is a file descriptor: at the process limit accept() begins to fail and the service stops taking work while every health check still passes.

What is the difference between shutdown(SHUT_WR) and close() on the wire?

On the wire, for a socket with one reference, nothing — both send a FIN. The difference is local and large. close() releases the descriptor, so you can never read the reply, and the socket becomes an orphan the kernel reaps when tcp_fin_timeout expires. shutdown(SHUT_WR) ends only the outgoing direction and leaves the descriptor open and readable, which is what makes request-until-EOF protocols possible — and because your process still holds it, the kernel attaches no timer at all, so a half-closed socket whose peer never closes waits for ever. Listing 11.4 shows both: two sockets in FIN-WAIT-2, one with a countdown and one without.

When would you deliberately send an RST instead of closing properly?

Rarely, and only when unsent data genuinely does not matter: a proxy tearing down a connection whose backend just died, a server shedding load under attack, a test harness that wants a connection to vanish leaving no state on either side. What makes it tempting is that SO_LINGER zero also skips TIME-WAIT, which looks like a cure for port exhaustion — and that is exactly where it turns dangerous, because you have removed the protection of section 11.4 to solve a problem better fixed by reusing connections or by making the server close first. You have also discarded whatever was still queued, so the peer may lose a response it had already been sent.

  • RFC 1337 — TIME-WAIT Assassination Hazards in TCPIETF

Practice · TCP: Closing, and the State Machine

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Capture a close of your own with tcpdump -ttt and count the segments.Four, unless the two middle ones merged. Say which happened.Easy
02Run ss -tan in a loop while you open and close one connection.watch -n0.1 works, or the loop from listing 11.2.Easy
03Find a socket in TIME-WAIT on a machine you use and read its timer with ss -tano.Predict the value ten seconds later, then check.Easy
04Count sockets by state: ss -tan state all | awk 'NR>1{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c.Do it on a busy machine. The shape tells you what the machine is.Easy
05Write a server that accepts and never closes, connect to it, watch CLOSE-WAIT appear.Then add the close() and watch it stop happening.Medium
06Reproduce the port exhaustion in listing 11.4 with a narrow ip_local_port_range.Twenty ports is enough. Note the exact errno.Medium
