08Force a socket into CLOSING, and explain to someone else how you did it.Both FINs must cross. Listing 11.3 hides one of them to arrange it.Hard
If TIME-WAIT is harmless, why does so much tuning advice exist about it?

Because the visible symptom and the real cause sit on different machines, and the number is enormous and easy to find. Somebody runs ss on a busy client, sees tens of thousands of sockets in a state whose name sounds like waiting, and reaches for a sysctl. The genuine failure — connect() returning EADDRNOTAVAIL because every local port is in TIME-WAIT for the same destination — is real but rare, and it is a four-tuple problem rather than a socket-count problem: 60,000 of them spread over many destinations exhaust nothing.

There is history too. tcp_tw_recycle did once shorten the state, appeared to work, and quietly broke every client behind a NAT device by relying on per-source timestamps that several clients could not share. Linux removed it, as the ls in listing 11.4 shows; the advice outlived the option. The durable fixes are all above the sysctl layer: reuse connections instead of creating them, spread over more destination addresses, widen the port range if you truly need to, and where you control the protocol, have the server close first — listing 11.4 changes nothing else and turns twenty connections into a hundred and twenty.

Why can TCP not close a connection in two segments — one FIN each?

Because a FIN is data in the sense that matters: it occupies a sequence number and must be delivered reliably, so it must be acknowledged. Listing 11.1 shows it exactly — a ten-byte request occupies seq 1:11, and the FIN sent at seq 11 comes back as ack 12. Without that acknowledgement a sender could never know the peer had heard that the stream ended, and a stream that ends without the reader knowing is a truncated file, not a closed connection.

What TCP can do is carry the acknowledgement of one FIN in the same segment as the other FIN, and it often does: when the peer’s application closes immediately on reading end-of-file the two merge and the close takes three segments. Listing 11.1 deliberately prevents that with a sleep(0.5), which is why the delayed acknowledgement goes out alone about 40 ms after the client’s FIN and the server’s FIN follows half a second later. It is the same piggybacking that makes the handshake three segments rather than four — and a reason counting packets is a poor way to identify what you are looking at. Read the flags.

Chapter Twelve · Part III

TCP Under Load

A connection that opens instantly can still be slow, and the reason is almost never the one people reach for. Bandwidth is the least common cause. This chapter is about the three that actually matter — the window, the round trip, and loss — and about ss -ti, which reports all three from a live socket and which almost nobody uses.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Explain why a fast link can carry a slow transfer
  • Calculate a bandwidth-delay product and say what window it demands
  • Read cwnd, ssthresh and retrans from a live socket
  • Describe what one lost segment costs, and why
  • Tell a loss problem from a latency problem from an application problem
  • Say which congestion control your machine is running, and what else it could
What this chapter could and could not induce

Two things are worth stating before any number appears. First, the lab’s “wire’ is a memory copy between namespaces, so its round trip is measured in microseconds and its bandwidth in gigabits — nothing like a real link. Every latency figure below is therefore arithmetic, worked from realistic numbers, and is labelled as such. Second, the usual tool for inducing delay and loss, tc netem, is not installed on the machine this book was built on, so it is not used anywhere here. Loss is induced instead with an iptables rule that discards a fixed proportion of arriving segments, which is real loss by a different mechanism, and every listing that uses it says so.

12.1 Four things that make a transfer slow

CauseWhat it looks likeWhat proves itFix
BandwidthThroughput sits at a hard ceilingThe ceiling is the same at any hourBuy more, or send less
LatencySmall transfers dominate; throughput scales with windowRTT is high but loss is zeroLarger window; move closer; fewer round trips
LossThroughput collapses far below the ceiling and is erraticretrans is non-zeroFind the dropping device
The applicationThe socket is idle; the network is fineapp_limited, or Send-Q stays at zeroFix the program

Table 12.1 The last row is the most common and the least suspected. If a socket is app_limited — a real flag ss will print — the kernel is saying it had nothing to send: the program is the bottleneck, and no amount of network tuning will help. Rows two and three are the ones this chapter can demonstrate.

12.2 The window, and why distance costs throughput

A sender may have many segments outstanding — sent but not yet acknowledged. The limit is the smaller of two windows: the receive window the far end advertises, and the congestion window the sender maintains for itself. Once that many bytes are in flight, the sender stops and waits for an acknowledgement.

That single rule sets a ceiling that has nothing to do with the speed of the link:

maximum throughput = window ÷ round-trip time

The quantity window × RTT is the bandwidth-delay product: how many bytes must be in flight to keep a pipe of a given speed and length full. Work it for a realistic link and the consequence is stark:

Round tripRough exampleThroughput with a 64 KB window
0.5 msSame datacentre~1000 Mbit/s
10 msSame country~52 Mbit/s
40 msAcross a continent~13 Mbit/s
150 msIntercontinental, or satellite~3.5 Mbit/s
600 msGeostationary satellite round trip~0.9 Mbit/s

Table 12.2 Computed from the formula above, not measured. This table is the answer to “we bought a gigabit link and the transfer still takes an hour”: with a fixed window, throughput falls linearly with distance, and no amount of bandwidth changes it. The fix is a bigger window — or fewer round trips, which is what HTTP/2 multiplexing and TLS 1.3’s single round trip are really buying (ch 16, ch 18).

12.3 A transfer with nothing wrong, watched from inside

12.4 One in seven segments dropped, and what it costs

Now the same transfer, over a path that loses fifteen per cent of the segments arriving at the receiver. The loss is imposed by an iptables rule on host-a rather than by tc, which is not installed here; the effect on the sender is identical, because the sender cannot tell why a segment failed to arrive.

Why loss is so much more expensive than it looks

Losing one segment in seven does not cost one seventh. It costs almost everything, for three compounding reasons. The window halves on every loss event, and then grows back slowly — so the sender spends most of its time far below the rate the path could carry. Ordered delivery stalls: the receiving application gets nothing after the gap until the missing segment is retransmitted and arrives, even though later segments are sitting in the receive buffer, which is head-of-line blocking and the subject of chapter 18. And a retransmission is a whole round trip, so on a 40 ms path each loss adds at least 40 ms of dead time. This is why “only two per cent packet loss” is never a reassuring sentence.

12.5 ss -ti as the first command

Almost every question in this chapter is answered by one command against a live socket. It is worth learning the six fields that matter and ignoring the rest.

FieldMeansWhat a bad value tells you
rtt:a/bSmoothed round trip / variance, msHigh a is distance. High b is an unstable path
cwndCongestion window, in segmentsSmall and staying small means loss, not bandwidth
ssthreshSlow-start thresholdPresent at all means this connection has lost something
retrans:a/bRetransmitting now / total everAny sustained value is a path fault, not tuning
unackedSegments in flightPinned at cwnd means window-limited
app_limitedThe kernel had nothing to sendPresent means the program is the bottleneck

Table 12.3 The last row ends more arguments than the rest combined. If app_limited appears, the network was never the constraint: the sender was waiting on the application. Note also that ssthresh is diagnostic by its mere presence — a connection that has never experienced congestion never sets one, so seeing it at all tells you loss has occurred, before you read a single number.

Checkpoint

A gigabit link between two continents delivers 3 Mbit/s. Nothing is lost. Why?

The window, almost certainly. With a 150 ms round trip and a fixed 64 KB window, throughput is capped at about 3.5 Mbit/s no matter how fast the link is — the sender fills the window, stops, and waits a seventh of a second for permission to continue. The fix is window scaling (ch 10) and letting the kernel grow the buffers, not more bandwidth. Check first with ss -ti: if unacked is pinned at cwnd and there are no retransmissions, it is window-limited.

ss -ti shows ssthresh on a connection you thought was healthy. What does that alone tell you?

That it has lost at least one segment. A slow-start threshold does not exist until a congestion event sets one, so its mere presence is a record that something was dropped, even if retrans currently reads zero because the loss was some time ago. It is the cheapest possible check for “has this path ever misbehaved”, and it costs nothing to look.

Why does two per cent packet loss cost far more than two per cent of throughput?

Three effects compound. The congestion window halves on every loss and recovers slowly, so the sender spends most of its time below the rate the path would carry. The receiving application stalls at the gap until the retransmission arrives, even though later data is already in the buffer. And each retransmission costs a full round trip. On a long path, a few per cent loss can remove most of the achievable throughput — which is why loss and latency together are so much worse than either alone.

Your monitoring shows the socket is fine but users say the page is slow. Where do you look?

At app_limited and lastsnd. If the kernel reports it had nothing to send, the network is idle and waiting for your program — a slow query, a lock, a blocking call. Listing 12.5 is exactly that state, and every network metric in it looks perfect. The related trap is measuring throughput on a connection the application never fills: you will measure your own code and conclude the network is fast.

Would switching to BBR fix a link that loses two per cent of packets?

Possibly, and it is the one case where the choice of algorithm genuinely matters. CUBIC and Reno treat any loss as a congestion signal and back off, which is wrong on links that lose packets for reasons unrelated to congestion — Wi-Fi interference, mobile handovers, a marginal cable. BBR models the path’s bandwidth and round trip instead and is far less disturbed by such loss. It is not a general-purpose “faster” setting, though: on a genuinely congested path it can be more aggressive towards competing flows, and it is a change to make with measurement, not by default.

Why is cwnd reported in segments rather than bytes?

Because congestion control counts packets, not bytes — the thing a queue overflows on is a packet, and the algorithms in RFC 5681 are defined in terms of segments. To convert, multiply by mss, which ss prints alongside it. A cwnd of 10 with an mss of 1448 is about 14 KB in flight — which is the standard initial window, and explains why the first few round trips of any connection are slow regardless of the link.

Why does the lab not use tc netem like every other tutorial?

Because tc is not installed on the machine this book was built on, and this book does not print a command it did not run. Rather than fabricate a plausible netem transcript, chapter 12 induces real loss a different way — an iptables rule that discards a fixed proportion of arriving segments — and says so in every listing that uses it. The sender cannot tell the difference: a segment that was dropped by a queue and a segment that was dropped by a filter are equally absent. What the lab genuinely cannot produce is realistic delay, so every latency figure in the chapter is arithmetic and labelled as such.

Is packet loss ever normal?

Yes, and expecting zero is the mistake. TCP has no other way to discover the capacity of a path: it increases its sending rate until something drops, then backs off. On a congested link, loss is the feedback signal, and a small steady rate of it is the system working as designed. What is not normal is loss that does not vary with load — that points at a fault rather than at congestion: a failing cable, a saturated wireless channel, a policer discarding traffic at a fixed rate, or a firewall dropping what it cannot keep state for. The distinction is testable: congestion loss falls when you send less, and a fault does not.

Chapter Thirteen · Part III

UDP

After three chapters on the machinery TCP builds — handshakes, sequence numbers, state, windows, retransmission — it is worth seeing what the alternative costs. UDP is eight bytes of header and no promises at all. That sounds like a toy, and it carries DNS, video, games, and the protocol your browser most likely used to fetch this page.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • State exactly what UDP provides and what it does not
  • Read a UDP header and account for every one of its eight bytes
  • Explain why a UDP exchange has no handshake and what that saves
  • Say what happens when nothing is listening, and why the sender may not find out
  • Choose between TCP and UDP for a given problem, with a reason
  • Explain why UDP amplification attacks are possible

13.1 Eight bytes, and nothing else

FieldBytesNotes
Source port2May be zero, meaning “no reply expected”
Destination port2The only demultiplexing this protocol does
Length2Header plus data. Redundant with IP’s length, and kept anyway
Checksum2Optional in IPv4, mandatory in IPv6

Table 13.1 That is the whole protocol. Compare it with TCP’s twenty-byte minimum header from chapter 10, which additionally carries sequence and acknowledgement numbers, a data offset, nine flag bits, a window, an urgent pointer and usually forty bytes of options. UDP has no sequence number, so it cannot detect loss or reordering; no acknowledgement, so it cannot retransmit; no window, so it cannot do flow control; and no flags, because there is no connection to open or close.

13.2 What you give up, stated plainly

TCP gives youUDP gives youSo the application must
Delivery, eventuallyNothingRetry, or not care
Bytes in the order sentWhatever order they arriveNumber its own messages, or not care
No duplicatesPossible duplicatesBe idempotent, or detect them
Flow controlNonePace itself, or overwhelm the receiver
Congestion controlNoneBack off voluntarily — or be a bad citizen
A byte streamMessage boundaries preservedNothing — this one is a gain

Table 13.2 The last row is the one people forget, and it is a genuine advantage. TCP is a stream: send two 100-byte writes and the receiver may get one 200-byte read, or 60 then 140, and must frame the messages itself. Every text-based protocol carries length prefixes or delimiters for this reason. UDP preserves the boundary — one sendto, one recvfrom, same size. Row five is the dangerous one: a UDP sender that does not implement backoff will keep transmitting into a congested network that TCP flows are politely retreating from, taking capacity from them.

“Unreliable” does not mean unlikely to arrive

The word causes real confusion. UDP datagrams on a healthy network arrive essentially as often as TCP segments do — they travel over the same links and queue in the same buffers. Unreliable is a statement about guarantees, not probability: UDP will not tell you whether a datagram arrived, and will not resend it if it did not. On a good path that difference is invisible. On a bad one it is total, and which of those you are on is not something you get to know in advance.

13.3 Nothing listening, and the error nobody sees

SituationTCPUDP, unconnected socketUDP, connected socket
Nothing listeningRST, refused at onceSilence until your timeoutRefused at once
Firewall DROPTimeoutTimeoutTimeout
Host downTimeoutTimeoutTimeout
WorkingHandshake, then dataReply arrivesReply arrives

Table 13.3 Row one is the only one that distinguishes anything, and it is why connect()ing a UDP socket is worth doing even though it sends no packets. It also explains a common diagnostic frustration: with UDP, “nothing listening” and “blocked by a firewall” look identical from the client unless you take that step, which is why nc -zu is far less informative than nc -z (ch 21).

13.4 Who uses it, and why they are right to

ProtocolWhy not TCP
DNS (ch 15)One small question, one small answer. A handshake would triple the cost, and a lost query is simply asked again
QUIC / HTTP 3 (ch 18)It needs its own transport semantics, and UDP is the only way to deploy one through equipment that will not pass a new IP protocol
Video and voiceA retransmitted frame arrives after the moment it was for. Late data is worse than no data
GamesPosition updates supersede each other. Resending a stale one is worse than useless
Syslog, metrics, tracesHigh volume, individually disposable, and must never block the application that emits them
DHCPThe client has no address yet, so it cannot make a connection at all

Table 13.4 Two different arguments run through this table. Rows one, five and six choose UDP because a connection is too expensive for what is being sent. Rows three and four choose it because reliability is actively wrong — when data has a deadline, a retransmission that arrives late has cost bandwidth to deliver something useless, and delayed the fresh data behind it. That is head-of-line blocking, and chapter 18 is about what it does to the web.

13.5 The dangerous property: amplification

UDP has no handshake, and therefore no proof that the source address in a datagram is real. An attacker can send a small query with someone else’s address in the source field, and the answer — which may be far larger — is delivered to that someone else. The attacker spends one small packet and the victim receives a large one.

The ratio is the amplification factor, and for some services it is enormous. A DNS query is tens of bytes; a response with many records can be thousands. Public services historically abused this way include open DNS resolvers, NTP’s monlist, memcached exposed to the internet, and SSDP on home routers. It is why:

  • A DNS resolver should serve only its own network, never the whole internet.
  • Providers are urged to implement source-address validation (BCP 38), dropping packets whose source cannot legitimately come from that direction.
  • New UDP protocols are designed with an anti-amplification rule. QUIC forbids a server from sending more than three times what it has received from an unvalidated address, which is a direct response to this problem.
  • Never expose a UDP service to the internet without meaning to. A TCP service exposed by accident is a risk to you; a UDP service exposed by accident is a weapon pointed at strangers.

Checkpoint

Why does a UDP client sometimes wait for its full timeout when nothing is listening?

Because on an unconnected socket the kernel cannot attribute the ICMP port-unreachable message to a particular operation — such a socket may legitimately receive from anyone, so an error concerning one previous sendto has nowhere to be delivered. The reply genuinely came back; the application simply never learns of it. Calling connect() on the UDP socket first fixes the peer address, and then the same code reports Connection refused immediately. connect() on UDP sends no packets at all.

Is UDP faster than TCP?

Not in the sense usually meant — both put the same bytes on the same wire at the same speed. What UDP avoids is latency from ceremony: no handshake before the first byte, no acknowledgement waiting, no retransmission stalling the data behind a lost packet, and no congestion window limiting the early transfer. For one small request-and-answer, that is most of the cost, which is listing 13.3. For a large bulk transfer, a well-implemented UDP protocol has to rebuild almost everything TCP does and ends up no faster, which is why QUIC is not a simple protocol.

Your metrics agent uses UDP and you are losing metrics under load. Whose fault is it?

Nobody’s — it is the design working as chosen. UDP was selected precisely so the agent never blocks the application it instruments, and the price is that datagrams are discarded when a buffer fills, silently. The right responses are to reduce the volume (aggregate before sending), enlarge the receive buffer, or accept the loss as the cost of not blocking. The wrong response is to switch to TCP without thinking, which converts “we lose some metrics” into “the application stalls when the metrics backend is slow” — a far worse failure.

Why is exposing a UDP service to the internet more dangerous than exposing a TCP one?

Because of amplification. TCP requires a handshake, so a server never sends a substantial response to an address that has not proved it can receive — a forged source address gets a SYN-ACK and nothing more. UDP has no such step, so an attacker can send small forged queries and direct large answers at a victim. An accidentally exposed TCP service is a risk to you; an accidentally exposed UDP service can be used as a weapon against third parties, which is why open resolvers and exposed memcached are treated as urgent problems.

What does UDP give you that TCP does not?

Message boundaries. One sendto becomes exactly one recvfrom of the same size. TCP is a byte stream with no notion of a message, so every protocol built on it must frame its own — length prefixes, delimiters, or chunked encoding — and getting that framing wrong is a classic source of bugs. UDP also gives you the freedom to define your own reliability, which matters when the built-in kind is the wrong kind.

DNS uses UDP but sometimes uses TCP. When, and why?

When the answer will not fit. Historically the limit was 512 bytes; EDNS(0) allows larger UDP responses to be negotiated, but there is still a ceiling, and beyond it the server sets a truncation flag and the client repeats the query over TCP. DNSSEC, with its signatures, made large answers common. TCP is also used for zone transfers, which are bulk data and exactly the case UDP is wrong for. Chapter 15 shows a truncated answer and the retry.

  • RFC 768 — User Datagram ProtocolIETF
  • RFC 8085 — UDP Usage GuidelinesIETF

Practice · UDP

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Send a UDP datagram with nc -u and capture it with tcpdump.Confirm the header arithmetic from listing 13.1.Easy
02Send to a closed UDP port and capture the ICMP that comes back.Then explain why your client did not report it.Easy
03Repeat that with a socket you called connect() on first.The error should now surface immediately.Easy
04Find every UDP service listening on your own machine.ss -uln. Ask why each one is there.Easy
05Capture a real DNS query and answer and measure both sizes.That ratio is the amplification factor for your resolver.Medium
06Write a UDP echo client that retries three times before failing.You have just implemented the smallest part of TCP.Medium
07Compare the packet count of one HTTP request over TCP with one DNS query.Listing 13.3 is the method.Medium
08Argue whether your own logging pipeline should use UDP, with evidence.The question is what happens when the backend is slow.Hard
If UDP is so minimal, why is QUIC built on it rather than on IP directly?

Deployability, not elegance. A genuinely new transport would need its own IP protocol number, and the internet is full of middleboxes — NATs, firewalls, load balancers — that pass TCP and UDP and drop anything else they do not recognise. A protocol that cannot traverse them cannot be deployed, whatever its merits. Building on UDP means every existing device sees ordinary UDP datagrams and forwards them, while the endpoints implement streams, reliability, congestion control and encryption above. It is the same lesson as chapter 0’s flag day: since 1983, any change to the internet must work through equipment that will never be updated.

Does UDP have congestion control at all?

The protocol has none, and that is the point of RFC 8085, which exists mainly to tell application authors that the responsibility is now theirs. An application sending a small, occasional datagram — a DNS query, a syslog line — can reasonably ignore this. An application sending a continuous high-rate stream cannot: without voluntary backoff it will keep transmitting into a congested path while TCP flows retreat, taking capacity from them and possibly causing collapse. This is why serious UDP protocols implement congestion control themselves. QUIC does, using the same algorithms as TCP; a naive video streamer often does not, which is one reason such traffic is treated with suspicion by network operators.

Chapter Fourteen · Part IV

MTU, MSS and Fragmentation

There is one number in networking that causes more baffling, intermittent, blame-shifting failures than any other, and it is 1500. A connection that opens perfectly and then hangs the moment real data flows is almost always this chapter, and the reason it is so hard to diagnose is that everything small works fine — ping, DNS, the handshake, the login page — right up until something big is sent.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Define MTU and MSS and convert between them
  • Predict when a packet will be fragmented and when it will be rejected
  • Read a fragmented packet in a capture and reassemble it by eye
  • Explain path MTU discovery and the one ICMP message it depends on
  • Diagnose an MTU black hole from its symptoms
  • Say why tunnels and VPNs make this common

14.1 Two numbers, and the arithmetic between them

TermMeansTypicalSet by
MTULargest payload a link will carry, in bytes1500The link technology
MSSLargest TCP payload in one segment1460Each end, from its own MTU
Ethernet frameMTU + 14 bytes of header1514Ethernet
IPv4 headerSubtracted from MTU to get MSS20RFC 791
TCP headerAlso subtracted20RFC 9293

Table 14.1 The arithmetic is MSS = MTU − 20 − 20 for IPv4 and TCP, giving 1460 on an ordinary Ethernet link. For IPv6 the IP header is 40 bytes, so the same MTU yields an MSS of 1440. Note what MSS does not account for: TCP options. A segment carrying timestamps has less room than the MSS suggests, which is why ss reports an advmss of 1460 while the actual payload maxes out around 1448.

14.2 Too big: fragmentation, seen whole

Why fragmentation is considered a mistake now

RFC 8900 is titled IP Fragmentation Considered Fragile, and the case against it is practical rather than aesthetic. Losing one fragment destroys the whole datagram, so a path with 1% loss can lose far more than 1% of fragmented traffic. Only the first fragment has the transport header, so stateless firewalls and load balancers cannot classify the rest. Reassembly is a memory burden on the receiver and has been the source of a long line of security bugs. And many networks simply drop fragments as a matter of policy. The modern approach is to avoid fragmentation entirely by discovering the path MTU and sending nothing larger — which is the next section, and which has its own failure mode.

14.3 Do not fragment, and how the sender finds out

14.4 The black hole

Path MTU discovery has one dependency, and it is a single ICMP message type. Block it — and it is blocked constantly, by administrators who believe all ICMP is a security risk — and the mechanism does not degrade. It fails silently and completely.

The two listings below differ by one firewall rule on the router. Everything else is identical: same topology, same narrow link, same transfer.

SymptomConsistent with an MTU black hole?
ping worksYes — ICMP echo is small
The connection opensYes — handshake packets are small
Small requests succeedYes
Large uploads or downloads hangYes. This is the signature
It works from some networks and not othersYes — only paths with a narrow link
ping -s 1400 -M do works, -s 1472 does notYes. This is the test
An error message appearsNo. Black holes are silent

Table 14.2 The sixth row is the diagnostic, and it takes ten seconds. Binary-search the payload size with ping -M do -s N until it stops working: the largest N that succeeds, plus 28 bytes of ICMP and IP headers, is the real path MTU. If that number is below 1500 and traffic is still being sent at 1500, you have found it.

14.5 Why this keeps happening: tunnels

An MTU below 1500 in the middle of a path is not rare or exotic. Anything that wraps your packet inside another packet must take room from the payload to make space for its own headers:

EncapsulationOverheadResulting MTU
PPPoE (many DSL lines)81492
IPsec, depending on mode and cipher~50–70~1430–1450
WireGuard60 (IPv4) / 80 (IPv6)1420 / 1440
GRE241476
VXLAN (used inside many clusters)501450
IPv6 over IPv4201480

Table 14.3 Any of these in a path gives exactly the topology of listing 14.5: a narrow link in the middle that neither endpoint knows about. This is why the symptom is so strongly associated with VPNs, and why “it broke when we moved to the overlay network” is a sentence with a specific meaning. The cloud makes it worse, because the tunnel is often invisible to you — it belongs to the provider.

Checkpoint

A connection opens, small requests work, large downloads hang. First command?

ping -M do -s 1472 <host>, then binary-search downwards. 1472 + 28 bytes of headers is exactly 1500, so if that fails and a smaller size succeeds, the path MTU is below 1500 and you have an MTU problem. It takes seconds and rules in or out the single most misdiagnosed failure in networking. If it succeeds at 1472, look elsewhere.

Why does blocking all ICMP break large transfers?

Because path MTU discovery is built on one ICMP message — Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed (type 3, code 4). It is the only way a router in the middle can tell a sender that its packets are too large, and the only way the sender learns the correct size. Blocking it does not make the mechanism degrade gracefully; the sender receives no information at all and keeps retransmitting packets that are silently discarded. “Block all ICMP” is a firewall policy that predates any real understanding of what ICMP does, and it produces this failure reliably.

Why is the MSS 1460 and not 1500?

Because MSS counts TCP payload only, and both the IP header (20 bytes) and the TCP header (20 bytes) must fit inside the link’s 1500-byte MTU alongside it. Over IPv6 the IP header is 40 bytes, so the same link gives an MSS of 1440. In practice the payload is often smaller still, around 1448, because TCP options such as timestamps occupy space the MSS figure does not account for.

Two hosts announce an MSS of 1460 each. Does that mean segments of 1460 will get through?

No, and this is the central misunderstanding of the chapter. Each host computes its MSS from its own interface, so the announcement describes the first link and the last link, and says nothing whatsoever about the ones between. If any intermediate link is narrower, the segments will not fit and the sender will only find out through path MTU discovery — if the ICMP gets back. MSS negotiation protects against a small MTU at the endpoints; nothing in TCP protects against one in the middle.

How does MSS clamping differ from path MTU discovery?

Path MTU discovery is reactive and end-to-end: the sender tries, fails, is told, and adapts — and depends on an ICMP message surviving the return path. MSS clamping is proactive and done by a middlebox: a router edits the MSS option in the SYN as it forwards it, so the endpoints negotiate a size that fits before any data is sent. It depends on nothing getting back, which is why it is the reliable fix. Its limitations are that it only helps TCP — UDP and QUIC get nothing — and that it requires the narrow link’s owner to have configured it.

Why do fragments make firewalls uncomfortable?

Because only the first fragment carries the transport header, so only the first has port numbers. A stateless filter cannot tell what the second fragment belongs to without holding reassembly state, which costs memory and has historically been a rich source of evasion techniques and denial-of-service bugs. Many networks therefore drop fragments outright as policy. That is a defensible decision, and it is also why relying on fragmentation to carry large packets is unwise — which is the argument of RFC 8900.

Practice · MTU, MSS and Fragmentation

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Find the MTU of every interface on your machine.ip link, or ifconfig on macOS.Easy
02Binary-search your real path MTU to a server you use.ping -M do -s N. On macOS the flag is -D.Easy
03Capture a fragmented ping and identify the identification, offset and flags.Listing 14.2 is the model.Easy
04Find the MSS in a real SYN from your own machine.tcpdump -nn "tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0".Easy
05Reproduce listing 14.5 and then remove the firewall rule to fix it.One rule is the whole difference.Medium
06Work out the MTU inside a WireGuard tunnel from table 14.3 and check it.Then test with ping -M do through the tunnel.Medium

If MTU problems are so common, why is 1500 still the number?

Because changing it is not something anyone can do unilaterally. The value is baked into Ethernet, into the expectations of every operating system, and into equipment that will never be updated — the 1983 flag-day argument from chapter 0, again. Jumbo frames of around 9000 bytes do exist and are genuinely useful, but only within a network where every device on the path agrees, which in practice means a datacentre or a storage network. On the public internet, a single link that has not been told will silently drop anything larger, and the failure looks exactly like listing 14.5.

Does IPv6 fix fragmentation?

It changes who does it, which helps. Routers in IPv6 are forbidden to fragment — only the sending host may, using an extension header — so the ambiguous middle case disappears and path MTU discovery is effectively mandatory rather than optional. The minimum MTU any IPv6 link must support is also raised to 1280, so there is a guaranteed floor to fall back to. What is not fixed is the dependency on ICMP: IPv6 path MTU discovery relies on Packet Too Big (ICMPv6 type 2), and blocking it produces exactly the same black hole. Since ICMPv6 also carries neighbour discovery, blocking ICMPv6 wholesale breaks the network far more visibly, which has had the useful side effect of making people stop doing it.

Chapter Fifteen · Part IV

DNS, End to End

Nothing in the network knows what a name is. A packet carries a 32-bit address and no room for anything else, so before any of the previous fourteen chapters can begin, something must turn www.example.com into four bytes. That something is a database with no complete copy anywhere, an authority tree split among everyone who ever registered a domain, and a cache in front of all of it.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Walk a delegation by hand, from a root server down to an authoritative one
  • Tell a referral from an answer by reading one line of a response header
  • Name the record types you will actually meet, and say what each is for
  • Explain what a TTL controls, and why nothing in DNS ever propagates
  • Trace a lookup through nsswitch, and say why getent and dig disagree
  • Say when DNS falls back to TCP, and how the client is told to

15.1 A tree, read backwards

Write the name with the dot it usually hides: www.example.com. That last dot is the root, and every name hangs beneath it. Names read right to left, and each dot is a place where authority can be handed to somebody else. A dot does not divide the data; it divides who is allowed to answer.

The root holds no website addresses at all — only a list of which servers run com., which run uk.. The servers for com. hold nothing inside example.com either; they hold a note saying which servers do. Records exist only at the bottom. What this replaced was one file, HOSTS.TXT, downloaded by every host from a single site, and it worked until the rate of change made a hand-edited file absurd.

TierWhat it knowsWhat it returnsWho runs it
Root — the . zoneWhich servers run each top-level domainA referral, never the address you asked forThirteen named servers, each anycast to many sites
TLD — com., uk.Which servers run each domain in itA referralThat TLD’s registry
Authoritative — example.com.The records themselvesThe answer, with aa setThe domain’s operator
Recursive resolverNothing at first; a great deal within minutesWhat it cached, or it goes and finds outYour ISP, employer, or a public service
Stub resolver — your machineThe address of a resolverIt does not answer. It askslibc, or systemd-resolved (§15.5)

Table 15.1 Only the third row holds data; the first two hold pointers, which is why the root zone fits comfortably on a phone. The fourth row is the only one keeping a copy of something it does not own, and both the convenient and the infuriating properties of DNS come from that row alone.

15.2 Walking the delegation by hand

A resolver doing this properly asks each tier in turn and follows the referrals itself. That is iterative resolution, and one header bit controls it: RD, recursion desired. Set it and you are asking the server to do the work; clear it with dig +norecurse and you are asking it to answer only from what it already holds, which is what a real resolver does at every step below. This runs on the host rather than in the lab — it is public information about public infrastructure, and the lab has no route to the internet.

Iterative (listing 15.1, by hand)Recursive (what your machine asks for)
RD bit in the query0 — +norecurse1 — the default
Who follows the referralsThe clientThe server
Round trips for the askerOne per tier, plus nameserver-name lookupsOne
What comes backA referral, until the last stepThe answer, or an error
Who does itResolvers, talking to authoritative serversEvery stub resolver on every client
Offered by authoritative servers?They answer only this wayNo, and no ra flag

Table 15.2 Two views of one walk from opposite ends, and confusing them is the commonest DNS mistake there is. An authoritative server that did offer recursion to the internet would be an open resolver — a reflection weapon (ch 13) and a poisoning target. dig +trace does the whole walk for you, which is useful for diagnosis and useless for learning what a delegation is.

15.3 What is actually stored

A zone is a set of resource records: a name, a class (always IN), a type, a TTL and type-specific data. Records sharing a name and type form an RRset, and the TTL belongs to the set rather than to any one record.

TypeHoldsThe thing people get wrong
A / AAAAOne IPv4 / one IPv6 addressIndependent records sharing a name. Several of either is normal, and is the crudest load balancing there is
CNAMEAnother name, resolved insteadIt cannot coexist with any other record at the same name
MXA mail exchanger and a preferenceLower preference wins, and it must name a host, never an address
TXTText, in strings of at most 255 bytesIt carries SPF, DKIM and every ownership proof ever invented, which is why TXT answers grow large (§15.6)
NSA server authoritative for this zoneIt appears twice — in the parent as the delegation, in the child as zone data. They can disagree
SOAZone parameters, once per zoneIts last field is not a default TTL
PTRA name, in in-addr.arpaNothing requires it to match the forward record

Table 15.3 Row two becomes an outage. A CNAME means “every question about this name is really about that name”, so nothing may sit beside it — and an apex always has an SOA and NS records. example.com can therefore never point at a load balancer’s hostname the way www.example.com can, which is why every provider sells a workaround named ALIAS or ANAME.

The lab has no route to a root server, so nothing in it can walk a delegation. A real DNS server answering real queries over the real protocol runs anywhere:

SOA fieldHereWhat it controls
Primary serverns.example.net.The master copy, for transfers and dynamic updates
Responsible mailboxhostmaster.example.net.An email address, first dot standing in for @
Serial2026082601Secondaries compare it; larger means “fetch the zone again”
Refresh / Retry1200 / 600How often a secondary checks the serial, and how soon after a failure
Expire604800How long a secondary serves with no contact at all
Minimum600The negative-caching TTL, whatever its name suggests

Table 15.4 The middle rows govern only the primary-to-secondary relationship, and do nothing if you have one server — which, with a hosted provider, you effectively do. The last row affects every user of the zone regardless. Running a zone properly is volume 20 of this series.

15.4 TTL, caching, and the word “propagate”

Every record carries a number of seconds — a statement by the zone’s operator that anyone may remember this for this long. A resolver holding an unexpired copy answers from it without asking anybody, and that one mechanism is what lets DNS survive a query volume no authoritative server could handle.

It is also the field’s most persistent misconception. DNS does not propagate. There is no push, no replication to caches, no notification, and no way for an authoritative server to reach a resolver holding an old answer. There is only expiry, so “it has not propagated yet” almost always means a cache is still inside a TTL that has not run out:

What listing 15.4 cannot show, and why

The resolver on the router is a caching forwarder, not a full recursive resolver: on a miss it sends the question to one configured server instead of walking the delegation itself. It has to be, because the lab has no route to a root server — which is why listing 15.1 ran on the host. No caching claim depends on that; the countdown, the lost aa flag and the query that never left the router are identical in a recursive resolver. What the lab cannot show is the miss path, where a real resolver performs the walk of listing 15.1 before it can answer at all.

The practical consequence is a scheduling rule rather than a DNS one. To move a service, lower the TTL a full old-TTL before the change and raise it afterwards, because the value that traps you is the one already handed out when you started. And when one office still sees the old address, query their resolver: the TTL it returns is exactly how many seconds remain.

15.5 The resolver path on a Linux host

None of this explains what happens when a program calls getaddrinfo(), and the answer is that DNS is only one of the things consulted. The C library reads /etc/nsswitch.conf, which lists sources to try in order; for hostnames that list is longer than most people expect, and DNS is at the end of it. Which is why dig and the rest of the system can disagree: dig is not a resolver-library client at all. It builds a DNS packet, sends it to a server and prints the reply, reading neither file. getent hosts goes through the library exactly as your application does.

15.6 UDP by default, TCP when it will not fit

DNS is the reason chapter 13 exists: one small question, one small answer, no state worth keeping, and a lost query that costs nothing to repeat. A handshake would have tripled the packet count for a transaction that fits in one datagram. So DNS runs over UDP, and the original specification capped a UDP DNS message at 512 bytes, chosen to sit safely below any plausible path MTU of the era (ch 14).

That cap has been under pressure ever since — it is why there are thirteen root servers rather than fifty, since the priming response listing them all with their addresses had to fit in 512 bytes. EDNS(0) lets a client advertise a larger buffer in a pseudo-record on the query. Failing that, the server sets the TC bit, returns almost nothing, and the client asks again over TCP.

UDPTCP
WhenAlways, firstWhen the reply had tc set, or for a zone transfer
Packets per question2A handshake, the exchange, a close
Size limit512 bytes, or what EDNS(0) negotiatedEffectively none, and many messages per connection
FramingThe datagram is the messageA two-byte length prefix before each message
Source forgeryTrivial — the basis of DNS amplification (ch 13)Prevented by the handshake
Blocked by firewalls?RarelyFrequently, by people who believe DNS is UDP-only

Table 15.5 The last row produces a nasty failure. Block TCP port 53 but not UDP and everything works until one answer grows past the limit — a new DKIM record, or DNSSEC switched on — and then that single name fails while every other name on the same server is fine. It is chapter 14’s MTU black hole in a different protocol: a fallback path nobody tested.

Why an over-large answer is now ordinary

DNSSEC attaches signatures to records, and a signed answer can be several times the size of an unsigned one; more than anything else, that is what made large responses normal. EDNS(0) keeps them on UDP, and the buffer a client advertises is a real trade: advertise too much and a big reply is fragmented at the IP layer, where a network that discards fragments will drop it outright (ch 14) — which looks, from the client, exactly like the server being down.

This book does not demonstrate DNSSEC validation: it needs a validating resolver with a trust anchor, which the lab cannot reach. What listing 15.1 does show is the ad flag, a resolver reporting that it validated an answer for you. The flag is not itself signed, so it is worth exactly as much as that resolver and the network between you and it.

Checkpoint

A response has ANSWER: 0 and several NS records in its authority section. What is it?

A referral — the normal reply from a root or TLD server to a query about a name below it, naming the servers to ask next. It is not an error; it is one step of an iterative walk. The confirming detail is the missing aa flag: the server is authoritative for its own zone, and the delegation records it handed you belong to somebody else’s. Get this from a server you expected to be authoritative, and the delegation and the zone disagree.

You changed an A record two hours ago and one office still gets the old address. What fixes it?

Waiting, and nothing else — DNS has no way to reach into a cache and invalidate an entry. There is no propagation to wait for, only expiry. Query that office’s resolver directly and read the TTL it returns: that is exactly how many seconds remain. The lesson for next time is scheduling, because the value that traps you is the one handed out before you touched anything. If the name is new rather than changed, suspect negative caching under the SOA minimum instead.

Why can the apex of a zone not be a CNAME?

Because a CNAME may not coexist with any other record at the same name, and an apex always has an SOA and a set of NS records — those are what make it a zone. The rule exists because a CNAME means “every question about this name is really about that name”, which is incoherent if the name has data of its own. So example.com cannot point at a load balancer’s hostname the way www.example.com can, which is why every provider sells a non-standard record to work around it.

getent hosts api.internal and dig api.internal disagree. Where do you look?

/etc/hosts first, then /etc/nsswitch.conf. The two take different paths deliberately: getent goes through the C library and tries every source in the hosts: line in order, while dig builds a DNS packet and talks to a server, reading neither file. A disagreement almost always means something earlier in that list answered first — usually a hosts-file line left from a migration, sometimes baked into a container image. On a systemd machine also try resolvectl query.

Why does DNS use UDP when a lost query gets no acknowledgement at all?

Because losing one costs almost nothing. The client retransmits after a short timeout, and it is asking a question that fits in one datagram and expecting an answer that usually does too — the whole transaction is two packets. A handshake would add three packets and a round trip before the question could be asked (ch 13). Reliability here is worth less than the round trip it costs, and DNS builds the only reliability it needs, ask again, out of a timer.

An administrator blocks TCP port 53, reasoning that DNS is a UDP protocol. What breaks, and when?

Nothing, until an answer exceeds the UDP limit — and then that one name fails while every other name on the same server keeps working. The trigger is usually growth in a single record set: another TXT record for a mail or ownership check, another address, or DNSSEC enabled on the zone. The server sets TC, the client tries TCP, the connection is refused or silently dropped, and the lookup fails with a timeout rather than an error.

Go deeper — the primary sources
  • RFC 1034 — Domain Names: Concepts and FacilitiesIETF
  • RFC 1035 — Domain Names: Implementation and SpecificationIETF
  • IANA root server listIANA

Practice · DNS, End to End

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Walk a delegation for a domain you use, from a root server down, with +norecurse.Listing 15.1 is the method. Three or four steps.Easy
02Look up all seven record types for one domain and read the TTLs.dig +noall +answer NAME A NAME MX NAME TXT, and so on.Easy
03Ask a public resolver the same question twice and watch the TTL fall.Then ask an authoritative server and see that it does not.Easy
04Compare getent hosts NAME with dig +short NAME on your own machine.Then read your hosts: line in /etc/nsswitch.conf.Easy
05Force a truncated answer and capture the TC bit on the wire.dig +noedns +ignore; tcpdump prints TC as |.Medium
06Find a name whose answer exceeds 512 bytes and prove it uses TCP.A domain with several TXT records, or a signed zone.Medium

08Work out how long before a migration you must lower a TTL, and justify the number.The answer is not the new TTL.Hard
Why does lowering a TTL an hour before a migration not help?

Because what governs a cache is the value in force when that cache last asked, not the one you are serving now. A resolver that fetched a record with a 24-hour TTL ten minutes before your change holds it for another 23 hours and 50 minutes, and has no reason to come back and find the shorter value. Lowering it only affects resolvers that query afterwards.

The procedure is therefore staged: lower the TTL, wait one full old TTL, make the change, raise it again once the new address has settled. Notice what that makes a long TTL — a commitment rather than a setting. A zone with a week-long TTL cannot be migrated on less than a week’s notice, which is the real reason low TTLs are common on records fronting user traffic.

If DNS has no complete copy anywhere, why do outages at one provider take down large parts of the web?

Because the distribution is by authority, not by redundancy. Each zone has exactly one set of servers authorised to answer for it, and if that set is unreachable nothing can substitute: no other server may invent the answer, and the caches that could have covered are good only until their TTLs run out.

So every domain delegated to a failing provider fails together — progressively, as caches drain, which is why such outages have a characteristically slow onset. What genuinely mitigates it is delegating a zone to nameservers at two independent providers, so the NS set in the parent names two organisations. That is standard for large operators and rare elsewhere, because it means keeping two configurations in step against an infrequent failure.

Chapter Sixteen · Part IV

TLS on the Wire

Everything about TLS is explained with the word “encrypted”, which is the word that hides the interesting part. A TLS connection announces which site you are visiting, in ordinary ASCII, before a single byte of protection exists — and it has to, for reasons that are nobody’s fault. This chapter builds a certificate and a server inside the lab, captures the handshake, and goes looking for the hostname in the hex.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Name what a passive observer learns from a TLS connection without breaking anything
  • Find the SNI hostname in the plaintext bytes of a real capture
  • Read the three disagreeing version fields in one ClientHello and say why they disagree
  • Count the round trips TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 need before application data moves
  • Explain why a TLS 1.2 certificate appears in a capture and a TLS 1.3 one does not
  • State precisely what a certificate proves, and what it does not

16.1 A connection you can take apart

TLS makes three promises at once, and they fail separately. Confidentiality: nobody on the path can read the data. Integrity: nobody can change it without being caught. Authentication: whoever answered proved control of the name you asked for. The third is what certificates are for, and the one routinely misread.

Everything here runs on a certificate generated inside the lab and thrown away afterwards; lab.example exists only in these two namespaces. Note the version the first command prints — TLS behaviour depends heavily on which OpenSSL you have, so the listing asks rather than assumes.

On the wireVisible on the path?Why
Destination address and portYesIt is the IP header. Routers need it (ch 4)
That this is TLS at allYesThe record type byte is unencrypted by definition
The hostname you asked forYesSent before any key exists — listing 16.2
Versions and ciphers offeredYesCapabilities precede agreement
The server’s certificate1.2 yes, 1.3 noListing 16.5 proves both halves
Size and timing of every recordYesEncryption hides content, never shape
URL path, headers, cookiesNoInside the protected stream (ch 18)
The response bodyNoThis is the part TLS is actually for

Table 16.1 An observer recording only the first six rows knows which service you contacted, when, how often, and how much passed each way — enough to identify most activity by pattern alone. That is why the hostname row matters more than it looks, and why the last two rows on their own are a narrower guarantee than “encrypted” suggests.

16.2 The hostname is not a secret

The Server Name Indication extension exists because of a scheduling accident. TLS was designed when one address meant one server, so the certificate could be chosen before the client said anything. Then addresses became scarce, virtual hosting became universal, and one address began serving hundreds of names — at which point the server had to know which name before it could pick a certificate and a key.

So the name travels in the very first message, which is the one message that cannot be encrypted, because no key has been agreed yet. That is not a bug or a weakness in the cipher. It is a chicken-and-egg problem in the shape of the protocol: to encrypt to the right server, you must first say which server you mean.

What this means away from the lab

All of that applies unchanged to https:// in a browser. Encrypting your DNS — DoH or DoT, chapter 15 — stops anyone on the path learning which names you look up, though the resolver you send them to necessarily still sees every one, which is the standing criticism of it. Either way it changes nothing here: the name is sent again, in the clear, in the ClientHello that follows. Blocking by SNI is how national filtering and many corporate web filters work, because it costs one plaintext field of one packet.

16.3 Three version numbers, and two of them are lies

A ClientHello answers a second question: how do two ends that know different versions of TLS agree on one? The old answer — the client states the highest version it knows, the server picks something no higher — stopped working. Middleboxes had been written to recognise the versions that existed when they were built, and dropped connections announcing anything newer. A protocol that cannot be upgraded without being discarded by equipment nobody can update is a frozen protocol. This is ossification, the same force that put QUIC on top of UDP in chapter 13. TLS 1.3’s answer was to leave the old fields where those middleboxes accept them and move the real negotiation somewhere they never learned to look:

BytesFieldSaysThe real answer?
16Record content type22 — handshake—
03 01Record layer versionTLS 1.0No. Frozen where every middlebox accepts it
01Handshake type1 — ClientHello—
03 03legacy_versionTLS 1.2No. Also frozen — its name says so
32 bytesclient_randomfresh entropyYes. Why no two handshakes look alike
20 + 32 byteslegacy_session_ida session to resumeNo. Decoration, echoed back to look familiar
01 00Compression methodsone method: noneYes. TLS 1.3 removed compression, after CRIME
00 00Extension type 0server_name — the SNIYes, and in the clear (listing 16.2)
00 2bExtension type 43supported_versionsYes. This is the real offer
03 04First version listed thereTLS 1.3Yes, with 03 03 after it as fallback

Table 16.2 The rows follow the order the bytes appear in listing 16.3, with the length fields left out — and one substantial omission: between the session id and the compression byte sits the cipher-suite list, a two-byte length followed by seventy bytes of suites, which is skipped here for room. Three are archaeology: two version fields say TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.2 and are ignored by both ends, and the session id is a decoy. The extension near the bottom decides. A protocol that has to lie about its own version to cross the network is telling you something about the network — the same thing chapter 8 said about NAT.

The ChangeCipherSpec that does nothing

Listing 16.4 shows a ChangeCipherSpec in both directions of a TLS 1.3 handshake. TLS 1.3 has no ChangeCipherSpec: the message was removed and its function is gone. It is sent anyway, and ignored on arrival, purely so a middlebox sees the record it expects from TLS 1.2 and leaves the connection alone. The standard calls this compatibility mode — a message whose whole purpose is to be misread by third parties.

16.4 One round trip instead of two, and a certificate you cannot see

A handshake is a sequence of flights: messages sent in one direction before the sender must stop and wait. Counting flights counts round trips, and round trips are what a handshake costs on a real path, where one crossing may be 80 ms and no amount of CPU will help. openssl s_client -msg logs each handshake message with its direction — >>> sending, <<< receiving — so every change of direction is half a round trip:

TLS 1.2TLS 1.31.3 resumed, 0-RTT
Round trips before application data210
Plus TCP’s own handshake111
Total before the request leaves3 RTT2 RTT1 RTT
Certificate on the wireIn the clearEncryptedNot re-sent
Cipher suites to choose fromHundreds, several brokenFive, all AEADFive
RenegotiationYes, and a vulnerabilityRemovedRemoved
CompressionOptional, and a vulnerabilityRemovedRemoved

Table 16.3 Row three is what a user feels: on an 80 ms path that is roughly 240 ms before the request leaves under TLS 1.2 and roughly 160 ms under TLS 1.3, on every new connection. The last three rows are the quieter improvement — TLS 1.3 is faster partly because whole features were deleted, and each of those had been the root of a named attack.

A timing measurement this lab cannot make

Those round-trip counts are read off the message order in listing 16.4, not measured, and this lab cannot measure them: its machines are namespaces on one kernel, so a crossing is tens of microseconds and both handshakes finish in a time dominated by process startup and RSA arithmetic. The usual remedy elsewhere is tc qdisc … netem, and tc is not installed on this machine — no listing in this book uses it; chapter 12, which genuinely needed loss, induced it with an iptables rule instead. Counting flights is the sounder measurement regardless: it sets the cost, and it does not vary with the path.

The other consequence is visible from outside. In TLS 1.2 the server’s Certificate goes out before either side has switched to encryption — and a certificate contains names. In TLS 1.3 everything after the ServerHello is encrypted, certificate included. Same server, same certificate, two versions, one search:

16.5 0-RTT, and the thing it trades away

A client that has spoken to this server before holds a ticket, and TLS 1.3 lets it use that ticket to send application data in the first flight, alongside the ClientHello, before the server has said anything. That is 0-RTT, or early data. The catch is structural rather than a bug: the key is derived entirely from the stored ticket, because nothing fresh from the server exists yet. A message needing nothing fresh from its recipient can be captured and sent again, and no amount of cryptography lets the server tell the replay from the original. It has to remember instead.

0-RTT gives youand costs you
LatencyA round trip off every resumed connectionNothing
Freshness—The request can be replayed. No server input went into its key
Forward secrecy—Early data has none — the ticket key decrypts it later
Server state—Single-use tickets or a replay cache, shared across the fleet
Application design—Only idempotent requests may go early. GET, not POST
Failure mode—Rejection is normal, so the client must be able to send it again

Table 16.4 Row two is why 0-RTT is off by default in most stacks and confined to safe methods where it is on. Listing 16.6 shows one server process rejecting a replay it recognises; a fleet behind a load balancer has that property only if the machines share the state, and a replay aimed at a different machine has not been seen before. RFC 8446 leaves the choice of anti-replay mechanism to the deployment, so the rule is simple: if executing the request twice would be a problem, do not let it go early.

16.6 What a certificate proves

Listing 16.1 built a certificate for lab.example on a machine with no relationship to that name, and every cryptographic operation in it was valid. It failed verification for exactly one reason: nothing the client already trusted had signed it.

A valid certificate provesIt does not prove
Someone proved control of this name to an issuer, at issue timeThat they still control it now
That issuer is trusted by your machine, directly or through a chainThat the issuer checked anything beyond control of the name
Whoever answered holds the matching private keyThat the key has not since been copied
The name you asked for is listed in the certificateThat the operator behind the name is honest
It has not expired and is not obviously revokedThat the site is safe, legitimate, or who you think it is
The connection cannot be read or altered in transitAnything about what happens at the far end

Table 16.5 The left column is a statement about a name; the right is everything people read into the padlock that was never claimed. A phishing site holding a perfectly valid certificate for a name that merely resembles yours is not a failure of TLS — the certificate proved precisely what it says, that whoever asked for it controlled that name. This is why browsers stopped displaying organisation names in the address bar: the field was being read as an endorsement it never was.

How a certificate is obtained — ACME, the HTTP-01 and DNS-01 challenges, renewal, and the fact that all of them reduce to “prove you can change something at this name” — belongs to volume 20 of this series, which runs a DNS zone. This chapter needs only a certificate that exists, which is why it makes one.

Encrypted Client Hello, and why it is not in this chapter

The plaintext hostname of listing 16.2 is a known problem with a work-in-progress answer: Encrypted Client Hello. The real ClientHello, hostname included, is encrypted to a public key the operator publishes in DNS and sent wrapped inside an outer ClientHello carrying a harmless shared name. An observer sees the outer name, which may be identical for every site behind a given provider; the server unwraps the inner one. It supersedes the earlier Encrypted SNI proposal, which encrypted only that one extension and leaked too much around it.

Not demonstrated in this book

Nothing in this chapter shows ECH working. It could not: the final command of listing 16.2 counts the options in this OpenSSL build whose names begin -ech, and the number it prints is the honest answer. A demonstration would also need a published DNS record carrying the key and a server that decrypts against it, neither of which this lab has — and deployment is partial, because client, server and DNS must all cooperate, and a resolver that drops the record silently turns it off. Treat the SNI as readable until you have verified otherwise for a specific connection.

Two conclusions follow, and neither is about cryptography. The hostname you visit is not private under TLS: if it must be, the protection has to come from elsewhere. And a certificate is a statement about a name, not about a party — the beginning of a trust decision, not the end of one. Chapter 20 reads a failing handshake out of a capture, and by then you will know which bytes to look at first.

Checkpoint

Why can the SNI hostname not simply be encrypted like everything else?

Because it is needed in order to choose the key. One address commonly serves hundreds of names, each with its own certificate, and the server cannot pick which certificate and private key to use until it knows which name the client wants. So the name must arrive in the first message, which is by definition sent before any key exists. It is a bootstrapping problem, not an oversight — and Encrypted Client Hello resolves it only by adding a key the client fetches in advance, from DNS, which is why it could never have been done inside TLS alone.

Your traffic is entirely TLS 1.3. What can a network operator still log?

The destination address and port, the fact that the connection is TLS, the hostname from the ClientHello, the versions and ciphers you offered, and the size and timing of every record in both directions — table 16.1. That is a complete list of which services you used and when, plus a good guess at what you did from traffic shape alone. What is genuinely hidden is content: path, headers, cookies, body. “Encrypted” is a claim about content, habitually heard as a claim about metadata.

A ClientHello says TLS 1.0 in one place and TLS 1.2 in another, yet the connection ends up TLS 1.3. Is something wrong?

No — that is a normal, correct TLS 1.3 ClientHello. The record-layer version and legacy_version are frozen at old values because middleboxes were dropping connections that announced anything newer, and both ends ignore them. The real negotiation is the supported_versions extension, type 43, which lists TLS 1.3 first; the server picks from it and states its choice in its own copy. Trust the version in the record header and you will misidentify almost every modern connection.

You capture a handshake and cannot find the server’s certificate in it. What does that tell you?

Most likely that it is TLS 1.3, where everything after the ServerHello is encrypted, certificate included — listing 16.5 shows the same certificate visible under TLS 1.2 and absent under TLS 1.3. Anyone who identified services by pulling certificates out of captures lost that technique, as did inspection appliances doing the same, which was partly the point. A capture alone can no longer tell you which certificate a server presented, so connect and ask: openssl s_client prints it.

Why is 0-RTT data replayable when the rest of the connection is not?

Because its key comes only from the ticket the client already held. Every other message in a handshake mixes in something fresh from the other side, so a replayed copy fails; early data cannot, because the server has not spoken when the client sends it. Cryptography therefore cannot distinguish an original from a replay, and the defence has to be memory — a single-use ticket or a replay cache, as in listing 16.6, shared across every machine that might receive the connection.

A colleague says the padlock means the site is safe. What is the precise correction?

It means the connection to that name is encrypted and integrity-protected, and that whoever answers on that name proved control of it to an issuer your machine trusts. It says nothing about who they are, what they do with what you send, or whether the name is the one you meant — a phishing domain can hold a valid certificate, obtained in seconds and entirely legitimately, because control of the name is the only thing ever checked. Listing 16.1 makes a valid certificate for a name the machine has no connection to; all it lacks is a signature from something already trusted.

Practice · TLS on the Wire
