If the SNI is readable anyway, what does TLS buy against a network observer?

A great deal, and much less than the word “encrypted” implies. It buys confidentiality and integrity for the content: an observer cannot read the path, the headers, the cookies, the credentials or the response body, and cannot modify any of them without the connection failing. That is the difference between someone knowing you contacted a bank and someone reading your balance and altering a transfer.

What it does not buy is metadata privacy. Address, port, hostname, timing, direction and byte counts all remain, and the sequence of request and response sizes while a page loads is often distinctive enough to identify which page was fetched, with nothing decrypted. Encrypted DNS closes one channel and ECH aims to close another, but traffic shape stays open regardless, because it is not a field anyone can encrypt. TLS protects what you said, not that you said it, or to whom.

Why did TLS 1.3 delete features rather than add them?

Because almost every serious TLS vulnerability of the preceding decade came from an option rather than from the core. Compression enabled CRIME. Renegotiation carried an authentication flaw. Static RSA key exchange had no forward secrecy, so one stolen key retroactively decrypted every recorded session. A long menu of legacy cipher suites meant a downgrade attack always had somewhere to downgrade to.

TLS 1.3 kept five cipher suites, all authenticated encryption, made forward secrecy mandatory, and removed compression and renegotiation. Fewer options means fewer combinations, fewer code paths and less for a negotiation attack to reach for — and the round-trip saving in listing 16.4 came partly from the same pruning, because a client with fewer things to ask about can guess correctly and send its key share immediately. It is the rare case where the faster protocol is also the smaller one.

Chapter Seventeen · Part IV

Firewalls

A packet filter has exactly two ways to refuse a packet: throw it away and say nothing, or send back an error. They are one word apart in the configuration, they give identical security — the packet does not arrive either way — and from the client’s chair they are two minutes apart. Everything else here is machinery around that choice. Netfilter rules belong to a network namespace, so every ruleset below is built in a throwaway one and torn down with it: this chapter can lock a host out of its own network in front of you, safely and for real.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Choose between DROP and REJECT, and predict what each costs the client
  • Read a refusal off the wire and name the device that sent it
  • Say which chain a packet traverses, and why FORWARD is the router’s
  • Prove a rule can never match, using nothing but its packet counter
  • Explain what connection tracking stores and which single rule depends on it
  • Say what a firewall cannot decide, and where that decision belongs instead

17.1 Two ways to say no

When a filter decides no, it can do only two things: discard the packet silently (DROP) or discard it and send back an error (REJECT). That is a decision about what you tell the sender, not about security — and it matters because the sender has no other way to find out. TCP has no delivery report, so a client that hears nothing cannot tell a filter from a dead host or a cut cable, and does the only thing it can: retransmit until it gives up.

--reject-withWhat it claims happenederrnoWhat the client printsWhen
— (DROP)nothing at all110Connection timed outafter minutes
icmp-port-unreachablenothing is listening there111Connection refusedat once
tcp-resetnothing is listening there111Connection refusedat once
icmp-host-unreachablethat host cannot be reached113No route to hostat once
icmp-net-unreachablethat network cannot be reached101Network is unreachableat once
icmp-proto-unreachableno such protocol here92Protocol not availableat once
icmp-admin-prohibiteda policy forbids this113No route to hostat once

Table 17.1 Generated by running each variant against a live client — the last two columns are what connect() returned; the first row is DROP, whose message listing 17.1 printed last. The error an application sees is chosen by whoever wrote the rule, so it is evidence about a configuration, not about the network. Connection refused is ambiguous by construction: a closed port and a deliberate refusal give the identical errno. And No route to host, which reads like a routing failure and sends people to traceroute (ch 7), is what a firewall says when it is honest.

So which should you use?

For anything a human or a service connects to, REJECT. A fast refusal is diagnosable; a hang is not. The usual argument for DROP — that silence hides you from scanners — is weak: an unanswered probe still reports as filtered rather than closed, so you are not hidden, only slow to scan, and a scanner does not mind waiting while your systems do. DROP earns its place at an internet edge, absorbing floods where every reply is bandwidth spent on an attacker’s behalf. Inside your own network, silence is a self-inflicted wound.

17.2 Which chain sees the packet

Netfilter hooks fixed points in the packet path, and the filter table uses three. The names describe the packet’s relationship to this machine, and what decides between them is the routing decision, which happens first:

ChainA packet reaches it whenWhat it is forHow it is got wrong
INPUTrouting decided the destination is one of this machine’s addressesProtecting the host itself — its SSH, its metrics port, its databaseLocking yourself out. Add the rule that lets you back in first
OUTPUTa local process generated itEgress control: stopping a compromised host reaching outBreaking your own DNS and package updates, then blaming the network
FORWARDrouting decided it belongs elsewhere and this machine will pass it onThe entire policy of a router, gateway or NAT box (ch 8)Writing that policy into INPUT, where no forwarded packet will see it

Table 17.2 The middle column is the whole distinction, and it is about destination, not direction: a packet arriving on an interface is an INPUT packet only if it is addressed to this machine. Everything else is FORWARD, which on a router is nearly all of it. Note what is missing — there is no “inbound” chain, because a reply to your own request arrives on the same interface as an unsolicited connection, and those are separated by state (§17.4), not by hook.

17.3 Order is the program, and the counter is the proof

A chain is not a set of rules but a list, evaluated top to bottom, in which the first match decides and everything below it is never consulted. That makes it an if / elif ladder, with the same failure mode: a broad condition near the top turns a narrow one below into dead code. In a firewall that dead code is silent — it parses, it appears in iptables -S, it survives review, and it does nothing.

What the counters showWhat it meansWhat to do
A rule you expect to match sits at 0Shadowed by something above it, or its match does not mean what you think--line-numbers, then -I it above the offender
The chain policy counter is risingTraffic is reaching the end of the chain and dying on the defaultThat is everything you have no rule for. Look before you allow
A DROP count climbs steadily and foreverSomething is retrying on a timer — a health check, an agent, a stale clientFind it. A firewall eating your own health checks is listing 17.1’s hang
Every rule is at 0 and traffic is still blockedWrong chain, wrong table, or wrong engine entirelyTry FORWARD too, then see listing 17.6

Table 17.3 Counters are the only observability a packet filter has, and iptables keeps them whether you want them or not. Read them before you change anything: deleting and re-adding a rule makes a new one with a fresh counter and destroys your evidence. When a rule and reality disagree, believe the counter — it records what the kernel did, the rule only what you asked for.

17.4 Stateful filtering, and the one rule everything hangs on

Try to write a default-deny INPUT chain without connection state and the problem appears at once. You want nothing inbound — but every outbound request produces an inbound reply, addressed to an ephemeral port the kernel picked at random (ch 9), from an address and port you did not know in advance. The only stateless rule that admits those replies is “allow all TCP to ports 32768–60999”, which admits the whole world with them. Connection tracking solves it by remembering: conntrack records each flow — addresses, ports, protocol, position in its lifecycle — so a packet can be classified not by what it contains but by whether you started it.

StateWhat conntrack means by itWhat a sane policy does
NEWThe first packet of a flow it has not seen beforeThis is what your rules actually decide. The rest follows
ESTABLISHEDA packet of a flow it has seen traffic on in both directionsAccept — or nothing you initiate ever receives an answer
RELATEDA new flow belonging to an existing one: ICMP errors about it, and data connections a protocol helper expectsAccept. Dropping it costs error reporting and path MTU discovery (ch 14)
INVALIDIt cannot be placed — a stray ACK, a packet for an expired flowDrop it explicitly, and log it if you are curious
UNTRACKEDExempted from tracking on purpose, in the raw tableFor high-rate traffic where the table itself is the bottleneck

Table 17.4 Read the first two rows together and every host firewall appears: accept ESTABLISHED,RELATED at the top, write the real policy against NEW below it, default-deny underneath. Note that “established” is conntrack’s word, not TCP’s — it applies to UDP and ICMP too, and means only “I have seen this flow go both ways”.

The table is finite, and that is a failure mode

Tracking buys its convenience with memory: one entry per flow, held until that flow’s timeout, bounded by nf_conntrack_max. A busy box that hits the limit drops new connections while existing ones continue perfectly — which presents as “it works for everyone already connected and refuses everyone else”, and which no amount of staring at the application will explain. Watch the entry count against the maximum; the kernel announces the overflow in dmesg. This is the honest case for NOTRACK on stateless high-volume traffic.

17.5 Two syntaxes, one engine

Everything so far was written in iptables and executed by nftables. On current distributions iptables is a compatibility front end that speaks the old syntax and programs the new kernel subsystem — and it says so, printing (nf_tables) after its version, as the listing below shows. The choice is therefore of language, not mechanism, and the mapping is mechanical enough that a translator ships with iptables itself:

Written in iptablesThe same rule in nft
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9401 -j DROPnft add rule ip filter INPUT tcp dport 9401 counter drop
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9401 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-resetnft add rule ip filter INPUT tcp dport 9401 counter reject with tcp reset
iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPTnft add rule ip filter INPUT ct state related,established counter accept
iptables -A INPUT -s 198.51.100.0/24 -p tcp --dport 9401 -j ACCEPTnft add rule ip filter INPUT ip saddr 198.51.100.0/24 tcp dport 9401 counter accept
iptables -A FORWARD -p udp --dport 9401 -j DROPnft add rule ip filter FORWARD udp dport 9401 counter drop
iptables -I INPUT 1 -p icmp --icmp-type echo-request -j ACCEPTnft insert rule ip filter INPUT icmp type echo-request counter accept
iptables -P INPUT DROPTranslation not implemented

Table 17.5 The right-hand column is produced by iptables-translate, not typed, so the two cannot disagree. Read the differences. nft has no -m modules: -m conntrack --ctstate is simply ct state. It names the address family explicitly (ip saddr), which is how one inet ruleset covers IPv4 and IPv6 at once instead of the parallel rulesets ip6tables forces on you. And every rule that translates carries counter — iptables counts always, nft only where you ask, so a hand-written rule without it gives none of §17.3’s evidence. The last row is the interesting failure: a chain policy has no translation, because in nft it is a property of the chain, not a command.

17.6 Security groups, and the thing a firewall cannot decide

A cloud security group is the same idea with the knobs removed: attach it to an instance’s virtual interface, list what may come in, and everything else is discarded — silently, which is why a wrong security group produces a connection that hangs rather than one that is refused, and why it is the first thing to check when a cloud service “times out”. Listing 17.6 is a security group written longhand.

Cloud security groupStateless network ACLiptables / nft on the host
Unmatched trafficDropped, silentlyDropped, silentlyWhatever the chain policy says
Deny rulesNone. Allow-list onlyYesYes
Does order matter?No. Any matching rule allowsYes, by rule numberYes — first match wins (§17.3)
Connection stateAlways statefulNone — return traffic needs its own ruleOnly if you ask (§17.4)
Enforced atThe virtual interface, outside the instanceThe subnet boundaryInside the instance
Survives root on the instanceYesYesNo — root can flush it
Can match onPorts, CIDRs, other security groupsPorts, CIDRsInterfaces, marks, sets, local uid, more

Table 17.6 Two rows explain why cloud firewalls feel easier. No deny rules and no order deletes §17.3 outright — you cannot shadow a rule in a set that has none — and always stateful deletes §17.4’s decision. What you give up is the last row. Operationally the decisive one is the second from last: a security group is enforced outside the instance, so an attacker who is root inside cannot remove it, which a host firewall can never claim.

Why authorisation does not live here

Every rule in this chapter matched on an interface, an address, a protocol, a port or a connection state. That is the entire vocabulary, and who is asking is not in it — listing 17.6 made the point from both sides, because a sender’s identity exists only on the machine that sent the packet.

  • An address is not an identity. NAT collapses an office behind one address (ch 8), a proxy makes every request appear to come from itself (ch 19), and a released cloud address goes back into a pool for somebody else. “Allow 203.0.113.0/24” means “allow whoever holds those addresses right now”.
  • A port is not a permission. Ports are demultiplexing (ch 9). One port carries every operation an API offers, so allowing it allows DELETE /users as much as GET /health — and past the handshake a middlebox sees only ciphertext (ch 16).
  • “Inside the network” is not a credential. A rule that trusts a range trusts every process on every host in it, including the one compromised this morning — the assumption that turns one foothold into a whole-estate incident.

None of which makes firewalls optional. Their job is reachability, and nothing else can do it: a service that cannot be reached cannot be attacked whatever bugs it contains, and every port you close is code you no longer have to trust. A firewall is the only control in this book that protects software you have not read.

But it is a floor. Reachability is decided once, at connection time, on facts about a network; authorisation has to be decided per request, against an authenticated principal, by code that can see what is being asked. Ask either to do the other’s job and you get the two classic failures: a flat network where one compromised host owns everything, or an application that trusts its callers because they arrived on the right port.

Checkpoint

One service hangs for two minutes and then reports Connection timed out. Another is refused instantly. What does each tell you?

The instant refusal tells you a packet came back — a reset or an ICMP unreachable — from something that received your SYN and answered. That is real information: something is reachable, and it declined. The hang tells you almost nothing, because it is your own kernel giving up after tcp_syn_retries retransmissions with no input at all, and a DROP rule, a dead host, a black-holed route and a cut fibre produce identical silence. The only ways to narrow it are the wire (listing 17.2) or the path (ch 7) — the message itself was written by your own machine.

If REJECT is so much friendlier, why does anyone use DROP?

Two defensible reasons and one bad one. At an internet edge, replying to unsolicited traffic spends your bandwidth and CPU on an attacker’s schedule and can be reflected at a third party, so absorbing it silently is correct; and silence does slow bulk scanning, since each probe costs a timeout. The bad reason is obscurity as a house style: an unanswered probe still reports as filtered rather than closed, so nothing is hidden, while your own health checks and deploys pay the two minutes in listing 17.1.

You added an allow rule, the syntax is right, the traffic is still blocked. What is the one command?

iptables -L -v -n --line-numbers, or nft list ruleset where the rules carry counters. If the allow rule shows 0 packets it has never been reached, something above it matched first, and the fix is to insert rather than append. If it shows a non-zero count and traffic still fails, the block is elsewhere — another chain, another table, another host, or the return path. That one number halves the problem before you have formed a theory.

Why does a default-deny INPUT chain not need a matching rule for every reply?

Because of the ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule and the connection tracking behind it. Conntrack records every flow the machine takes part in, so a returning packet is classified by whether this machine started the exchange rather than by its contents. Without it you would have to admit inbound traffic to the whole ephemeral port range, which admits everyone. Note the failure mode in listing 17.5: outbound packets still leave normally and only the replies die, so it presents as the remote end being down.

You harden a router by filling its INPUT chain, and traffic through it is unaffected. Why?

Because the routing decision comes first, and it sends packets addressed to this machine to INPUT and everything else to FORWARD. On a router almost nothing is in the first category, so an INPUT chain protects the router’s own management plane — its SSH, its metrics, its routing daemon — and filters not one forwarded packet. Listing 17.3 puts both counters side by side. Policy about traffic through a device belongs in FORWARD, always.

“We do not need authorisation checks; the service is only reachable from inside the VPC.” What is wrong with that?

It confuses reachability with permission. The rule matched an address and a port, and neither says who is asking — that fact exists only on the sending machine and never reaches the wire, which is why an owner match is rejected in an INPUT chain at all. So the sentence really reads “every process on every host in this range may do anything this service offers”, including the host compromised this morning. It is brittle a second way too: put one load balancer in front (ch 19) and every request arrives from an allowed address by definition.

Practice · Firewalls

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Block a port on a test host with DROP, then with REJECT, and time a client against each.Listing 17.1 is the method.Easy
02Capture the wire for both and identify what came back in each case.tcpdump -nn "port N or icmp". One capture will be one-sided.Easy
03Print your own ruleset with nft list ruleset and again with iptables -L -v -n.If they disagree, listing 17.6 explains why.Easy
04Find a rule on a host you administer whose packet counter is zero.Then decide whether it is shadowed, unmatchable, or simply idle.Easy
05Build a default-deny INPUT chain, delete the ESTABLISHED,RELATED rule, and watch what breaks.On a machine you can reach physically or through a console.Medium
06Write one rule twice — in iptables, then nft — and check yourself with iptables-translate.The counter keyword is the difference people forget.Medium
07Put a rule in a router’s INPUT chain, prove with counters that forwarded traffic ignores it, then move it to FORWARD.Listing 17.3. Predict both counters before you look.Medium
08Take one security group you rely on and write down, per rule, what an attacker who is root on an allowed host could do.The answer is the gap between reachability and authorisation.Hard
If DROP and REJECT give identical security, why is the choice treated as a security decision?

Because of an argument about information that was much stronger when it was made. A REJECT confirms a host exists and is responding, and when scanning was slow, forcing an attacker to wait out a timeout per port was a real cost imposed on them. It is a small cost now: scanners are massively parallel and do not care how long an individual probe takes, and the probe still comes back distinctly as filtered rather than closed, so the host is not hidden, only slower to enumerate. The cost of silence, meanwhile, falls entirely on legitimate traffic.

The honest formulation is that DROP is a resource decision rather than a secrecy one. At an internet-facing edge under load, every reply is bandwidth and CPU spent at an attacker’s discretion, and can be aimed at a third party whose address they forged. Behind that edge, where what hits your rules is overwhelmingly your own misconfigured systems, the same silence buys nothing and costs diagnosis time. Most real rulesets should contain both, chosen per rule rather than as a house style.

Where does a firewall belong in a design that already authenticates every request?

At the front, still, doing a job authentication cannot do. Authentication protects the operations your application deliberately exposes; it does nothing about the ones exposed by accident. A debug endpoint, an admin port bound to all interfaces, a database never meant to be routable, a dependency with a pre-authentication parsing bug — each is a reachable code path that per-request checking cannot guard, because the check sits behind it.

What strong authentication changes is the claim you may make for the firewall. It is no longer “this service is safe because only the app tier can reach it” but “this service is authenticated, and separately, very few parties can send it a packet”. Those are independent statements, and neither failing alone should be catastrophic. That independence is the whole point of defence in depth, and why the answer to “which layer should stop this?” is usually both, for different reasons.

Chapter Eighteen · Part V

HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

One problem, solved three times, at three layers. HTTP/1.1 is text you can type at a socket by hand, and its flaw is that a connection carries one exchange at a time. HTTP/2 replaced the text with binary frames so one connection could carry many at once — then found that TCP would not permit it. HTTP/3 gave up on TCP altogether. Follow head-of-line blocking down the stack and you have the whole history.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Type an HTTP request by hand and read a response straight off the wire
  • Explain what persistent connections changed, and what Connection: close still does
  • Say why HTTP pipelining failed and why browsers opened six connections instead
  • Read an HTTP/2 frame header and name the stream a frame belongs to
  • Explain why HTTP/2 still blocks, and identify the layer responsible
  • Say what QUIC moved out of the kernel and why it had to ride on UDP

18.1 A protocol you can type

Almost every protocol in this book is binary and you meet it through a decoder. HTTP/1.1 is the exception: a line of text, then more lines of text, then a blank line. That was deliberate — a protocol you can produce with a keyboard is one anyone can implement and debug.

The cost is parsing. Text has no length field, so a receiver scans for delimiters and copes with every server that is slightly wrong. Most request-smuggling vulnerabilities come from two implementations disagreeing about where a message ended.

PartLooks likeRules
Request lineGET /hello.txt HTTP/1.1Method, target, version. Always first
Status lineHTTP/1.0 200 OKVersion, code, and a phrase nothing should parse
Header fieldsHost: 203.0.113.20Name, colon, value. Names case-insensitive
Blank line\r\nThe only marker that the header section ended
BodyThe file’s bytesContent-Length, chunked encoding, or the close

Table 18.1 The last two rows carry the danger. The blank line is the only thing dividing headers from body, so a field value containing a CRLF can invent one. And the body’s length comes from whichever of three mechanisms applies, so a front end and a back end can disagree about where a request ended (ch 19). HTTP/2’s explicit frame length removes that bug class.

18.2 One connection, three requests

HTTP/1.0 opened a connection, sent one request, read one response and closed. For a page with forty images that is forty handshakes and forty slow starts (ch 12), and forty sockets left in TIME_WAIT (ch 11). On a link with a 100 ms round trip the handshakes alone cost four seconds before an image byte moves.

HTTP/1.1 made the connection persistent by default. There is no Connection: keep-alive below, because keeping the connection is not the thing you ask for. Closing it is.

Persistent connections are why Host: is mandatory

These two changes arrived together and are related. Once a connection outlives one request, the destination address no longer says which site a request is for, so the request must. Host: made virtual hosting possible, and virtual hosting let thousands of sites share one address — part of why chapter 4’s shortage was survivable as long as it was. TLS solved the same problem with SNI (ch 16).

18.3 The first head-of-line block

Removing the handshakes does not let two things happen at once. HTTP/1.1 is strictly request, response, request, response: one outstanding request per connection.

Pipelining was the specified fix — write several requests without waiting, read the responses in order. It has been in the standard since 1997 and no mainstream browser enables it. Here is why.

The workaroundWhat it boughtWhat it cost
Six connections per originSix requests in flight at onceSix handshakes, six congestion windows competing
Domain shardingSix more connections per hostnameMore lookups and handshakes, diminishing returns
Sprite sheetsMany small images in one requestNo icon appears until the whole sheet loads
Concatenating scriptsOne large file, not forty small onesOne byte changes and the whole bundle is refetched
Inlining as data: URIsAn asset costing no requestUncacheable, and base64 makes it a third larger
PipeliningSeveral requests per connectionHead-of-line blocking, and broken proxies. Never deployed

Table 18.2 Every row buys back parallelism the protocol would not give. The 1999 specification recommended no more than two connections per server; browsers ignored it and settled on six. The first five rows are work done by the site author rather than the protocol — the strongest argument that the protocol was wrong.

18.4 HTTP/2: frames, streams and a shared header table

HTTP/2 keeps every piece of HTTP’s meaning — methods, paths, status codes, fields — and throws away the way it is written down. In its place a binary framing layer, every frame beginning with the same nine bytes.

BytesFieldWhat it does
0–2Length24 bits. The payload size, so nobody scans for a delimiter
3TypeDATA, HEADERS, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, and six more
4FlagsType-specific. END_STREAM is 0x01, END_HEADERS is 0x04
5–8Stream identifier31 bits, one reserved. Which conversation this frame is

Table 18.3 The last field is why HTTP/2 exists: because every frame names a stream, frames from different requests can be interleaved on one connection in any order and still be sorted out at the far end. Stream 0 is the connection itself; client streams are odd and server streams even, so neither end collides with the other.

The lab has no production HTTP/2 server, and this book will not print a transcript it did not produce, so the listing uses about thirty lines of Python implementing just enough of the protocol to hold a conversation. The client is real — curl, driving the same nghttp2 library that has talked to production servers for a decade. Two honest limits: the server never decodes the compressed headers it receives, so it answers by stream number rather than by path, and it speaks HTTP/2 in the clear, which curl will do with --http2-prior-knowledge but a browser will not — there, HTTP/2 is always inside TLS and chosen by ALPN (ch 16).

FrameStreamPurpose
SETTINGS0Table and window sizes. Sent first, acknowledged
HEADERSnA request or response, HPACK-compressed
DATAnBody bytes. END_STREAM means that is all
WINDOW_UPDATE0 or nFlow control — per stream, not just per connection
RST_STREAMnCancel one request without harming the others
GOAWAY0Stop opening streams; this is the last I will honour

Table 18.4 Every frame in listing 18.4 is one of these. RST_STREAM is something HTTP/1.1 could not express: cancelling one request meant closing the connection and abandoning everything else on it. WINDOW_UPDATE gives each stream a window of its own, so one large download cannot starve the small requests beside it.

18.5 The block HTTP/2 could not remove

HTTP/2’s streams are independent to HTTP/2. They are not independent to TCP, which knows nothing about them: underneath the frames there is one connection, one sequence space and one absolute promise — the receiving application gets the bytes in the order they were sent, or it waits. So a lost segment holds everything sent after it in the receiving kernel, including frames from streams that lost nothing. Their bytes are in the machine; the application cannot have them.

The listing runs the same two requests twice, the second time with an iptables rule that discards the segment carrying stream 1’s body on its first three arrivals — three, because this lab’s round trip is microseconds and one loss would be repaired too fast to see.

Where it blocksWhat is blockedRemoved by
HTTP/1.1 — one response at a timeEvery later request on itHTTP/2 streams — listing 18.4
TCP — in-order delivery of one byte streamEvery stream sharing the connectionQUIC — section 18.6
QUIC — in-order delivery within a streamOnly the stream that lost a packetNothing. This is the right amount
The application — a resource others wait forWhatever depends on itNothing at the transport layer

Table 18.5 The chapter in one table, and the third row needs precision: QUIC does not abolish head-of-line blocking, it reduces its scope to one stream. Losing a packet inside a large image still delays the rest of that image — those bytes must be in order — but the stylesheet sharing the connection stops being punished for it. The fourth row is the kind of blocking no protocol version can reach (ch 21).

18.6 HTTP/3: streams that are genuinely independent

If the problem is TCP, the fix is not to use TCP. QUIC provides what HTTP/2 assumed it already had: several ordered byte streams, each with its own sequence numbering, flow control and loss recovery, in one connection. A packet lost on one stream delays that stream alone.

HTTP/3 is HTTP/2’s semantics on those streams, with a smaller framing layer because QUIC has taken over multiplexing, flow control and cancellation. Header compression is redone as QPACK, because HPACK’s shared table assumed everything arrived in order — the assumption QUIC gives up.

There will never be another IP protocol number

A transport that is not TCP or UDP needs an IP protocol number of its own, and that is what stops it working. The equipment between any two hosts — NAT devices (ch 8), firewalls (ch 17), load balancers, carrier gateways — forwards protocols 6 and 17 and discards the rest. Not out of malice: a NAT has nowhere to record a mapping for a protocol whose ports it cannot find. SCTP has been standardised since 2000 and is still undeployable for that reason. So QUIC is a transport disguised as a datagram protocol, and every middlebox sees ordinary UDP and forwards it — chapter 0’s flag-day argument in its final form, in which change must arrive dressed as something the old equipment already understands.

The lab has no internet, so this runs on the host against a public site — and checks first, because not every build of curl has HTTP/3.

HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3
Message formatText, CRLF-delimitedBinary framesBinary frames
TransportTCPTCPQUIC over UDP
Requests at onceOneMany, interleavedMany, interleaved
Connections per originAbout sixOneOne
Header compressionNoneHPACKQPACK
EncryptionOptionalTLS, in every browserAlways. Built in
Head-of-line blockingIn HTTP itselfIn TCP, underneathWithin one stream only
Survives an address changeNoNoYes — connection IDs, not addresses

Table 18.6 The last row gets the least attention and may matter most. A TCP connection is identified by four numbers, two of them yours, so moving from Wi-Fi to mobile destroys every connection you had; a QUIC connection is identified by a connection ID both ends carry, so the download continues. That works only because QUIC’s state lives in the application rather than the kernel’s socket table.

Checkpoint

HTTP/1.1 made connections persistent. Why did that not make pages load in parallel?

Because persistence removes the handshakes, not the serialisation. One exchange at a time means the client may not send its next request until the previous response has been read to the end, so a slow response holds up everything behind it — listing 18.3 shows a fast request waiting on a slow one it has nothing to do with. Pipelining did not fix that, because the responses still had to come back in request order. Parallelism in HTTP/1.1 came from opening more connections, which is why browsers open six.

What does the stream identifier in an HTTP/2 frame header buy you?

Permission to interleave. Because every frame names its conversation, the sender may put frames from different requests on the wire in any order and the receiver can still reassemble each one — so a fast response need not queue behind a slow one, and one request can be cancelled without disturbing the others. That single field is the difference between listing 18.3 and listing 18.4.

Someone says HTTP/2 “eliminated head-of-line blocking”. What is wrong with that?

It eliminated head-of-line blocking in HTTP and inherited it from TCP, a different layer that was never consulted. TCP delivers one byte stream strictly in order, so a lost segment stops the kernel handing up anything sent after it, including frames from streams that lost nothing; listing 18.5 catches the receiver holding such bytes and reporting them in a SACK block. In one respect HTTP/2 made things worse: consolidating six connections into one means a single loss affects every request rather than a sixth.

QUIC needs nothing that UDP provides. Why is it built on UDP?

Because it is the only way through. A new transport needs an IP protocol number, and equipment along any real path — NAT devices, firewalls, carrier gateways — forwards TCP and UDP and discards what it does not recognise, usually because it cannot find ports to build state around. SCTP has been standardised since 2000 and is still undeployable for this reason. UDP gives QUIC two port numbers and, more valuably, invisibility — chapter 0’s flag-day argument again.

Does HTTP/3 abolish head-of-line blocking?

No, and saying so is the same overstatement as saying HTTP/2 did. QUIC reduces the scope of the blocking to a single stream: losing a packet inside a large image still delays the rest of that image, because those bytes genuinely must arrive in order. What changes is that the stylesheet and the API call sharing the connection are no longer delayed by it — the minimum the data itself demands, which is why table 18.5 has a row whose last column says nothing.

A page is slow. When is upgrading to HTTP/3 the wrong answer?

Whenever the loss rate is low, which is most of the time on a wired network. Everything HTTP/3 improves over HTTP/2 concerns behaviour during loss; on a clean path the two perform similarly, and HTTP/3 can be slower because its work happens in userspace. It is also wrong when the real problem is above the transport — a render-blocking stylesheet, an uncached call, a slow query — the last row of table 18.5 and, in practice, the usual finding (ch 21).

Practice · HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Type an HTTP request by hand into nc and read the response.Remember the \r\n, and the blank line at the end.Easy
02Run curl -V and say whether your build supports HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.The Features line, and the library names above it.Easy
03Fetch one site with --http1.1, --http2 and --http3 and compare the header case.-sI prints headers only.Easy
04Find a site that sends alt-svc and read what it advertises.curl -sI, then look for h3=.Easy
05Reproduce listing 18.3 and explain the timings to somebody else.Run B is the control. Run A is the result.Medium

08Argue whether your own service should enable HTTP/3, with a measurement.What is your users’ loss rate? If you cannot answer, that is the finding.Hard
If HTTP/2 solved the wrong layer, why was it worth doing?

Because it removed a real cost immediately and needed nobody’s cooperation. Most of table 18.2 is build steps that exist to compensate for a framing layer, and HTTP/2 made them unnecessary while running over the same TCP every network already carried. It could be deployed by upgrading a web server and a browser.

The honest reading is that HTTP/2 fixed the blocking it could reach and made the blocking it could not reach more visible: consolidating six connections into one concentrated the damage from a single loss. A fair trade on a good network, a bad one on a lossy mobile link, and exactly the evidence that motivated QUIC. Layers do not get fixed in the right order. They get fixed in the order somebody can deploy.

Why is QUIC implemented in userspace when TCP is in the kernel, and what does that cost?

Because that is what makes it changeable. TCP’s behaviour lives in every operating system on earth, so a change to it takes a decade to reach the machines that matter — the trap chapter 0 describes. QUIC lives inside the application, so a browser vendor can ship a new congestion controller in a release. It is also why QUIC encrypts nearly all of its own header: middleboxes that cannot read its internals cannot come to depend on them, and TCP lost that freedom precisely because its header was readable.

The cost is measurable. TCP’s data path is kernel code tuned for forty years; it avoids a copy between kernel and userspace and can push segmentation and checksums onto the network card. QUIC handles every datagram in userspace and encrypts each packet individually, so on a clean network a well-tuned TCP stack can still win on raw throughput. QUIC’s advantages are where TCP cannot follow: loss recovery that does not stall unrelated streams, one round trip to an encrypted connection instead of two, and surviving a change of address.

Chapter Nineteen · Part V

Proxies and Load Balancers

Between a browser and the server it believes it is talking to there is now, almost always, at least one machine that is neither. It holds the certificate, it decides which of several identical servers gets the request, and it rewrites enough of the traffic that the server behind it can no longer tell who asked. Most of what is baffling about a production web tier — one address in every access log line, a redirect loop that only happens over HTTPS, a cache that empties itself the day you add a node — is a consequence of that machine.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Tell a forward proxy from a reverse proxy by reading one line of the request
  • Say what “layer 4” and “layer 7” actually mean, and what each cannot do
  • Explain why the backend logs the proxy’s address, and fix it without creating a hole
  • Choose between terminating, passing through and re-encrypting TLS
  • Write a health check that does not lie in either of the two usual directions
  • Pick a balancing algorithm, and say why a cache needs a different one

19.1 One program, pointed two ways

A proxy accepts your connection and makes a different one on your behalf. That is the whole definition, and notice what it leaves out: which end of the conversation the proxy belongs to. A forward proxy is configured into the client, so it must be told which server to reach on every request. A reverse proxy is deployed by the site: the client is told nothing, the public name points at it, and its upstream is in its own configuration. Below, one program is used both ways.

Forward proxyReverse proxy
Configured intoThe clientThe site’s infrastructure
Works forThe client’s ownerThe site’s owner
Client knows it existsYes, it was toldNo. DNS points at it
Server knows it existsNoIt is all the server talks to
Request lineAbsolute: GET http://host/pOrigin form: GET /p
Host: namesThe originThe proxy
Upstream comes fromThe requestIts own configuration
Typical jobsEgress filtering, anonymityTLS, load spreading, caching, rate limits

Table 19.1 Every row follows from the first. Chosen by the client, a forward proxy can be asked for any destination, so it is an access-control point, deployed to say no to something. Chosen by the site, a reverse proxy has a fixed set of upstreams the client cannot influence, so it is a capacity and safety device. The rest of this chapter is about reverse proxies.

Why a corporate proxy logs the hostname of every HTTPS site but never the page

The absolute-form trick collapses for https://: a client will not hand a URL to a machine it is not trusting with the plaintext. It sends CONNECT example.com:443 instead, and the proxy copies bytes blindly while the handshake happens end to end through it. So the proxy logs exactly one thing per session — the hostname and port on that line. Not the path, not the cookies, and nothing it can cache, which is why transparent HTTP caches stopped being useful as the web moved to TLS (ch 16).

19.2 L4 and L7, the only two layer numbers used precisely

The seven-layer model from chapter 1 is mostly a vocabulary working engineers ignore. Two of its numbers are exceptions, used with real precision, because they name the only two places where it is useful to cut a connection open.

Layer 4 decides on the TCP four-tuple and nothing else, once per connection, when the SYN arrives; afterwards it is a pipe, blind to URLs, cookies and status codes. Layer 7 reads the application message, which means reassembling the byte stream, which means terminating the connection and being the peer — and it can then decide once per request. Layer 4 comes in two varieties usually spoken of as one thing, and they differ enormously.

L4 by rewriting (DNAT)L4 by relaying (socat)L7 (a real proxy)
DecidesPer connectionPer connectionPer request
Backend sees as clientThe real clientThe balancerThe balancer
Routes on URL or cookieNoNoYes
Retries elsewhere on failureNoNoYes
Non-HTTP trafficAnything over TCPAnything over TCPOnly what it parses
Sees TLS plaintextNoNoOnly if it terminates TLS
State per flowOne conntrack entryTwo socketsTwo sockets and buffers
Return traffic must pass itYesYesYes

Table 19.2 Row seven is why large front doors live in column one: rewriting a header costs a table lookup, proxying costs two sockets and a copy per byte, and the Linux kernel’s own IPVS works this way. Row eight is the constraint that bites — the reply is addressed to the real client, so if the backend has any route to it avoiding the balancer, the reply escapes untranslated and the client, seeing a packet from an address it never dialled, answers with a RST.

19.3 The address the backend sees

The moment a proxy terminates the connection, the backend’s getpeername() stops being a fact about the visitor and becomes a fact about the proxy. Everything quietly built on that address breaks at once and silently — access log, geo-IP lookup, rate limiter, block list — and none of them error. They all just report the load balancer, forever. The fix is for the proxy to write the real address into the request it forwards, and X-Forwarded-For is the header everyone uses. But a request header is something the client can set too, and that is where the trouble starts.

MechanismLives inWorks forNotes
X-Forwarded-ForRequest headerHTTP onlyUniversal, unstandardised, client-writable. Leftmost entry is the claimed original
Forwarded (RFC 7239)Request headerHTTP onlyThe standardised version, carrying for=, proto= and host=. Almost nobody emits it
PROXY protocolBefore the payloadAny TCP protocolv1 one readable line, v2 binary. Both ends must agree
X-Forwarded-ProtoRequest headerHTTP onlySays the request arrived over TLS although this hop did not
TPROXYNothing in the payloadAny TCP protocolThe proxy uses the client’s address as its own source

Table 19.3 Row three exists because rows one and two need an HTTP request to put a header in. With TLS pass-through, or in front of a database, there is nowhere in the protocol to add anything — so the PROXY protocol prepends its line to the TCP stream itself, ahead of the first byte of TLS. Both ends must be configured to match, or every connection becomes a parse error.

The redirect loop that only happens in production

The edge terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP. The backend notices the request arrived over HTTP and redirects to the HTTPS version of the same URL. The browser follows, arrives at the edge over HTTPS, the edge forwards plain HTTP again — forever. It never happens in development, because there is no proxy there. The cause is one missing header, X-Forwarded-Proto: https, which the edge must set and the framework must be told to trust — a setting that is off by default for exactly the reason line 3 above demonstrates.

19.4 Who terminates the TLS

A reverse proxy that wants to read a URL needs the plaintext, and if the connection is encrypted there is one way to get it: hold a private key and be the TLS server (ch 16). That requirement produces the three arrangements every load balancer offers, and choosing between them is choosing where the plaintext may exist — terminate at the edge and speak plain HTTP to the backends; pass through and copy bytes you cannot read; or re-encrypt, terminating one session and opening a second. All three run below against the same request, with a capture on the backend link.

Terminate at edgePass throughRe-encrypt
Private key lives onThe balancerEvery backendBalancer and backends
Routes on URL or cookieYesNoYes
Routes on hostnameYes, from HostYes, from the SNIYes
Backend link carriesPlaintextCiphertextCiphertext
Can cache or add headersYesNoYes
Crypto costOnceNone at the edgeTwice
Renewal touchesOne placeEvery backendEdge, plus an internal CA

Table 19.4 Row three surprises people: an L4 balancer can route on the hostname without terminating anything, because the client puts the name it wants in the ClientHello’s Server Name Indication field, in the clear, before any key exchange. That is how one address fronts hundreds of TLS sites behind a pass-through balancer. Row seven is why pass-through costs more than it looks.

19.5 Health checks, and the two ways a naive one lies

A load balancer’s value is not that it spreads traffic — anything can spread traffic. It is that it stops sending traffic to a server that is broken, which requires an opinion about which servers are broken, and that opinion is only as good as the question asked. Three backends below: one fine, one that answers /health cheerfully while failing every real request, and one that accepts connections and then does nothing at all — the state a process reaches when its thread pool is exhausted, which is far more common than crashing.

The checkCatchesMissesCosts
ICMP echoA dead machineEverything about the serviceNothing
TCP connectA stopped process, a wrong portDeadlock, GC pause, lost dependency, error responsesNothing
/health, constant replyA stopped or wedged processAny broken dependencyOne request
/health, checks dependenciesMost real breakageUntested code pathsLoad on that dependency: every backend, every balancer, every interval
Real requests, codes watchedWhat users experienceLittleUsers find it first

Table 19.5 The table does not simply improve downwards. Row four is where a health check becomes an outage amplifier: if every backend asks the same database whether it is well, the moment it hiccups they all fail together and the balancer removes all of them. Test what this instance can be individually broken at, and nothing shared. Two other numbers matter as much as the check: the probe timeout must be shorter than the interval, and the detection time users feel is interval × threshold.

19.6 Choosing a backend

Once several backends are healthy, something must pick one. The algorithms are short, and the differences only appear when the backends are not identical — which in production they never are, because one is always on a noisier host or halfway through a garbage collection. The listing puts the same twelve requests through the same three backends twice, changing only the selection rule; one backend is deliberately slowed with an eight-hundred-millisecond sleep, because in the lab everything else finishes in microseconds and there would otherwise be nothing to see.

AlgorithmPicks byGood forFails at
Round-robinTurn takingIdentical backendsAny backend slower than the rest
Weighted round-robinTurns, in proportionBackends of known sizesWeights that were true last year
Least connectionsFewest in flightRequests of varying costVery short requests: the count is always 0 or 1
Least time / EWMAIn-flight count weighted by latencyMixed hardware, noisy neighboursCold after a restart — it needs history
Two random choicesSample two, take the less busyMany balancers, many backendsLittle; near least-connections for far less coordination
Consistent hashA hash of a key, on a ringBackends with state: caches, shardsOne hot key overloading one node

Table 19.6 Row five is cheap and counter-intuitive: with several independent balancers, “send it to the least busy backend” makes them all pile onto the same one at the same instant, while sampling two at random and taking the better of the pair avoids that almost entirely. Row six is a different kind of algorithm — the others equalise load, and this one deliberately does not, because equalising load across a set of caches destroys what made them caches.

Checkpoint

Every line of your access log shows the same client address. What happened, and what is the fix?

Something in front of the application terminated the connection, so the address it sees is that proxy’s: getpeername() is telling the exact truth about who connected. The fix is for the proxy to record the original address in X-Forwarded-For, or the PROXY protocol if the traffic is not HTTP, and for the application to be configured to read it. Both halves are needed — a proxy setting a header nobody reads looks identical to the broken case, and an application trusting a header no proxy sets is listing 19.3 line 3 waiting to happen.

A colleague wants a layer 4 load balancer “so we can send /api to the API servers”. What is wrong?

A layer 4 device decides on the four-tuple when the SYN arrives, and at that moment no request exists — the client has not sent a byte of HTTP. Paths, headers and cookies are layer 7, and reading them means terminating the connection, which is the definition of a layer 7 proxy. What a layer 4 device can route on is the destination port and the SNI hostname in a TLS ClientHello, which is often mistaken for URL routing: it is one field, deliberately sent in the clear.

Why can a client put any address it likes in X-Forwarded-For, and what stops that mattering?

Because it is an ordinary request header, and anything that speaks HTTP can send one; headers carry no authentication. What stops it mattering is a rule about position: the proxy at the edge, whose peer is genuinely untrusted, must overwrite the header rather than append to what it was handed. Proxies further in may append, since everything reaching them came from a proxy you operate. On the reading side, count entries from the right by the number of proxies you run, and never trust the leftmost.

Your balancer health-checks with a TCP connect, all backends report healthy, and users get errors.

A TCP connection is completed by the kernel from the listen backlog and requires nothing from the application, so a process that has deadlocked, exhausted its thread pool or is in a long garbage-collection pause accepts connections as promptly as a working one — listing 19.5 shows two such backends both reporting UP. The check must exercise the layer users use: an HTTP request, with a timeout, whose response code is examined, against an endpoint touching something this instance can individually be broken at.

You add a fourth node to a three-node cache pool and the hit rate collapses. What did the balancer do?

It almost certainly selected the node with hash(key) % n, and n changed. Under modulo, changing the pool size renumbers nearly everything: three nodes to four moves about three quarters of the keys, and each is a miss whose data is fetched again while the copy that already exists sits unused on the old node. Consistent hashing puts keys and nodes on one ring, so adding a node disturbs only the arc it lands in — about 1/n, the minimum possible.

Who holds the private key in each of the three TLS arrangements, and which lets the balancer route on a URL?

Terminating at the edge: the balancer holds it and can route on anything in the request. Pass-through: every backend holds one and the balancer holds none, so it can route on address, port and SNI hostname only. Re-encrypt: the balancer holds a key for the public name, the backends hold their own — usually from an internal CA — and it routes on anything, because it decrypts first. The trade is how many places the key exists against how much the balancer may do, and no arrangement avoids it.

Practice · Proxies and Load Balancers

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Send a request through a forward proxy and capture the request line it receives.Look for the absolute form.Easy
02Find the X-Forwarded-For handling in a proxy configuration you already run.Append or overwrite — and does that suit its position?Easy
03Send a forged X-Forwarded-For to a service you own and read its log.Use a documentation address such as 192.0.2.99.Easy
04Build the socat relay from listing 19.2 and confirm the backend sees the relay.One command, and a backend that prints its peer.Easy
05Reproduce the DNAT door and read the connection-tracking entry it creates./proc/net/nf_conntrack. Both tuples are on one line.Medium
06Write a health endpoint that checks exactly one dependency, and defend the choice.What happens when it fails for every backend at once?Medium
07Work out what your own cache pool does when a node is added or removed.If the answer is % n, measure the hit rate across a deployment.Medium
08Implement least-connections and two-random-choices and compare them under a slow backend.Listing 19.6 is the harness; change only the selection rule.Hard
Should the load balancer terminate TLS?

Usually yes, for operational reasons rather than cryptographic ones. Terminating at the edge puts certificate renewal in one place, removing a whole category of outage, and it lets the balancer do what you bought it for: route on the URL, retry elsewhere when a backend fails, add and strip headers, rate-limit per client, and speak HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to the browser while speaking plain HTTP/1.1 to an application that has heard of neither (ch 18). None of that is possible on ciphertext.

The argument against is that the backend link then carries plaintext, and listing 19.4 shows how legible. Whether that matters depends on who else is on that network: in a segment you own it is a reasonable risk, and in a shared or cloud one it is not. That is what re-encrypt is for, and its real cost is not the second handshake but the internal CA you now have to run.

Why is layer 4 still used at all, when layer 7 can do so much more?

Cost per byte, and blast radius. A layer 7 proxy holds two sockets, two buffers and application state per connection and copies every byte through user space; an L4 forwarder of the rewriting kind holds one table entry and lets the kernel move the packet. At the scale where a front door handles millions of concurrent connections that difference decides how many machines it needs, which is why the outermost tier of a large network is almost always layer 4, with layer 7 proxies behind it.

The second reason is that a layer 4 forwarder cannot misunderstand your protocol, because it never parses it: anything over TCP passes unaltered. Every layer 7 proxy in a path is a program that must correctly parse whatever it is handed, and disagreements about header parsing between two proxies in a chain are a well-known source of request-smuggling bugs.

Chapter Twenty · Part VI

Reading a Capture

Every claim in the nineteen chapters before this one was checked by capturing the packets and looking at them. This chapter is about the looking — not the manual page but the method: capture once into a file, then interrogate the file until it answers, rather than re-running an intermittent failure hoping for a better filter next time.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Build a tcpdump command line and say what each flag adds
  • Write a capture to a file and read it back with a different filter
  • Express host, network, port, direction and protocol conditions in BPF
  • Select packets by TCP flag bit, including SYNs without SYN-ACKs
  • Find the six lines in a capture that usually contain the answer
  • Capture on a busy host without filling the disk or dropping packets

20.1 Building the command line

A tcpdump command line is three parts in this order: options, an interface given with -i, and a filter expression. Everything that is not an option belongs to the filter, which is why an unquoted filter containing brackets or a & is mangled by the shell before tcpdump sees it. Quote the filter, every time.

The options split in two. Some decide which packets you get — -i, -c, -s and the filter; the rest decide how much of each is printed. Confusing them is why someone captures for ten minutes and cannot answer the question: they raised the verbosity when they should have widened the filter.

One flag below is a lab artefact and not something you will ever type. tcpdump normally drops privilege after opening its capture socket, switching to an unprivileged account so the code that parses hostile packets has no rights; this lab has no such account, so every capture here says -Z root to make it stay put.

FlagWhat it doesReach for it when
-i eth0One interface; -i any means all of themAlways
-nnNo host lookups and no port-name lookupsAlways
-eThe link header: both MACs, EtherTypeARP, VLANs (ch 2)
-v / -vvThe IP header: TTL, id, DF, lengthTTL and MTU (ch 7, ch 14)
-XHex and ASCII of the contentsYou need the actual bytes
-qOne short line per packetCounting, spotting shape
-c NStop after N packetsAny capture on a busy host
-s NStore only the first N bytes of eachHeaders matter, payloads do not
-w fWrite raw packets to a file, not textAlmost always
-r fRead packets from a file, not an interfaceAnalysis

Table 20.1 The two most often skipped cost the most. Without -nn the tool makes DNS queries while capturing and can print its own queries into your capture. Without -c, an unbounded capture on a production host fills a root filesystem at three in the morning.

20.2 Write it once, read it many times

A live capture is a one-shot. The traffic happens once, so a filter that was slightly wrong means reproducing an intermittent failure to try again — and you must choose how much detail to print before you know what you are looking for.

-w removes the problem. It writes the raw packets to a file, undecoded, and -r reads them back with any flag and any filter at all. Capture and analysis become separate activities happening in different places: you capture on the server and analyse on your laptop. Every listing after this one reads the file built below.

The file is the deliverable, not the transcript

There is a temptation to run tcpdump | tee capture.txt and send someone the text. Do not. Text is one decoding, at one verbosity, with one filter applied, and what it left out is gone. A .pcap is the packets: the recipient can raise the verbosity, dump the bytes, or open it in a tool you do not have.

20.3 The filter language

The filter is not a grep over the output. It is a small program compiled to bytecode and run inside the kernel against every packet, which is why filtering costs almost nothing and why filtering early is how you survive a busy host. Filters are built from primitives joined by and, or and not; a primitive is usually a direction, a kind and a value, as in src host 10.0.0.1. Omit the direction and it matches either.

PrimitiveMatchesNote
host 203.0.113.20Source or destination is that addressThe commonest filter there is
src host X / dst host XOne direction onlyhost is optional: src X works
net 203.0.113.0/24Either address is in that networkCIDR or a mask (ch 4)
port 9201Either port is 9201, TCP or UDPSay tcp port if you mean one
src port 9201Traffic from that port — the server sideThe cheapest way to see one direction
portrange 9200-9209Any port in the rangeA service with a block of ports
tcp, udp, icmp, arpThat protocolip, ip6, vlan too
and, or, not&&, ||, ! also workBracket freely

Table 20.2 Two of these mislead. port 9201 matches UDP as well as TCP, and matches the port at either end. And negation does not compose as expected: not host A and not host B is what you want; not (host A and host B) matches nearly everything.

20.4 Filters that read bits

Everything so far filtered on fields the language names. Underneath, BPF addresses any byte at any offset, written proto[offset] or proto[offset:size]: tcp[13] is the flag byte, ip[8] the TTL. That byte is wanted so constantly that tcpdump names it tcp[tcpflags] and names each of its bits — which is where a capture stops being a transcript and becomes a diagnostic tool.

NameBitSet onRead it as
tcp-fin0x01A polite closeI have no more to send (ch 11)
tcp-syn0x02Both packets of a handshakeA connection is opening (ch 10)
tcp-rst0x04A refusal or an abortSomething went wrong. Always look
tcp-push0x08Most packets that carry dataDeliver this to the application
tcp-ack0x10Everything after the first SYNUseless alone, essential in combination
tcp-urg0x20Almost nothing, everIf you see it, be suspicious

Table 20.3 The two forms you will actually type are tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0, “SYN set, never mind the rest”, and tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn, “SYN set and ACK clear”. The first counts handshake packets, the second counts attempts; the two diverging is itself a finding.

tcpdump does not flag retransmissions — you spot them

A retransmission has no bit of its own: it is an ordinary packet whose sequence number covers bytes already sent, and you recognise it by noticing you have seen that number before. The repeated SYNs to 9208 in listing 20.2 all carry the same seq — same connection, same number, later timestamp. Wireshark labels these for you, but the label is a heuristic and the sequence numbers are the evidence.

20.5 The six lines that contain the answer

A capture from a real server is long, and reading it is hopeless: by line three hundred you have lost the thread. The answer is almost always in a handful of specific lines, so go and get exactly those. The list is short deliberately — six filters you can type from memory at two in the morning.

Look forThe filterWhat it settles
1. The first SYNtcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-synThat the client tried, when, and to which address
2. The first responsesrc host SERVER and tcp port PSYN-ACK means something is there; RST means refused; silence means dropped
3. The first data packetThe payload-length expression from 20.4That the connection was used, not merely opened, and how long the application took
4. Any RSTtcp[tcpflags] & tcp-rst != 0Who gave up. A reset mid-conversation is a different fault from one instead of a handshake
5. Any retransmissionA sequence number you have seen beforeThat packets are being lost, and in which direction (ch 12)
6. The last packet| tail -1How it ended: FIN is clean, RST is an abort, an unanswered retransmission means it stopped

Table 20.4 Work down that list and the failure is classified before you have read a hundred lines. Four of the six concern the beginning and the end rather than the contents, which is where the information is: the middle of a healthy conversation is thousands of packets saying the same thing.

The lab cannot show you a realistic round-trip time

Line 2 of table 20.4 has a second use: the gap between the SYN and the SYN-ACK is the round-trip time to that server, measured for free. This book cannot demonstrate it honestly. Both machines are namespaces on one kernel joined by a virtual cable, so the round trip is tens of microseconds — visible in listing 20.2, where the whole conversation occupies under a millisecond — and the traffic shaper one would normally reach for to induce delay is not installed on this machine. The technique is unaffected: subtract the two timestamps, or let -ttt do it.

20.6 Capturing on a busy host without drowning

Everything above ran on a network carrying only what we put on it. A production host may be moving a gigabit per second — roughly a gigabyte of capture file every eight seconds — and the packets you want are a few dozen. Three independent levers help: a tight filter, the big one, because it runs in the kernel and rejected packets are never copied to userspace at all; -s N, which keeps only the first N bytes of each packet; and -c N, a hard bound. The listing runs one four-megabyte transfer past three captures at once: everything on the port; only the packets that open or close a connection, at 96 bytes each; and the same again at a snapshot length that is too short.

A capture is not the wire

It is a copy taken at one point in one kernel. Segments larger than the MTU are offload; [|tcp] is your own snapshot length; a gap may be the kernel dropping rather than the network; sequence numbers starting at 1 are relative to the SYN, and -S shows the real ones. And nothing at all usually means the wrong interface — so before concluding traffic is absent, ping and watch it appear.

When to stop using tcpdump

tcpdump keeps no memory of a connection, so it cannot label a retransmission, reassemble a stream spread over forty packets, or chart throughput. Those questions want a tool that keeps state.

The questionToolWhy
What is on this interface right now?tcpdumpAlready installed, starts instantly
Capture it and take it awaytcpdump -wNothing else belongs on a production host
Which conversations, and how much each?WiresharkIt keeps per-conversation state
Was that a retransmission?WiresharkIt tracks sequence numbers across the file
What did the application actually send?Wireshark“Follow stream” reassembles the bytes
Where is this TLS handshake failing?WiresharkIt decodes the handshake properly (ch 16)

Table 20.5 The division is about where each tool runs, not which is better. tcpdump belongs on the server: small, present, no display needed. Wireshark belongs on your laptop: large, stateful, interactive. The bridge is the .pcap from 20.2.

Checkpoint

Why -nn rather than -n?

The second n stops port numbers being looked up in /etc/services, and that lookup is the more damaging because it is silent and usually wrong — listing 20.3 prints 9201 as wap-wsp-wtp. The file records what was registered decades ago, not what is running. On a live capture there is a second reason: resolution means DNS queries, which leave through the interface you are capturing.

Should you send a colleague the .pcap or the text you saw?

The .pcap, essentially always. Text is one decoding at one verbosity with one filter applied, and what it omitted is unrecoverable: if they need the bytes, the TTL, or a packet your filter excluded, you must reproduce the failure. The caution is that a full-payload capture may contain credentials — -s 96 hands over the headers without the contents.

tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0 returned twice as many packets as you expected. Why?

Because it matches the SYN-ACK too: the SYN bit is set on both packets of a handshake, so a healthy connection contributes two matches, not one. To count connection attempts, require the ACK bit to be clear as well — tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn. Keep both counts: if attempts greatly outnumber SYN-ACKs, something is not answering.

A capture shows a TCP segment of 65,160 bytes on a link whose MTU is 1500. Is the MTU wrong?

No, and nothing is broken. tcpdump taps inside the kernel, above the point where segmentation offload hands a large buffer to the card and the card cuts it into MTU-sized frames; the reverse happens on receive. The wire carried 1500-byte frames, and the capture recorded the buffer. So do not reason about MTU (ch 14) from a capture taken on an endpoint.

Your capture shows loss. How do you know it is the network’s loss and not yours?

By reading the summary tcpdump prints when it stops. “Packets dropped by kernel” is what was thrown away because the capture buffer filled and tcpdump was not reading fast enough; a non-zero count means holes indistinguishable from network loss. The fixes are the three levers of 20.6, plus -w rather than formatting text on screen, which is far more expensive per packet than people expect.

A connection “does not work”. The capture shows a SYN and then nothing. What have you learned?

That this is not an application problem. Nothing answered, which rules out a server present and refusing — that returns a RST immediately, as port 9209 does in listing 20.5. Silence means the SYN was discarded without an error, which is what a firewall DROP rule does by design (ch 17). The next question is where: capture at a second point, and if the SYN leaves your host and never arrives, the two files bracket the fault.

Practice · Reading a Capture

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Capture ten packets on your own machine with -nn and read every field of one line.Name each part before moving on.Easy
02Capture to a file with -w, then read it back three times with three filters.The point is that the traffic only happens once.Easy
03Run one read with -n and one with -nn, and find a port name that is wrong.Anything above 8000 in /etc/services is good hunting.Easy
04Find every SYN your machine sent in a minute, without the SYN-ACKs.tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-syn|tcp-ack) == tcp-syn.Easy
05Write one filter for “to that host, on that port, in that direction, not ICMP”.Bracket it, then check it matches what you meant.Medium
