07Capture one exchange with -s 96 and with the default; compare the file sizes.Then check what the small one can still answer.Medium
08Take one capture of a real failure and answer all six rows of table 20.4 from it.Those six lines are your report.Hard
When should the filter go in the capture and when in the read?

Put it in the capture only when you must, and keep it as wide as you can afford. A capture filter is destructive: packets it rejects are never written, and if the answer was in traffic you excluded, the only remedy is to reproduce the failure. On a quiet host, capture everything and filter on the read.

On a busy host you have no choice, because the kernel cannot copy a gigabit a second to userspace and will drop packets trying. The compromise is to bound the capture by subject rather than detail: host 10.1.2.3 keeps the whole conversation, including the ARP and ICMP around it, and still discards almost everything. Do the narrowing on the read, where a mistake costs one press of the up-arrow.

The capture is clean at both ends and the users still say it is broken. Now what?

First make sure “clean” means what you think. Check the drop counters on both captures, because a capture that lost packets looks clean in the sense that nothing bad is visible. Then confirm both files contain the conversation being complained about, matched by port and by time.

If the packets are healthy at both ends, the network has done its job and the problem is above it — and the capture is the fastest way to prove it. A clean handshake, a request, and a response four seconds later means the server took four seconds to think. Time in a capture is attributable: the gaps belong either to the path or to an endpoint, and which is usually obvious from where the gap falls (ch 21).

Chapter Twenty-One · Part VI

Diagnosis

Every network problem arrives as a sentence from someone who is not looking at the network: it is down, it is slow, it works sometimes. Those three sentences describe three investigations with almost nothing in common, and the most expensive mistake in this chapter is starting the wrong one. What follows is a method — classify the symptom, walk a fixed ladder of questions, change exactly one thing — demonstrated against faults broken on purpose in the lab.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Sort a report into one of three symptom classes before running any command
  • Walk the ladder — link, address, route, neighbour, port, application — and name the command for each rung
  • Tell “nothing answered” from “something refused”, and say what each one rules out
  • Read ss -ti and decide between latency, loss and the application
  • Recognise the fingerprints of the commonest intermittent faults
  • Change one thing at a time, and prove that the change was the cause

21.1 Three questions, and only then a command

The instinct when something breaks is to run a command, usually ping, because it is the one everybody knows. That is not a method, and it fails in a specific way: ping answers a question about reachability, and most production complaints are not about reachability. Answering the wrong question quickly feels like progress, which is why a bad diagnosis can take a day.

So the first move costs nothing and is not a command. Decide which of three sentences you have:

The reportWhat it really meansFirst commandWhat it is not
It is downNothing works, consistently, and probably for everyoneWalk the ladder from the link upwardsNot a performance question. Measure nothing
It is slowIt works, but a request or a transfer takes too longss -ti on a socket while it is slowNot usually a bandwidth question (ch 12)
It is intermittentSome requests succeed and some do not, with no obvious patternMake it countable before you make it stopNot a single fault. Something in the path varies

Table 21.1 The commonest wasted afternoon in networking is a bandwidth test run against a complaint that turns out to be latency or loss; the second commonest is reasoning about an intermittent fault as though it were a permanent one — testing, seeing it work, declaring it fixed. Classification is not bureaucracy. It selects the evidence you are about to gather.

For “it is down” there is a fixed ladder, and its order is not arbitrary: each rung depends on the ones below it, so an answer at any level makes everything above it irrelevant. Six questions, six commands, asked here of a network where nothing is wrong — because you cannot recognise a bad answer if you have never looked at a good one:

RungQuestionCommandA good answerA bad answer
1 LinkIs the interface alive?ip -br linkUP and LOWER_UPDOWN, or NO-CARRIER
2 AddressDo I have the right one?ip -br addrAddress and the expected prefix lengthNo address, or the wrong mask
3 RouteWhich way out?ip route get <dst>A next hop, a device and a sourceNetwork is unreachable
4 NeighbourDo I know the next hop’s MAC?ip neighREACHABLE or STALEFAILED, or INCOMPLETE
5 PortIs anything listening?ss -ltn on the serverA LISTEN row on the right addressNothing, or bound to 127.0.0.1
6 ApplicationDoes it answer correctly?curl, or the real clientThe expected replyAn error the application produced itself

Table 21.2 Two rungs are worth arguing about. Rung 4 is skipped by almost everyone and is where a duplicate address or a stale cache hides (ch 3): a FAILED entry for your own gateway is a whole diagnosis in one line. Rung 5 must be run on the server, because a listening socket is a fact about the server’s kernel and cannot be observed from anywhere else — and half of all “the firewall is blocking us” escalations end there, with a service that was never started or was started on loopback only.

21.2 It is down

“Down” is the kind class. The fault is present every time you look, so evidence is free and the only way to fail is to gather it in the wrong order. Work upward, and treat every answer as eliminating everything below it. Two faults follow, both broken on purpose, both producing a total outage, and both reported by users in exactly the same words.

Rungs 1 to 4 fail with errors. Rung 5 is different: a port can fail in three ways that the application reports as only two, and telling them apart decides who gets paged.

What the client seesOn the wireMeansFix
Connection refused, instantlyRST from the serverHost up and reachable; nothing bound to that portStart the service, or check the port number
Connection refused, instantlyICMP port unreachableA firewall rejected it, politelyChange the rule. The service may be running perfectly
TimeoutNothing comes backA DROP rule, a routing fault, or a dead hostFind out how far the packets get
No route to hostICMP host unreachableA router on the path has no route, or ARP failed on the last hopRouting, or the neighbour table (ch 3, ch 6)
Network is unreachableNothing was sentYour own routing table refused. Entirely localRungs 2 and 3

Table 21.3 Rows one and two are indistinguishable to the application, which is why a capture is worth taking even for a trivial-looking failure. Row three is the ambiguous one and the reason DROP is a contentious policy: it withholds information from legitimate users as effectively as from attackers, which is why many networks prefer REJECT internally and DROP only at the edge. Row five saves you opening a ticket with somebody else — nothing left your machine, so nothing outside it can be at fault.

21.3 It is slow

“Slow” is where the wrong command does the most damage, because the wrong command is obvious and easy to run. A bandwidth test measures how fast a single, greedy, long-lived transfer can go. Almost nothing in production looks like that, and a link can pass one at full speed while every real request on it is slow, for reasons the test is structurally unable to see. There are four causes and they need different fixes (ch 12). One command reports on three of them at once, from a live socket, without adding a single packet:

Field in ss -tiA bad value looks likeDiagnosisWhat will not help
rttHigh, and stableDistance, or a queue on the pathMore bandwidth
rtt variation (second number)Large next to rttA congested queue, or a wireless linkRetrying faster
bytes_retrans / bytes_sentA noticeable percentageLoss. Find the device droppingTuning either endpoint
cwndA few segments after seconds of transferLoss again, from the other sideA larger receive window
Send-QZero, while the user waitsThe application. It is not sendingAnything at all on the network
Send-QFull and staying fullThe network cannot drain it — genuinely the pathBlaming the application

Table 21.4 Rows five and six are the same field and opposite conclusions, which is why looking at it beats any amount of speculation. Read them in order: retransmissions first, because loss makes everything else lie; then round-trip time; then Send-Q. Only if all three are healthy should you start asking about the capacity of the link.

Why a bandwidth test is usually the wrong first command

It answers a question nobody asked. A speed test opens a greedy transfer, often several in parallel, and reports the maximum it achieved — a number insensitive to almost everything that makes real traffic slow. It says nothing about latency, because it measures a sustained stream; nothing about a chatty application, because it is the opposite of one; and it can even hide loss, because parallel streams recover collectively in a way one stream does not. It also takes time and capacity on a network somebody is already complaining about. ss -ti is instantaneous, generates no traffic, and reports on the connection that is actually slow.

21.4 It is intermittent

This is the hard class, for one reason: the thing that varies is not the thing you are changing. You test, it works, you declare victory, and it fails again an hour later for somebody else. Two rules make it tractable.

Make it countable before you try to make it stop. “Sometimes” is not data. Run the failing operation fifty times and count. One in three is a pool with a bad member; one in a thousand is something else; and if the loop never fails, the trigger is a property you have not reproduced — a size, a source address, a time of day, a particular client.

Then look for something in the path with more than one state. An intermittent fault almost always means the packets are not all taking the same journey, or that a device in the middle keeps state and loses it. Here is the first of those:

FaultFingerprintCommand that confirms it
One bad member of a poolA fixed fraction of requests fail, immediately and identicallyBypass the service address and probe each member
DNS to a broken backendFails for some clients, or after a restart; ping and the app disagreedig +short for every record, then probe each address (ch 15)
MTU black holeConnects fine, small requests fine, anything large hangsping -M do -s N, binary search (ch 14)
Stateful device forgettingLong-lived idle connections die; short ones never doIdle the connection deliberately, then send
Conntrack table fullNew connections fail under load, existing ones survivenf_conntrack_count against nf_conntrack_max; kernel log
Asymmetric routingOne direction works; fails only where a stateful device sitsCapture on both paths and compare what each sees

Table 21.5 Rows four, five and six are one mechanism in three costumes. A stateful firewall or NAT forwards a packet only if it can find the connection that packet belongs to; if it cannot, the packet is discarded in silence. The state may be missing because it expired, because the table was full when the entry should have been made, or because the opening packet went down a different path and this device never saw it. In all three cases both endpoints still believe the connection is healthy.

Two of those are worth watching happen — the black hole and the forgetful firewall — because they share the property that defeats ordinary debugging: the fault is in the middle, and neither end can see it.

What the lab could not do: fill the connection-tracking table

Row five of table 21.5 is not demonstrated above, and the reason is a limit of this book’s lab rather than a gap in the argument. nf_conntrack_max is read-only inside the unprivileged user namespace the lab runs in — the write is refused — so the ceiling cannot be lowered to a value a listing could reach, and filling the real one would mean opening the hundreds of thousands of connections its default allows. The documented behaviour: when the table is full the kernel discards the packet that would have created a new entry and logs nf_conntrack: table full, dropping packet. The symptom is distinctive — new connections fail while established ones continue happily, because those already have entries — and the check is to compare nf_conntrack_count with nf_conntrack_max under /proc/sys/net/netfilter/ on the device in the middle, never on either endpoint.

21.5 The table, and the discipline

Everything above collapses into one page. The value of a table like this is that it removes a decision at the moment you are least able to make one.

SymptomFirst commandIf it answers well, look at
Network is unreachableip route get <dst>Nothing else. The fault is local, at rung 2 or 3
Nothing works from this machineip -br addr; ip route get <dst>The far end — climb the ladder there too
Ping works, the service does notss -ltn on the serverFirewall rules, and their counters
Connection refusedss -ltn on the serverWhether a REJECT rule is impersonating it
Connect times outtcpdump at each hop in turnHow far the packets get before they stop
Works, but slowss -ti on the live socketRetransmissions, then RTT, then Send-Q
Connects, then hangs when data flowsping -M do -s 1472 <dst>The path MTU, and who is hiding it
A fixed share of requests failA loop of fifty, countedEach pool member, probed directly
Idle connections die, short ones do notIdle it deliberately, then retryEvery stateful device between the two ends
Works from here, not from thereip route get from bothAsymmetric paths, and per-source firewall rules

Table 21.6 Read the middle column as an instruction to gather one piece of evidence, not as a fix. None of these commands repairs anything; each eliminates a large region of the search space, which is the only thing that reliably shortens an outage. The ping -M do row is the best ten seconds in the table: a large share of “the application is broken” escalations are chapter 14 in disguise.

Change one thing at a time. Under pressure the temptation is to change four things at once because one of them will surely work. Something then starts working and you have learned nothing: you do not know which change mattered, you cannot write an honest incident report, and you have three unexplained modifications in production that will surprise somebody in six months. A fault you fixed without understanding is a fault you will meet again.

  1. Write down the symptom before touching anything, precisely enough to test. “Large downloads from host-b stall after about 1400 bytes”, not “the network is bad”.
  2. Make one change, and say out loud what you expect it to do.
  3. Test the original symptom, not a proxy for it. A successful ping does not prove a stalled download is fixed.
  4. If it did not help, put it back. Accumulated debris is why the second outage is always harder than the first.
  5. When it works, prove it. Undo the fix and check the symptom returns. That minute is the difference between a diagnosis and a coincidence.
Bisect the path, not the configuration

When the ladder does not settle it, stop reasoning about which setting is wrong and start narrowing where the packets stop. Capture at the sender, the first router, the last router, the receiver. Each capture answers one question — did the packet get this far — and each answer halves the path. Listing 21.2 is this method at its smallest: one tcpdump at the far end proved the request arrived, eliminating the entire outbound path in a single command. It beats inspecting configuration because a capture cannot be out of date, cannot be overridden by something you forgot about, and does not require you to guess correctly first.

Checkpoint

A user reports a total outage. What do you do before running any command?

Decide which of the three sentences it is, and restate the symptom in a form you can test. The classification is usually wrong on arrival — a report of “down” frequently turns out to be a timeout on one specific operation, which is a completely different investigation. Ask what exactly fails, from where, since when, and for whom. That last question is the most valuable in the list: if it fails for one client and not another, you have an intermittent or path-dependent fault, and the ladder is the wrong tool.

ping to a server works, but connecting to its port times out. What has that ruled out?

Rungs one to four, in both directions. A successful echo reply proves the link is up, both addresses are right, routing works outbound and back, and neighbour resolution succeeded on each segment — a reply cannot return along a broken return path. So the fault is at rung five or above: nothing bound to the port, a DROP rule discarding the segments, or a service bound to loopback only. The next command is ss -ltn on the server, then iptables -L -v -n to see whose counter moves when you retry.

Why does Connection refused not tell you the service is stopped?

Because two different things produce it and the application cannot distinguish them. A kernel with nothing bound to the port answers with a TCP reset; a firewall with a REJECT rule answers with an ICMP port-unreachable message. The C library maps both to ECONNREFUSED, which is why listing 21.3 shows two ports reporting identical errors for entirely different reasons. Only a capture separates them, and the distinction decides whether you restart a service or edit a rule.

A transfer is slow. Why is ss -ti a better first command than a bandwidth test?

Because it reports on three of the four causes at once, instantly, from the connection that is actually slow, without putting an extra packet on a network somebody is already complaining about. It gives you the kernel’s own measured round-trip time, the retransmission counters that prove or disprove loss, the congestion window, and Send-Q, which says whether the application is even trying. A bandwidth test measures one thing — the ceiling of a greedy transfer — and that is the least common cause of slowness in production.

Fifty requests, fifteen fail, and each failure is instant. What does that shape suggest?

A pool with a bad member, and roughly one member in three. A fixed fraction of failures is the signature of something distributing requests across several destinations: a load balancer, a DNS name with several address records, or a client library holding a list of servers. The instant failure narrows it further — the bad member is answering with a reset rather than swallowing packets, so it is reachable and simply has nothing bound. Probe each member directly, and distrust the balancer’s own statistics, which count dispatches and not successes.

You changed three things and the problem went away. What is wrong with that?

You have not fixed anything you can describe. You cannot say which change mattered, cannot write an accurate incident report, cannot tell whether the other two have introduced new problems, and cannot prevent the fault recurring. You have also left two unexplained modifications in a production system, which is how the next outage becomes harder than this one. Revert to a single change, confirm the symptom returns, then re-apply the one change and confirm it goes away. A fault that disappears without being understood has not been fixed; its schedule has merely changed.

Practice · Diagnosis

Type them. Reading a command and running it are different skills, and only one of them is the one you need at 2am.

01Run all six ladder commands against a host you can reach, and write down each answer.Listing 21.1 is the model. Know the healthy shape first.Easy
02Break your own default route on a test machine and identify it from the symptom alone.ip route del default. Note that the error is immediate and local.Easy
03Find one service on your machine bound to 127.0.0.1 and one bound to 0.0.0.0.ss -ltn. Say which one a colleague could reach.Easy
04Add a REJECT rule and a DROP rule on a test port, and tell them apart from a client.You will need a capture. Listing 21.3 is the method.Easy
05Run ss -ti during a real download and read rtt, cwnd and the retransmit counters.Compare a nearby server with a distant one.Medium
06Binary-search the path MTU to three servers and see whether any is below 1500.ping -M do -s N. Add 28 for the headers.Medium
07Write the fifty-request loop from section 21.4 and run it against a service behind a load balancer.Count. Then probe each backend the DNS name resolves to.Medium
08Take a fault you diagnosed recently and write down which command eliminated which possibilities.If no command eliminated anything, you were guessing.Hard
Why is a timeout so much less informative than an error, and what do you do about it?

An error is a report from something that made a decision. Network is unreachable means your own routing table declined; Connection refused means a remote kernel or firewall answered you; No route to host means a router on the path gave up and said so. Each identifies who decided, and therefore where to look. A timeout is the absence of a decision, and is consistent with a DROP rule anywhere on the path, a dead host, a broken return route, an MTU black hole, a stateful device that lost its state, or a machine that is simply overloaded — the client cannot distinguish them because it received nothing at all.

The response is to stop asking the endpoints and start asking the path. A timeout means packets are disappearing somewhere, and somewhere is a location: capture at successive points and find the last place the packet exists. Listing 21.2 does this at the smallest possible scale, where a single tcpdump on the far end converted “100% loss, no error” into “the request arrives and no reply is generated”, eliminating the entire outbound path in one command. The technique works whether the path has two hops or twenty.

Both endpoints report a connection as ESTABLISHED, but nothing gets through. How?

Because ESTABLISHED is a belief held independently by each end, not a shared fact. TCP state lives in two kernels and changes only when packets arrive; if nothing arrives, nothing changes, so a connection where neither end has sent recently looks perfectly healthy to both even if every device between them has forgotten it exists. There is no heartbeat in TCP by default — that is what the optional keepalive is for, and it is off unless the application asks, with a default idle period measured in hours.

Listing 21.6 shows exactly this: a stateful firewall expired its entry during an idle period, so the next segment matched no connection and was discarded along with every retransmission of it. The same missing state can arise because a table filled up and the entry was never created, or because the opening packet took a different path and this device never saw it — the asymmetric-routing case. The lesson is that endpoint state is evidence about the endpoints and nothing else. When both ends disagree with reality, the answer is in the middle, and you find it with a rule counter or a capture on the device that keeps the state.

Chapter B · Reference

The Networking Cheat Sheet

Everything the previous twenty-three chapters spent pages establishing, compressed into tables arranged for finding something in at three in the morning. Nothing here is new. Rows are cross-referenced back to the chapter that earned them, so a lookup that raises a question has somewhere to go.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to
  • Convert a prefix length to a mask and a usable host count without doing arithmetic
  • Translate a command you know on Linux into its macOS or Windows equivalent
  • Recognise a reserved address range on sight and name the RFC that reserved it
  • Write a tcpdump or ss filter that selects exactly what you meant
  • Read an ICMP type and code, or a TCP flag byte, straight out of a capture
  • Go from a symptom to the one command that narrows it, without guessing

B.1 The layers, and what lives at each

This chapter is a lookup table, not a chapter. Use the section headings as an index and read only the row you came for. Two things are worth knowing before you trust any of it. Everything inside a terminal block below was run — in the lab from chapter A, by the build that produced this page — and the four listings exist to check the tables beside them against a real network stack rather than against memory. Nothing in the macOS or Windows columns was run by anything. This book’s lab is Linux network namespaces, and there is no honest way to capture a PowerShell transcript from inside one; those columns are documented equivalents, and are flagged again where it matters.

LayerUnitIts addressHeaderWhat decides where it goesDevicesCh

Table B.1 Read the address column downwards and the shape of the whole subject appears: each layer has its own namespace, and none of them can see any other’s. That is precisely why the two translation protocols exist — ARP converts an IP address into a MAC (ch 3), DNS converts a name into an IP address (ch 15) — and why both are such fertile sources of failure, because each is a join between two systems that otherwise know nothing about one another. Chapter 1 reads four of these layers off one captured packet, byte by byte; for the OSI numbering, and why its layers 5 and 6 collapsed into one, see table 0.3.

Table B.2 Every number in this table was computed by the build, not typed, so it cannot be wrong in the way a hand-copied mask table usually is. Three ways to use it. Usable hosts is two fewer than the address count for every prefix down to /30, because the all-zeros address names the network and the all-ones address is its broadcast — neither can be given to a host. The wildcard column plus one is the block size: a /26 has wildcard 0.0.0.63, so /26 networks begin at .0, .64, .128 and .192, which is the whole of subnetting arithmetic (ch 5). And the mask is just the prefix written the long way — /24 and 255.255.255.0 are the same 32-bit number (ch 4).

† The last two rows are the exceptions, and the figures in them are conventions rather than arithmetic. A /31 has no room for a separate network and broadcast address at all, so RFC 3021 declares that on a point-to-point link both addresses are simply used as host addresses; Linux implements this, and it halves the address cost of every router-to-router link in a large network. A /32 is one address — not a subnet but a host route, which is how loopback addresses, anycast service addresses and per-container routes are expressed.

Table B.3 Two practical uses. Reading a capture, this table tells you instantly whether an address can possibly have come from the public internet — a packet sourced from 169.254 or 100.64 is telling you something about the sender’s situation before you have read any other field. Writing a firewall or an allocation plan, it tells you which ranges are safe to use and which will collide with something. The one people are surprised by is 127.0.0.0/8: the entire sixteen million addresses loop back, so 127.0.0.2 and 127.9.9.9 are as local as 127.0.0.1, which is occasionally useful for binding several services to distinct loopback addresses on one port.

Table B.4 The eight bold rows are the ones to commit to memory: between them they describe a machine’s entire position on a network. Which route will be used for this address is the most under-used command among them: it does not print the routing table, it runs the actual lookup for one destination and tells you the answer, including the source address the kernel will choose — and it works when the table is too long to read. Note the empty cells in the net-tools column: route has no equivalent of ip route get at all, and ifconfig cannot remove one address from an interface that has several. sudo, and an elevated prompt on Windows, are omitted throughout to keep the cells readable; everything that changes a setting needs one.

One of these four columns was executed. Three were not.

Listing B.1 below is this build running eight of table B.4’s Linux commands — the two Linux columns against each other, on one machine, in one moment, in the lab from chapter A. The macOS and Windows columns were executed by nothing at all. This volume’s lab is built from Linux network namespaces; it cannot run pfctl or Get-NetTCPConnection, and inventing a plausible transcript for them would break the only rule this book has. They are given as documented equivalents, and the sensible way to use them is as a search term rather than as a command to paste. Two are worth a warning in particular: netstat on macOS is the BSD one and takes different flags from the Linux one with the same name, and netsh on Windows has been in slow replacement by PowerShell cmdlets for a decade, so both spellings are given where both still work.

PortTransportServiceWorth knowing

445tcpSMBNever expose it. This is the port ransomware worms travel on
465, 587tcpSMTP submission587 with STARTTLS, 465 with implicit TLS. Both are client-to-server, unlike 25

27017tcpMongoDB

Table B.5 Ports fall into three ranges, and only the first is enforced by anything: 0–1023 are the system ports, and on Unix a process needs privilege to bind one, which is the entire reason web servers are started as root and then drop it; 1024–49151 are registered with IANA, and the registration is a convention with no teeth; 49152–65535 are the dynamic or ephemeral range. Linux ignores that last boundary — listing B.2 prints the range the kernel actually draws outgoing ports from, and it starts well below 49152, inside the registered range. That is why a service can occasionally fail to start because an unrelated outgoing connection has already taken its port (ch 9).

B.5 ICMP: what the network says when it says no

TypeCodeNameWhat it means, and where you meet it
00Echo replyThe answer to a ping (ch 7)
30Destination unreachable — network unreachableA router along the way has no route at all
31… host unreachableThe last router had a route but could not ARP for the host (ch 3)
32… protocol unreachableThe host does not implement that IP protocol number
33… port unreachableNothing is bound to that UDP port. The one ICMP an application usually never sees (ch 13)
34… fragmentation needed and DF setCarries the next link’s MTU. Block this and large transfers hang forever (ch 14)
39, 10, 13… administratively prohibitedWhat a firewall REJECT sends when told to be polite (ch 17)
40Source quenchDeprecated by RFC 6633. Routers must no longer send it
50–3Redirect“There is a better router on this segment.” Usually disabled, because it is trivially forgeable
80Echo requestWhat ping sends (ch 7)
90Router advertisementRarely used in IPv4
100Router solicitationRarely used in IPv4
110Time exceeded in transitTTL reached zero. This message is how traceroute works (ch 7)
111Fragment reassembly time exceededSome fragments arrived, one never did (ch 14)
120–2Parameter problemA header field the receiver could not make sense of
13, 140Timestamp request, replyLeaks the host clock. Commonly blocked
17, 180Address mask request, replyDeprecated; the mask now comes from DHCP

Table B.6 Three rows do real work and the rest are trivia: 8 and 0 are ping, 11/0 is traceroute, and 3/4 is path MTU discovery. The last of those is the reason “block all ICMP” is such a damaging firewall policy — it does not degrade the mechanism, it removes it, and the failure that results is silent (ch 14). Listing B.3 selects on three of these rows using icmp[0] and icmp[1], the type and code bytes, and prints one of them decoded — so at least part of this table can be checked against real packets rather than taken on trust.

ICMPv6 renumbers everything. 1 is destination unreachable, 2 is packet too big, 3 is time exceeded, 4 is parameter problem, 128 and 129 are echo request and reply, and 133 to 137 are neighbour discovery — router solicitation and advertisement, neighbour solicitation and advertisement, redirect. That last group is why blocking ICMPv6 wholesale does not merely break path MTU discovery, it breaks address resolution and therefore the network (ch 3).

B.6 TCP: the flag byte, and the states it drives

HexFlagtcpdumpMeans
0x01FINFNo more data from this sender. Half of a close (ch 11)
0x02SYNSOpen a connection; the sequence number field holds my initial sequence number (ch 10)
0x04RSTRThis connection does not exist. Stop immediately, no acknowledgement expected (ch 11)
0x08PSHPDeliver to the application now rather than waiting for a full buffer
0x10ACK.The acknowledgement field is meaningful. Set on every packet after the first
0x20URGUThe urgent pointer is meaningful. Effectively unused, and a perennial security curiosity
0x40ECEEECN echo — a router marked congestion rather than dropping (ch 12)
0x80CWRWCongestion window reduced, in reply to an ECE (ch 12)
0x02SYN[S]The first packet of a connection
0x12SYN+ACK[S.]The second packet — 0x10 + 0x02
0x10ACK[.]The third packet, and most packets thereafter
0x18PSH+ACK[P.]Data, with a request to deliver it promptly
0x11FIN+ACK[F.]An orderly close (ch 11)
0x14RST+ACK[R.]What a closed port answers with (ch 9)

Table B.7 All eight flags live in a single byte at offset 13 of the TCP header, which is what makes tcp[13] such a useful filter — and listing B.3 checks two rows of this table against real packets, selecting exactly the SYN with tcp[13] == 0x02 and exactly the SYN-ACK with tcp[13] == 0x12. Read tcpdump’s notation as a set: the bare . means ACK and nothing else, so [P.] is push-and-acknowledge, and anything with no letters at all is impossible.

Statess calls itWho is hereIt leaves whenAlarming?
LISTENLISTENA server that has called listen()A SYN arrivesNo
SYN-SENTSYN-SENTA client that has called connect()A SYN-ACK arrivesPiling up means the far end is not answering (ch 10)
SYN-RECEIVEDSYN-RECVA server that answered a SYNThe final ACK arrivesThousands of these is a SYN flood (ch 10)
ESTABLISHEDESTABBoth ends, with data flowingSomeone sends a FINNo
FIN-WAIT-1FIN-WAIT-1The end that closed firstIts FIN is acknowledgedNo
FIN-WAIT-2FIN-WAIT-2The closer, waiting for the other FINThe peer’s FIN arrivesStuck here means the peer never closed its half
CLOSE-WAITCLOSE-WAITThe end that received a FINIts application calls close()Yes. A pile of these is an application bug, not a network one (ch 11)
LAST-ACKLAST-ACKThe passive closer, after sending its FINThe final ACK arrivesNo
CLOSINGCLOSINGBoth ends closed simultaneouslyThe ACK arrivesRare, legal, harmless
TIME-WAITTIME-WAITThe end that closed first, afterwardsA timer expires — nothing elseNo, and it is not a leak (ch 11)

Table B.8 Two rows account for nearly every state-related incident. CLOSE-WAIT is the diagnostic gift of the whole table: the kernel has done everything it can and is waiting for your code to call close(), so a growing count of them points at a specific bug in a specific process rather than at the network. TIME-WAIT is the opposite — it is the one state that leaves on a schedule rather than in response to a packet, it belongs only to the end that closed first, and it exists so that a delayed packet from the old connection cannot be mistaken for part of a new one on the same four-tuple. Listing B.2 shows a real TIME-WAIT socket with its timer counting down.

Table B.9 -n is not optional. Without it ss resolves port numbers through /etc/services and will state, with total confidence, that port 9101 is bacula-dir — a name from a registry that has nothing to do with what is actually running. The four state groups in the last row are worth knowing because they save typing: synchronized is every state except SYN-SENT, connected is everything except LISTEN and CLOSED, and bucket covers the minimal sockets that TIME-WAIT and SYN-RECV live in. The one recipe deliberately missing is ss -s: its summary line is genuinely useful on a normal machine, but its socket total is read from a counter that is not per-namespace, so inside a container it reports a number belonging to the whole host.

Table B.10 A capture filter is not a search. It is compiled to BPF and run in the kernel, so a filtered capture never copies the unwanted packets to userspace at all — which is why filtering at capture time costs almost nothing and filtering afterwards costs everything. The two flags this book learned the hard way are at the top. -nn matters because with a single -n a port number is still looked up in /etc/services and printed as a name that has nothing to do with the service you are debugging. -Z root matters more than it looks: without it tcpdump tries to drop to an unprivileged user and fails, and it does this even when merely reading a saved file, which is a confusing way to lose an afternoon (ch 20).

B.9 The same rule, in nft and in iptables

What it doesiptablesnft
Drop everything arriving for one TCP portiptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9101 -j DROPadd rule ip filter INPUT tcp dport 9101 counter drop
Refuse it audibly, with a TCP resetiptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9101 -j REJECT --reject-with tcp-resetadd rule ip filter INPUT tcp dport 9101 counter reject with tcp reset
Allow one source network to reach itiptables -A INPUT -s 203.0.113.0/24 -p tcp --dport 9101 -j ACCEPTadd rule ip filter INPUT ip saddr 203.0.113.0/24 tcp dport 9101 counter accept
The stateful rule every ruleset starts withiptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPTadd rule ip filter INPUT ct state related,established counter accept
Allow ping iniptables -A INPUT -p icmp --icmp-type echo-request -j ACCEPTadd rule ip filter INPUT icmp type echo-request counter accept

A UDP portiptables -A INPUT -p udp --dport 9102 -j ACCEPTadd rule ip filter INPUT udp dport 9102 counter accept

Log it, without deciding anythingiptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 9101 -j LOG --log-prefix "blocked: "add rule ip filter INPUT tcp dport 9101 counter log prefix "blocked: "

Forward an inbound port to another hostiptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 9101 -j DNAT --to-destination 203.0.113.20:9102add rule ip nat PREROUTING tcp dport 9101 counter dnat to 203.0.113.20:9102
Clamp the MSS to the path MTUiptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtuadd rule ip mangle FORWARD tcp flags syn / syn,rst counter tcp option maxseg size set rt mtu

Table B.11 The right-hand column was not typed. Every cell in it was produced by running iptables-translate on the cell to its left, in the lab, during the build that made this page — so the two columns cannot drift apart, and the translation is the one the tool itself endorses. Only the surrounding nft '…' shell quoting has been removed. Notice that nft writes an explicit counter where iptables counts unconditionally: in nftables counting is a thing you ask for, which is why a large nftables ruleset can be cheaper than the iptables one it replaced. Notice also how much of iptables’ vocabulary was module names — -m conntrack --ctstate, -m multiport --dports, -m limit — and how all of it becomes ordinary expression syntax on the right (ch 17).

One thing the tool declines to translate: iptables -P INPUT DROP. A default policy is a property of a chain in nftables rather than a rule in it, so there is nothing to convert; the equivalent is to give the chain policy drop when you create it.

B.10 Names, and the web

TypeNo.HoldsWorth knowing
A1One IPv4 addressSeveral A records at one name is the oldest load balancer there is
AAAA28One IPv6 addressPronounced “quad A”. A client with both will usually try v6 first
CNAME5Another nameCannot coexist with any other record at the same name, which is why it cannot go at a zone apex

CAA257Which CAs may issue for this nameChecked by the CA at issuance, not by the browser

Table B.12 The row that causes the most operational grief is CNAME, and the reason is in the second half of its cell: a name holding a CNAME may hold nothing else, and every zone apex must already hold SOA and NS records, so example.com can never be a CNAME while www.example.com can. That single rule is the origin of every provider-specific workaround with a name like ALIAS or ANAME — and of the HTTPS record, which was standardised partly to give the apex a way to point at a service properly.

HTTP/1.1HTTP/2HTTP/3
Current RFC911291139114
Semantics defined byRFC 9110 — shared by all three→→
TransportTCPTCPQUIC, over UDP
FramingText, delimited by CRLFBinary framesBinary frames
Requests in flight at onceOne (pipelining exists, and is unused)Many, multiplexed on one connectionMany, multiplexed on one connection
Head-of-line blockingAt the request level — one slow response blocks the connectionRemoved at the HTTP level; still present in TCPRemoved at both levels

Table B.13 Follow the head-of-line blocking row across, because it is the whole history of these three protocols in one line: HTTP/1.1 blocks at the request level, HTTP/2 fixes that and inherits the same problem one layer down in TCP’s in-order delivery, and HTTP/3 could only fix that by abandoning TCP entirely. The last two rows have a practical consequence worth remembering: HTTP/3 lives on UDP 443, so a firewall or a cloud security group that allows TCP 443 and nothing else does not break anything visible — clients simply fall back to HTTP/2 and nobody is told (ch 18).

B.11 From a symptom to the first command

The symptomAsk this firstBecause it separatesCh
“The name does not resolve”dig +short NAME @1.1.1.1A broken record from a broken resolver — if the public resolver answers and yours does not, the zone is fine15
“It resolves to the wrong address”dig NAME, then check the TTLA stale cache from a stale record. A large remaining TTL means you are waiting, not broken15
“No route to host”ip route get ADDRNo route at all from a route that exists but leads nowhere6
“Connection refused”ss -tlnp on the serverNothing listening from listening on the wrong address. A RST came back, so the network worked9, 11
“Connection timed out”tcpdump -nn -i any host ADDR, at both endsDropped on the way out, dropped on the way in, and dropped on the way back17, 20
“It works locally but not remotely”ss -tlnp and read the addressA service bound to 127.0.0.1 from one bound to 0.0.0.09
“It connects, then hangs on anything large”ping -M do -s 1472 ADDRAn MTU black hole from everything else. Ten seconds, and it is the most misdiagnosed failure there is14
“Intermittent, and direction-dependent”ip neigh, repeatedlyA duplicate address or a flapping MAC from a routing problem3
“Slow, and the latency is high”mtr -n ADDRA slow link from a slow host — and shows you which hop7
“Slow, and the latency is fine”ss -tin on the senderRetransmission and a collapsed window from an application that is simply not sending12
“Fast at first, then slow”ss -tin, watch cwnd and retransCongestion control reacting from a receiver that stopped reading12
“TLS fails, HTTP works”openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername NAMEA certificate problem from a name problem from a protocol-version problem16
“The firewall is empty and packets still vanish”nft list ruleset, not iptables -LRules in tables iptables cannot see — listing B.417
“It works from the server, not from outside”ss -tlnp, then nft list ruleset, then the cloud security groupThree layers of filtering that all look identical from a client17
“Some sites work, some do not”ping -M do -s 1472 to eachA path with a narrow link from a name or a routing problem14
“Nothing at all on the wire”tcpdump -nn -i any with no filterA packet that never left from one that was dropped in transit20, 21

Table B.14 There is one rule behind every row: the first command should divide the problem in half, not confirm what you already believe. That is why ss -tlnp appears three times — it settles, in one line and without touching the network, whether anything is listening and on which address, and half of all “the network is down” reports die there. The other half of the method is knowing which failures are informative: a refused connection proves the whole path worked, right up to a host that answered with a reset, while a timeout proves nothing at all and is consistent with a firewall, a routing error, a dead host and a wrong address alike. Chapter 21 turns this table into a method.
